0.title: About this report · B0001
0.text: Prepared for Little Orange Fish, Huntsville, Alabama, the backbone organization for the North Alabama Mental Health Coalition [397], as the regional companion to its Alabama Mental Health Systems Report. The statewide report describes the system from Montgomery outward. This one starts in two counties, Madison and Cullman, and asks the same questions of the institutions a resident there would actually meet.

1.title: About this report · B0002
1.text: How to read this report. Part I is a short guide to the region and to the three different maps that are all called WellStone's service area. Part II works through the eight domains used in the statewide report, each applied to Madison and Cullman counties. Part III adds the four sections on systems outside the Department of Mental Health: children and families, justice, housing and social determinants, and payers. Part IV describes the thirteen surrounding counties whose crises route to Huntsville, sets out how the parts depend on one another, and lists what could not be read, confirmed or found.

2.title: About this report · B0003
2.text: Status and intended use. This is a draft for review. It has not been approved by Little Orange Fish and has not been peer reviewed. It is independent of WellStone and of every other organization it describes: none of them supplied material, saw the text or endorsed it, and nothing here is a position of the North Alabama Mental Health Coalition or of any member organization. It contains no clinical guidance and no political advocacy. Where it describes a policy choice, it describes it as the public record does.

3.title: About this report · B0004
3.text: A note on method and AI. The research and writing were done with Claude on 4 October 2026, working only from public sources: agency pages and documents, budgets, court records, organizations' own published reports and data, and local press where no primary document could be opened. Each statement of fact was recorded with the passage that supports it before any prose was written, and the bracketed numbers in the text lead to those sources. The sources were read through an automated reader that returns extracts, so quoted passages are the reader's rendering of the document and a few tables need checking by eye; those are listed in Appendix C. WellStone's own website refused the reader for all but a handful of pages, which is why much of what is said about its programs rests on the Department of Mental Health's documents and on press reports. Sentences marked as analysis are the report's own reading of the evidence.

4.title: Why a regional edition · B0005
4.text: The statewide report describes itself as a baseline for "a planned North Alabama regional edition built on the same template" [397]. This is that edition. The reason for writing it is simple enough: a state figure for Alabama is an average over 67 counties, and the two counties described here differ sharply from each other on most of the measures that matter. A reader who knows only where Alabama ranks learns little about Madison County, and less about the rural county to its south.

5.title: Why a regional edition · B0006
5.text: The region also has something the state as a whole lacks, which is a single organization at the center of the public system. WellStone is the community mental health center for both counties, and its own strategic plan names the residents of Madison and Cullman as its catchment [1] [2]. It runs the area's crisis center, its 988 call center and a pediatric crisis unit described at its opening as the first of its kind in the state [3] [4] [122]. A report on the region is therefore partly a report on one provider. It is written as a description of a system of systems all the same, because most of what decides whether a person gets help, keeps housing or stays out of jail is decided somewhere else: in a probate court, a hospital emergency room, a school, a city budget.

6.title: One service area, three maps · B0007
6.text: Ask what WellStone's service area is and the public record gives three answers.

7.title: One service area, three maps · B0008
7.text: The first is two counties. The Department of Mental Health's county-by-county emergency list assigns Madison and Cullman, and only those two, to WellStone as their community mental health center [2]. The Department's directory of Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics lists full-scope clinic sites at WellStone's Huntsville and Cullman campuses [5]. Together the two counties had 527,525 residents in the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimates, a sum this report computed from the county figures [6].

8.title: One service area, three maps · B0009
8.text: The second is fifteen. The Department's Crisis Centers page lists fifteen counties under "Serving" for WellStone Emergency Services and WellStone Pediatric Crisis Care, at one address on Memorial Parkway in Huntsville: Madison and Cullman, plus Cherokee, DeKalb, Etowah, Fayette, Jackson, Lamar, Lawrence, Limestone, Marion, Marshall, Morgan, Walker and Winston [3]. Two other Department pages give the same list, one of them describing the thirteen as "surrounding counties" [7] [8]. For routine care those thirteen belong to four other community mental health centers [2]. Summed from the same Census estimates, they hold 792,981 people, so three of every five residents of the crisis catchment live outside the two counties whose local governments appoint WellStone's board [6] [1]. The catchment's southern edge meets the counties assigned to the Birmingham and Tuscaloosa crisis centers, and to its west lie Colbert, Franklin and Lauderdale, three of the seven Alabama counties the Department's own map shows with no crisis center at all [3] [7].

9.title: One service area, three maps · B0010
9.text: The third answer is "Region 1," which turns out to mean three different things. The Department's mental illness services map draws a Region 1 of twenty counties and seven centers; its county membership is printed only in the map image, and this report relies on the statewide edition's reading of it [9]. The Department's Regional Offices page lists a Region I Community Services office in Decatur covering thirteen counties, which include Madison and Cullman but leave Fayette, Lamar, Marion, Walker and Winston to a Region II office in Tuscaloosa [10]. And the crisis intervention training program run by NAMI Alabama has its own Region 1 of eighteen north Alabama counties, with Huntsville Police as its training hub and WellStone Emergency Services as its crisis center [11].

10.title: One service area, three maps · B0011
10.text: None of this is unusual for a state that built its regional lines one program at a time, but it has a practical consequence. The fifteen counties are not a unit in any of the other regional schemes read for this edition. They fall into three public health districts [12] and are answered by more than one 2-1-1 center: Huntsville's takes calls from Madison and five of the ring counties, while Cullman's calls are answered from Birmingham [13]. Even Madison and Cullman, which share a mental health center, belong to different councils of governments, different homelessness continuums and different 2-1-1 centers [395] [311] [13]. No Department page and no press report read for this edition lists the counties the Huntsville 988 center answers, though WellStone has said that Cullman callers reach it [4] [14] [41]. Throughout this report, "the core" means Madison and Cullman and "the ring" means the other thirteen; Region 1 is used only as a benchmark and always with its size stated.

11.title: Two counties side by side · B0012
11.text: Madison County had an estimated 433,516 residents on 1 July 2025, up 11.7% since the 2020 census base, and Cullman County had 94,009, up 7.0% [15] [16]. Huntsville alone, at 233,627, is two and a half times the size of Cullman County; the city of Madison grew 19.4% in five years to 67,968, and the city of Cullman 13.4% to 20,799 [17] [18] [19]. In 2020 Madison County had 484.2 people per square mile and Cullman 119.6 [15] [16]. County Health Rankings counts 17.1% of Madison's population as living in a rural area and 75.6% of Cullman's [20].

12.title: Two counties side by side · B0013
12.text: The people are different too. By race alone Madison County is 65.8% White and 24.6% Black; Cullman County is 93.0% White and 1.6% Black [15] [16]. Hispanic or Latino residents are 7.6% of Madison and 5.8% of Cullman, more than three times Cullman's Black share [15] [16]. Madison has 34,400 veterans to Cullman's 4,727 [15] [16]. Cullman is older, with 20.0% of residents 65 or over against Madison's 17.0%, and far fewer of its adults hold a bachelor's degree: 19.7% against 46.4% [16] [15].

13.title: Two counties side by side · B0014
13.text: Money follows the same line. Median household income is $86,499 in Madison County and $62,656 in Cullman, poverty 9.6% and 14.1%, and the share of people under 65 with no health insurance 8.3% and 11.9% [15] [16]. One in ten Madison residents under 65 has a disability; in Cullman it is 13.5% [15] [16].

14.title: Two counties side by side · B0015
14.text: It would be easy to stop there, with a prosperous metro county and a struggling rural one. The city figures spoil that picture. Inside Madison County, median household income is $134,655 in the city of Madison and $74,714 in Huntsville; poverty is 4.3% in one and 12.6% in the other, and Huntsville's uninsured rate of 10.6% is closer to Cullman County's 11.9% than to its own suburb's 4.4% [18] [17] [16]. The city of Cullman, for its part, has a poverty rate of 19.9%, the highest of the five places compared [19]. The gap between the two counties is real, and the gap inside Madison County is wider. That is the reason the regional map in this edition goes below the county line.

15.title: How the region got here · B0016
15.text: The local system is younger than it looks. Its institutions date from the 1960s, but most of what a person in crisis would meet today was built after 2020.

17.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0018
17.text: One service area is really three. WellStone is the mental health center for two counties and the crisis center for fifteen, and none of the other regional boundaries read for this edition matches either [2] [3].
17.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

18.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0019
18.text: The front door got faster. The wait for a first evaluation at WellStone fell from 18 days to under one during 2025, the only measured change in access found for the region [50].
18.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

19.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0020
19.text: Crisis care was built in four years. Mobile crisis teams, an adult crisis center that reports over 150 admissions a month and a pediatric crisis unit all date from 2020 or later, alongside a 988 call center [31] [33] [1] [43] [4].
19.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

20.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0021
20.text: The pressure moved downstream. What WellStone's plan and the probate court now ask for is stabilization for committed adults, group homes and supervised housing; a probate court official put the wait for a group home at 100 days or more in May 2025 [1] [51].
20.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

21.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0022
21.text: Cullman carries the heavier burden with fewer services. Its suicide rate is 20.7 per 100,000 against Madison's 15.3; its hospital has no inpatient psychiatric unit, and no drop-in center or NAMI affiliate is listed there [52] [53] [54] [55].
21.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

22.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0023
22.text: The workforce shortage shows as beds that cannot be staffed. A month after it opened, the pediatric unit could staff six of its 24 beds, and nursing is one of WellStone's three named unmet needs [56] [1].
22.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

23.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0024
23.text: The clinic payment model pays for Medicaid patients only. The state requires a certified clinic to serve everyone and pays its daily rate only for Medicaid enrollees. In Madison County 18% of residents were eligible for Medicaid at some point in FY2024 [373] [57] [58].
23.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

24.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0025
24.text: Supportive housing fell as homelessness rose. The Huntsville continuum counted 549 homeless people in 2022 and 718 in 2025, while its permanent supportive housing went from 334 beds to 190 [59] [60] [61].
24.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

25.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0026
25.text: Diversion is the purpose, and no count of it was found. No count has been published of people diverted from jail or the emergency room by the crisis center or the police co-responders [62] [63].
25.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

26.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0027
26.text: The federal grants behind two recent programs have reached the end of their periods. Federal awards for the clinic model and for outpatient commitment ended in September and July 2026 [39] [37].
26.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

27.title: What the evidence shows, in brief · B0028
27.text: Most of what a planner needs is not published. There is no county split of people served, no crisis outcome, no jail caseload, no return for WellStone after FY2021 [64] [62] [65] [66].
27.section: What the evidence shows, in brief

28.title: Using the report · B0029
28.text: For advocacy. Each section ends with gaps drawn from the evidence and names the body that holds the relevant decision or the missing number. A request to a city council, a county commission, a probate judge or a legislator can therefore be specific about what is asked and of whom. The dates on the grants, the budget lines and the plan cycle show when those decisions fall.

29.title: Using the report · B0030
29.text: For planning. The tables of actors show who owns the adjacent piece. The dependency map in Part IV shows where a change in one domain will be felt in another. The Open Items page lists what would have to be measured before anyone could say whether a program is working.

30.title: Using the report · B0031
30.text: For the next edition. This is a baseline. Its figures are dated, its sources are linked, and its gaps are listed so that a later edition can show what changed and what was finally counted. Organizations described here are invited to correct it.

31.title: Scope · B0032
31.text: The statewide report describes who decides in Montgomery: the Department, the Legislature, the Governor and the federal courts. This section asks who decides locally. In Madison and Cullman counties that means one nonprofit board, five local governments, two probate courts and a handful of planning documents, and the question in each case is whom the body answers to and what it has put in writing.

32.title: The center and its board · B0033
32.text: Alabama delivers public mental health care through community mental health centers that the Department of Mental Health calls "the designated points of entry" for mental health and substance use services [21]. The centers are governed by boards formed under Act 310 of 1967, which provides for public corporations to be formed to contract with the Department [21]. WellStone is the 310 board for mental illness and substance use in both counties. It says it was incorporated in 1969 under that act, operated for more than 25 years as the Mental Health Center of Madison County, and took the WellStone name in 2014 [1] [23]. The Cullman Area Mental Health Authority merged into it on 1 October 2017, and Cullman's executive director became the combined organization's chief operating officer [26] [1].

33.title: The center and its board · B0034
33.text: The board has eighteen members. Six are appointed by the City of Huntsville, six by the Madison County Commission, three by the City of Cullman and three by the Cullman County Commission [1]. The Cullman City Council's minutes show the mechanism at work: in March 2026 it reappointed a member for a term ending in 2032 [67]. The City of Madison, which had a $45,000 appropriation to WellStone on its council agenda for FY2024, appoints no one [1] [68]. Neither do the thirteen ring counties whose residents the Department assigns to the crisis center this board governs [3]. That is not an oversight in anyone's bylaws. The crisis center was added in 2021–22 to an organization incorporated in 1969 for one county and merged with a second in 2017, and nothing in the public record read for this edition shows the board's makeup being revisited.

34.title: The center and its board · B0035
34.text: WellStone states that it is certified by the Department, and the Department says it moved to the Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic model in 2024 [1] [46]. Its chief executive is Jeremy Blair [69]. Its planning process, by its own account, takes input from the board, employees, a Human Rights Committee, clients and families, local government and partner agencies [1].

35.title: The center and its board · B0036
35.text: Mental illness is one of three 310 plans on file for the two counties. The Madison County 310 Board, created by Huntsville and the County Commission in 1990, coordinates intellectual disability services, and the Cullman County 310 Authority does the same in Cullman [70] [71]. Both report local government funding without stating amounts [71] [72].

36.title: What local government does · B0037
36.text: Local governments reach mental health mainly through their budgets and their police. Huntsville's council voted in May 2021 to fund clinicians who ride with its police crisis intervention officers, and the city describes a Homeless Services Team of peer specialists, social workers and officers [63] [73]. Its adopted FY2027 General Fund budget of $360,593,840 carries $14,788,543 for outside agencies, with another $17,015,229 for outside agencies from its lodging and liquor fund; the release names no agency, and the appropriations book that does could not be opened [74]. Domain 2 sets out what is known about the amounts.

37.title: What local government does · B0038
37.text: Madison County's role shows most clearly in its jail. When the Commission approved its FY2027 budget in September 2026 it renewed the jail's health care agreement with Southern Health Partners, at an annualized base cost of about $3.74 million for up to 1,235 inmates, and added a mental health nurse paid from opioid settlement funds [75]. In Cullman, the County Commission agreed in 2018 to support the Stepping Up Initiative and authorized the sheriff to sign an agreement with WellStone for services to people repeatedly jailed; WellStone withdrew its screening from the jail in 2019 and Cullman was again a Stepping Up site in 2020–21; no source read says whether the arrangement continues today [76] [291] [290]. The Cullman City Council's minutes for January to July 2026 that mention WellStone or mental health record a board appointment, an event permit and a resident's comment, and no appropriation; a press account of the city's FY2027 budget lists a community service contract with WellStone and gives no amount [67] [100].

38.title: What local government does · B0039
38.text: Cullman County voters have also been asked directly to pay for mental health. A local amendment on the November 2024 ballot would have added a 15% tax on medical cannabis sales, with a third of the revenue going to the county's legislative delegation for mental health. It failed, 19,660 to 18,569 [44].

39.title: Commitment and the courts · B0040
39.text: Involuntary commitment is a probate court matter in Alabama, and the two courts differ sharply in how much they have built around it. Cullman County's probate court lists commitments among its case types and publishes no procedure, forms or counts [77]. In late 2023 the Cullman sheriff told the state's opioid settlement commission that the county no longer had facilities to take people who need mental evaluations [78].

40.title: Commitment and the courts · B0041
40.text: Madison County's court went further. It announced an assisted outpatient treatment program in partnership with WellStone, to start on 3 February 2020 and paid for from the passport application fees the court collects; a later account dates the program to late 2019 [30] [81]. A person enters it only after a commitment petition, an assessment, a physician's confirmation that outpatient care is appropriate, a written treatment plan and a hearing [30]. As designed, participants were to have a case manager and a therapist and to report every 30 days for up to 150 days [79]. The probate judge told a reporter in 2023 that the $35 passport fee funded two case managers, one for the patient and one for the family [80].

41.title: Commitment and the courts · B0042
41.text: The court then helped change state law. Its judge helped draft House Bill 70 of 2022, sponsored by a Huntsville representative, which added a ground for taking a person to a facility (being unable to meet medical and physical needs) and allowed courts to mandate outpatient care; it took effect in July 2022 [81] [36]. The judge has said the law lets the court move inpatients to outpatient status once they are stabilized [80].

42.title: Commitment and the courts · B0043
42.text: How much demand the court faces is known only from press reports. The probate judge said in February 2020 that over 300 people had been committed the previous year [79]. A January 2023 report gave 309 petitions in 2019 and 414 in 2021 [80]. A May 2025 television report said involuntary commitments peaked at 589 in 2023 and named no source for the figure [51]. These count different things (people, petitions, commitments) and should not be read as one series. The same 2025 report describes the process as it now runs: a person held on an intent to commit has a hearing at about the third or fourth day and by then is at Huntsville Hospital or WellStone; inpatient commitment lasts up to 150 days and can be renewed to 300, which the judge called very rare because of bed availability [51].

43.title: Commitment and the courts · B0044
43.text: On results the press reports disagree. One account, written the year the bill was drafted, said about 63 people had been through the outpatient program and about 10% had returned to the court, against nearly 50% of people committed in the traditional way [81]. The 2023 report gives repeat cases as 86 of 414 petitions in 2021 against 142 of 309 in 2019 [80]. No evaluation of the program has been published.

44.title: Commitment and the courts · B0045
44.text: Cullman County has tried a specialty docket of its own. A mental health court for nonviolent offenders began in Cullman County in late May 2022 under the presiding circuit judge, with WellStone as a partner; participants plead guilty first and can have charges dismissed by meeting milestones the court sets [82]. Section 10 takes up the courts in detail.

45.title: What is written down · B0046
45.text: Three planning documents describe the region's needs, and they do not agree on what matters most.

46.title: What is written down · B0047
46.text: WellStone's FY2026–27 strategic plan, signed by its board president on 18 November 2025, names three unmet needs: adequate housing for clients, funding for medications for adults with no third-party reimbursement, and recruiting and retaining nurses [1]. Its priorities for expansion are crisis stabilization for adults under civil commitment, supervised housing, integration of behavioral and primary care, and satellite access points [1]. Its four goals, by contrast, are internal: financial stability, customer experience, business processes and the number of clinicians certified in evidence-based treatments. None sets a target for the population served or for an outcome [1].

47.title: What is written down · B0048
47.text: Cullman Regional Medical Center's 2025 community health needs assessment ranks mental health first and substance use second among thirteen areas of opportunity [83]. Of the 47 community representatives it surveyed, 62.2% rated mental health a major problem, and one wrote that there were "few resources for mental health treatment other than incarceration" [83]. The hospital's implementation plan, adopted on 11 March 2025, takes on mental health as one of seven needs and leaves substance use out [84]. Its strategies are to support partners, implement a suicide prevention program, continue its outpatient psychiatry clinic and keep a dedicated behavioral health area in its emergency room [84].

48.title: What is written down · B0049
48.text: In Madison County the nearest equivalent is the needs assessment United Way ran in mid-2024 with a team from Alabama A&M University [85]. Its executive summary lists transportation, pollution and recycling, and services for abused and neglected children as the three areas residents most often said needed improvement. Mental health is not among them, though the report recommends investment in crisis intervention, counseling and community-based support [86]. No community health needs assessment from Huntsville Hospital was found.

49.title: Key actors · B0050
49.text: Actor Role in local governance WellStone, Inc. board of directors Governs the community mental health center, crisis center and CCBHC for both counties; 18 members appointed by four local governments [1] Alabama Department of Mental Health Certifies and contracts with the center; designates it a point of entry [1] [21] City of Huntsville Appoints six board members; funds the police co-responder program [1] [63] Madison County Commission Appoints six board members; contracts for jail health care [1] [75] City of Madison Had a $45,000 appropriation to WellStone on its FY2024 agenda; appoints no board members [68] [1] City of Cullman and Cullman County Commission Appoint three board members each [1] [67] Madison County Probate Court Hears commitments; runs assisted outpatient treatment with WellStone [30] Cullman County Probate Court Hears commitments [77] Madison County 310 Board; Cullman County 310 Authority Plan intellectual and developmental disability services [70] Cullman Regional Medical Center; United Way of Madison County Publish the two local needs assessments [84] [85]

50.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0051
50.text: Representation has not followed the catchment. The board that governs a fifteen-county crisis center is appointed by four governments in two counties [1] [3]. No public document describes how the other thirteen counties, or their four mental health centers, take part in decisions about the center their residents are sent to.

51.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0052
51.text: The plan's goals are the organization's, and the needs are the community's. WellStone's plan names housing, medication funding, nursing and commitment stabilization as needs and priorities, and then sets goals for financial stability, customer experience, business processes and clinician certification [1]. Nothing in the plan says who is responsible for the needs it names.

52.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0053
52.text: One court has built a program; neither publishes its numbers. Madison County's outpatient commitment program is known mainly through press reports and a federal award record, and Cullman's court publishes no procedure, forms or counts for commitments [80] [37] [77].

53.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0054
53.text: Cullman's own assessment ranks substance use second, and its hospital's plan leaves it out [83] [84].

54.title: Scope · B0055
54.text: The statewide report follows the money from the Legislature to the Department. This section follows it the rest of the way: what reaches the two counties, from whom, and how much of that a resident could find out. The answer to the last question shapes the whole section. Capital spending is well documented because ribbon-cuttings are news. Operating money is visible only in fragments, and no Form 990 data for the organization at the center of the system appear in the public database for any year after FY2021 [66].

55.title: What the buildings cost · B0056
55.text: The crisis system in Huntsville began with a state decision. On 28 October 2020 the Department named WellStone one of the first three crisis center awardees, funded from an $18 million appropriation in the FY2021 General Fund budget [32]. The permanent building on South Memorial Parkway opened in September 2022 at a reported cost of $10 million: $3 million from the state, $2 million from the Madison County Commission, the City of Huntsville and the City of Madison together, and about $5 million left to a capital campaign called Be the Rock [87]. When the doors opened, the campaign had raised close to $550,000 [88]. Its web page publishes no goal, no total and no donor list, and in December 2024 WellStone's development director described it as winding down [89] [90].

56.title: What the buildings cost · B0057
56.text: The pediatric unit followed. It cost $9 million, which WellStone credits to the Legislature, the Department and campaign donors without giving any of the three shares [91]. Madison County's federal pandemic recovery plan lists a $1,000,000 grant to WellStone under mental health services [92]. In Cullman, WellStone opened a renovated and enlarged building in April 2024; neither local paper reported what it cost or who paid [41]. A 16-bed residential detoxification program, River Crossing, opened on 24 June 2025 in a renovated facility, and the Department says its beds are funded by a grant from the state opioid settlement fund without printing the amount [45].

57.title: What the buildings cost · B0058
57.text: The state's evaluation office gives the clearest picture of how the crisis center's own spending changed. Capital made up 74.5% of WellStone's crisis center expenditure in FY2021 and 78.6% in FY2022; by FY2024 operations and administration were 87.3% [62]. The same office says the state funds each of its six crisis centers at $7,000,000 a year [62]. The enacted FY2027 budget carries $36,000,000 for the "Existing Six Crisis Diversion Centers," which would be $6,000,000 apiece if divided evenly; neither document reconciles the two figures [93].

58.title: WellStone's books · B0059
58.text: The most recent year for which WellStone's Form 990 data are public is the one that ended in September 2021. It reported revenue of $25,940,539, expenses of $20,991,369 and net assets of $17,628,969 [66]. Revenue had been $14,013,123 in the last year before the Cullman merger and $19,585,170 in the first year after it [94]. For fiscal years 2022 through 2025 the public database shows single-audit records and no Form 990 data, and flags the FY2025 audit with a significant deficiency in internal controls; the audits themselves could not be opened [66].

59.title: WellStone's books · B0060
59.text: WellStone's own annual report for FY2021 is the only place found where it has broken revenue down by source: $9,882,565 from state government, $8,654,700 from patient fees, $2,639,254 from local government and $1,026,303 from the federal government, plus other revenue the extracted text does not show in full [95]. That year included local capital contributions to the crisis center, so it may not represent a normal one. The current strategic plan lists the same kinds of sources with no amounts at all [1].

60.title: WellStone's books · B0061
60.text: Federal grants are the exception, because the federal government publishes them. The Department of Health and Human Services' grants database shows three awards to WellStone between fiscal years 2021 and 2025, totaling $9,575,938 [96]. A two-year community mental health center grant awarded in 2021 at $4,288,700 was later reduced to $2,502,021 [97]. A four-year grant to implement the CCBHC model, with a project period ending 29 September 2026, brought $3,974,261 in four installments [39]. The third award, $3,099,656 over four years to July 2026, paid for the assisted outpatient treatment program with the Madison County Probate Court and Huntsville Hospital as named partners [37]. On their stated project periods all three had ended by the date of this report, and nothing in the public record says what replaces them.

61.title: WellStone's books · B0062
61.text: WellStone reports providing nearly $3.4 million in uncompensated care in fiscal year 2025; its FY2021 report gave $3.5 million [48] [95].

62.title: Local public money · B0063
62.text: Local appropriations can be pieced together for some governments and some years. The City of Huntsville's FY2026 budget allotted WellStone $900,000, from which the council moved $36,000 to another agency by amendment [98]. The city's FY2025 and FY2027 releases name no amount for WellStone, and the appropriations books that would show it sit behind a path the reader cannot open [99] [74]. The City of Madison's FY2024 appropriation, as proposed on its council agenda of 23 October 2023, was $45,000, with $15,000 to Crisis Services of North Alabama on the same agenda [68]. No annual operating appropriation from the Madison County Commission to WellStone was found, and the Commission's budget could not be read; its recorded contributions are a share of the crisis center's capital cost and a $1,000,000 pandemic recovery grant [87] [92].

63.title: Local public money · B0064
63.text: In Cullman the trail is fainter. The city's FY2027 budget authorizes community service contracts with twenty organizations, among them "Cullman Area Mental Health (Wellstone)," a name nine years out of date, and the amounts were not reported [100]. The county's FY2027 budget of $94,621,043 was adopted with no appropriation to WellStone or mental health mentioned in the press account, and its commission agenda of 22 September 2026 listed a Southern Health Partners agreement of $849,156.24, without stating its scope; that company is the jail health contractor in Madison County [101] [102].

64.title: Local public money · B0065
64.text: Opioid settlement money is the newest local stream, and the two counties have spent it differently. Huntsville's first allocations, approved unanimously in 2023, gave $850,000 to the Huntsville Hospital Foundation, $810,000 to First Stop and $750,000 to WellStone, chosen, its finance director said, because they were existing partners with programs aimed at the crisis [40] [103] [104]. Madison County is using settlement funds for an additional mental health nurse in its jail [75]. Cullman County gave a one-time $250,000 to the Good Samaritan Health Clinic and $150,000 over three years to the district attorney's drug court; the City of Cullman pledged to match the clinic gift and in June 2026 appropriated $125,000 to a women's recovery nonprofit [105] [106] [107]. At state level the Department gave WellStone $660,000 of a $3,000,000 settlement appropriation to expand staffing and hours at the north Alabama 988 call center [45]. In the third round of state settlement grants, two Cullman organizations received awards, as did Huntsville organizations including the Partnership for a Drug Free Community and Not One More Alabama; WellStone was not among the grantees [108].

65.title: Rough benchmarks · B0066
65.text: Any per-person figure for the region has to be computed, because nobody publishes one, and the results below are this report's arithmetic. Huntsville's FY2026 allotment to WellStone after amendment, $864,000, is about a quarter of one percent of the city's operating budget [98]. WellStone's FY2021 revenue comes to roughly $49 for each of the 527,525 residents of its two counties, a figure that sets a 2021 numerator over a 2025 population and should be read as an order of magnitude [66].

66.title: Key actors · B0067
66.text: Funder What it pays for locally Alabama Legislature and Department of Mental Health Crisis center operations; opioid settlement grants [93] [62] [45] U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (SAMHSA) CCBHC, community mental health center and assisted outpatient treatment grants to WellStone [96] City of Huntsville Annual appropriation to WellStone; co-responder partnership; opioid settlement allocations [98] [34] [40] City of Madison A $45,000 appropriation by agreement on its FY2024 council agenda [68] Madison County Commission Crisis center capital; pandemic recovery grant; jail health care [87] [92] [75] City of Cullman; Cullman County Commission Community service contract with WellStone; opioid settlement grants to a free clinic and drug court [100] [105] [106] Be the Rock capital campaign Private gifts toward the crisis center and pediatric unit [88] [91]

67.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0068
67.text: Four years without a public return. The region's principal provider has no Form 990 data on the public record after FY2021, a period in which it opened a crisis center, a pediatric unit and a detox program and was certified as a Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic [66] [42].

68.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0069
68.text: Grant-built programs reach the end of their grants. The assisted outpatient treatment award ran to 30 July 2026 and the CCBHC implementation grant to 29 September 2026 [37] [39]. Whether Medicaid's new clinic payment, local budgets or nothing at all picks up those costs is not stated anywhere this review could read.

69.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0070
69.text: Capital was raised in public; operating support is settled in budget lines that are hard to find. Of five local governments, one published an amount for FY2026 that a reader could open [98].

70.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0071
70.text: Settlement money has gone to different places in each county. Huntsville funded homelessness services, a hospital foundation and WellStone; Cullman funded a free clinic, a drug court and a recovery nonprofit [40] [105] [106] [107]. No published account of how the funds were used was found, though Huntsville requires utilization reports from its recipients [104].

71.title: Scope · B0072
71.text: This section follows the continuum the statewide report uses, from prevention through outpatient care, crisis response, inpatient treatment and recovery supports, and asks at each step what exists in Madison and Cullman counties and how much use it gets. The short version is that the front of the system changed a great deal between 2020 and 2025 and the back of it did not.

72.title: Who was served · B0073
72.text: The Department's annual reports count the people WellStone serves for mental illness: 9,301 in FY2021, 9,460 in FY2022, 9,795 in FY2023 and 9,700 in FY2024 [109] [110] [111] [43]. The FY2025 report gives 11,659, with a footnote saying adult mobile crisis services are now included [64]. That year was also WellStone's first full one as a Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic, a status the state certified in July 2024, and the report's clinic table gives 13,700 for WellStone out of 30,275 for the state's two clinics [42] [64]. One reading of that page attached a different number, 6,627, to WellStone's clinic row; the page prints each heading beneath its table, and 6,627 belongs to the 988 call center table above it. The table is listed in Appendix C for checking by eye.

73.title: Who was served · B0074
73.text: WellStone's own figures for the same year are "over 12,000" in its strategic plan and "more than 13,500" in a May 2026 press account, and in 2024 it was describing 14,000 clients a year [1] [48] [112]. None of the sources divides its count between the two counties. On the Department's FY2025 figures, this report calculates that the center reached between 2.2% and 2.6% of the two counties' residents, depending on which count is used [64].

74.title: Who was served · B0075
74.text: Substance use is the one series that fell. The Department counted 1,248 people served by WellStone for substance use in FY2021 and 1,087 in FY2024, a decline in each year between [109] [43].

75.title: The community base · B0076
75.text: WellStone delivers the publicly funded outpatient system in both counties. Its plan lists counseling, case management and intensive in-home teams for adults, the Nova Center for Youth & Family for children, crisis services and community education [1]. The Department's directory shows two sites offering the full range of clinic services, at 4040 Memorial Parkway SW in Huntsville and 1909 Commerce Avenue in Cullman [5]. In spring 2026 WellStone opened its first clinic in the city of Madison, offering individual, group and intensive outpatient therapy to adults and referring out for psychiatry, primary care and detox [48] [113]. In November 2025 it had put a van on the road, which it called the state's first mobile mental health clinic, starting at First Stop and the Downtown Rescue Mission [47]. It also runs NOVA-Huntsville, one of Alabama's three programs for a first episode of psychosis [114].

76.title: The community base · B0077
76.text: The clearest measured change of the period is in how fast a new patient is seen. The Department told legislators in January 2026 that WellStone's wait for an initial evaluation fell from 18 days in January 2025 to less than one day in December, and the wait for a first therapy session from 33 days to eight [50]. These are two points in time for one clinic, reported without a method note, but no other measurement of access over time was found for the region.

77.title: Crisis response · B0078
77.text: The statewide report describes crisis care as someone to contact, someone to respond and a safe place to go. All three now exist in Huntsville, and the crisis center and the response teams were built after 2020.

78.title: Crisis response · B0079
78.text: Someone to contact. One of Alabama's four in-state 988 call centers is at WellStone [4]. The Department's FY2025 table gives it 6,627 of the 35,118 recorded for the four centers, without saying whether the unit is calls or people; the report's text counts 40,053 calls statewide, a difference it does not explain [64]. The Department's board was told in November 2025 that the state answer rate had been above 90% since July; no rate is published for Huntsville alone [115]. Crisis Services of North Alabama runs a separate 24-hour HELPline and manages 2-1-1 for Madison and five other north Alabama counties, Cullman not among them [116].

79.title: Crisis response · B0080
79.text: Someone to respond. Mobile crisis started in Cullman, which got a state-funded adult team as a rural pilot announced in June 2020; a team member said in September 2022 that it had intervened in more than 150 crises that summer [31] [117]. Huntsville's adult team came later, with the 2022 federal grant [118] [119]. WellStone's child and adolescent teams cover both counties and served 498 young people in FY2025, more than half of the 936 served by all such teams in Alabama [120] [64]. Alongside these, the Huntsville City Council voted on 13 May 2021 to put two master's-level WellStone clinicians in patrol cars with crisis-trained officers, at a time when police said they answered 150 to 200 mental health calls a month [34]. Two clinicians were riding by February 2022 [63]. No count of what the co-responders have done since has been published.

80.title: Crisis response · B0081
80.text: A safe place to go. A temporary diversion center opened on WellStone's campus in May 2021; in February 2022 its chief executive described it as having ten inpatient and ten observation beds [33]. The permanent building, WellStone Emergency Services, had its ribbon cut on 19 September 2022: 25,000 square feet, built for up to 15 temporary observation beds and up to 24 extended observation beds, starting with 16 [38] [88]. At the temporary site the center had averaged 45 to 50 people a month [88]. By September 2024 the adult unit was admitting 175 a month, and WellStone's plan of November 2025 says "over 150" [121] [1]. The Department counts 1,879 people served there in FY2025, which is consistent with those monthly figures [64]. That count covers all fifteen counties of the catchment.

81.title: Crisis response · B0082
81.text: The pediatric unit, described at its opening as the first of its kind in the state, opened next door in late September 2024 with 24 beds for ages 12 to 18 [122] [43]. A month later a staffing shortage meant it could treat six children at a time [56]. It averaged about 25 patients a month through the end of 2024 [43]. For its first full year there are two numbers: the Department's count for FY2025 is 520, and a press report of February 2026 gave 400 individuals served since opening and said the unit had begun taking children as young as eight [64] [69]. At the opening, the Department's commissioner said the state probably needs two or three more such units [122].

82.title: Crisis response · B0083
82.text: What none of these sources reports is what a planner would most want to know. The state evaluation office's 2025 report on the crisis centers gives no admissions, lengths of stay, law enforcement drop-offs or diversion figures for Huntsville [62].

83.title: Inpatient care · B0084
83.text: The region lost its state hospital a decade ago. Officials announced on 13 January 2015 that North Alabama Regional Hospital in Decatur, with 74 beds, would close by 30 June of that year; patients were to be served instead by hospital acute units, crisis stabilization units, intermediate care run by community centers, or Bryce Hospital in Tuscaloosa [24]. The Department's own report records that with the closure all remaining state hospitals were in Tuscaloosa [123].

84.title: Inpatient care · B0085
84.text: What remains is hospital-based and thinly documented. Huntsville Hospital describes inpatient units for adults and seniors, reached through medical clearance and an assessment in its emergency department, and publishes no bed count [124]. Its parent system's audited statements identify psychiatric beds in only one place: Decatur Morgan West, in the next county, licensed for 64 [125]. Unity Psychiatric Care in Huntsville has 20 beds for people 55 and older [126]. The hospital association's listing for Crestwood shows no psychiatric service, and its listing for Cullman Regional shows outpatient psychiatry only [127] [53]. Cullman County, in other words, has no inpatient psychiatric unit; its hospital has a dedicated behavioral health area in the emergency room, opened in 2022 [128]. A television report in May 2025 said sixty mental health beds are in Madison County and serve patients from across north Alabama, without saying which beds it counted [51]. The state's health planning rule places Madison, Morgan and Cullman in a ten-county North Region for psychiatric bed need and prints no inventory by facility [129].

85.title: Inpatient care · B0086
85.text: This is where the pressure now sits. WellStone's plan names crisis stabilization for adults under civil commitment as its first priority for expansion [1]. The probate court's director of mental health programs said in May 2025 that the wait for a group home is at least 100 days and that she wanted more beds for stabilization and a step toward group homes [51]. When the state spent opioid settlement money on civil commitment and crisis residential beds, none went to Madison or Cullman [45].

86.title: Substance use treatment · B0087
86.text: The Department's directory lists fourteen substance use entries in Madison County and six in Cullman, including an entry at each county's jail [130] [131]. WellStone's part includes entries in that directory and, since 24 June 2025, River Crossing, a 16-bed residential withdrawal management unit in Huntsville funded from the state opioid settlement [64] [45]. Private providers carry much of the rest: Bradford's Madison campus, for one, offers medical detox, residential treatment and medication-assisted treatment [132]. Several well-known local recovery programs, among them The Pathfinder, His Way and the Downtown Rescue Mission, do not appear in the Department's directory, which shows only that they are not in the directory, not that they do not operate [130].

87.title: Prevention, recovery and continuity · B0088
87.text: Prevention is present and uncounted. WellStone held the Department's substance use prevention award for both counties in FY2024 [133]. Its Heads Up program has taught Mental Health First Aid at the University of Alabama in Huntsville since 2023, with about 100 faculty and staff trained by September 2026, which is the only local count of that training found [134]. NAMI's Madison County affiliate and Crisis Services of North Alabama both list prevention education and publish no numbers [135] [136].

88.title: Prevention, recovery and continuity · B0089
88.text: Recovery supports cluster in Huntsville. The Department lists five drop-in centers for people with mental illness in the state and one in north Alabama, Our Place on Max Luther Drive; it lists Huntsville as a location of the peer-run Recovery Organization of Support Specialists; neither has a Cullman site [54] [137]. Not One More Alabama offers family and recovery support from Huntsville [138]. WellStone's 2022 federal grant promised a peer "living room" offering walk-in support to 400 people, and no source says whether it opened [39].

89.title: Prevention, recovery and continuity · B0090
89.text: Continuity, the hand-off from one level of care to the next, is described and unmeasured. People leaving the crisis center were to be assigned a care manager, according to a report at its opening [139]. The federal clinic model requires 15 to 17 outcome measures, follow-up after hospitalization among them; the first demonstration year ended in mid-2025 and no result for WellStone has been published [42].

90.title: Veterans and the military · B0091
90.text: Madison County's 34,400 veterans and the workforce of Redstone Arsenal have a parallel system that leans on the civilian one at its edges [15]. Fox Army Health Center's behavioral health department takes self-referrals on weekdays; when it cannot provide the care needed, and it gives a child psychiatrist as the example, patients are sent off post through TRICARE [140]. For after-hours emergencies its page tells patients to go to the nearest emergency room or to WellStone Emergency Services [141]. The VA lists three sites in Huntsville and none in Cullman; its Huntsville clinic offers outpatient mental health care and its Vet Center free counseling without VA enrollment [142] [143] [144]. WellStone's 2022 grant committed it to intensive community care for service members and veterans, with a target of 50 served by September 2023, and no result has been reported [39].

91.title: Key actors · B0092
91.text: Actor Role in the continuum WellStone Outpatient care, 988 call center, mobile crisis, adult crisis center, pediatric crisis unit, detox, first-episode psychosis [1] [4] [7] [43] [120] [45] [114] Crisis Services of North Alabama 24-hour HELPline; 2-1-1 for Madison and five other counties [116] Huntsville Hospital Adult and senior inpatient units; emergency assessment [124] Decatur Morgan West (Morgan County) 64 licensed psychiatric beds [125] Unity Psychiatric Care 20 inpatient beds for people 55 and older [126] Cullman Regional Medical Center Emergency behavioral health area; outpatient psychiatry [128] [53] Bradford and other private providers Detox, residential and medication-assisted treatment [132] Our Place; Recovery Organization of Support Specialists Drop-in center and peer recovery support, Huntsville [54] [137] Fox Army Health Center; VA clinic and Vet Center Care for military and veteran populations [140] [143] [144] Huntsville Police Department Co-responders with WellStone clinicians [34]

92.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0093
92.text: The pressure has moved downstream. Access to a first appointment improved and crisis admissions more than tripled, while the things WellStone's plan and the probate court both ask for are what follows a crisis: stabilization beds for committed adults, group homes and supervised housing [50] [121] [1] [51].

93.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0094
93.text: Cullman has the first half of a continuum. It has a clinic, mobile crisis teams and an emergency room area; its hospital has no inpatient psychiatric unit, and the Department lists no drop-in center or peer recovery organization location there [145] [53] [54] [137].

94.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0095
94.text: Volume is reported; results are not. Counts exist for the crisis center, the pediatric unit and the call center. Length of stay, where people came from, where they went next and whether they came back do not [62].

95.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0096
95.text: Grant commitments have no published follow-up. The peer living room, the veterans program and the mobile crisis response targets written into the 2022 grant are on the federal record as promises, and their outcomes are not [39].

96.title: Scope · B0097
96.text: The statewide report measures Alabama's shortage with federal designations and national ratios. Those tools work poorly at county scale, as this section shows, so it leans on a plainer kind of evidence: what local providers have said they cannot staff. It then looks at where the region's future clinicians are being trained.

97.title: The shortage, measured three ways · B0098
97.text: Start with the federal designation. Cullman County is a mental health professional shortage area for its low-income population, with a score of 16 [52]. Madison County has no area designation at all, and is the only county in Alabama without one [52]. That does not mean Madison has enough clinicians. The designation counts only psychiatrists, and the threshold is a population of at least 30,000 for each one, or 20,000 where needs are unusually high [146] [147]. A low-income designation like Cullman's says something narrower: that too few providers take Medicaid and sliding-fee patients for the size of the low-income population [146]. A county with a medical school campus and a large private market can clear the bar while its uninsured residents wait.

98.title: The shortage, measured three ways · B0099
98.text: The second measure is the provider ratio, and here two published numbers exist for each county, and a third for Cullman. County Health Rankings' March 2026 figures give 474 residents per mental health provider in Madison and 568 in Cullman, against 639 for Alabama [52]. The Kids Count county profiles print 500 and 609 for 2024 [148] [149]. Cullman Regional's needs assessment reports 132.0 providers per 100,000 residents in Cullman County, against 140.9 for the state and 312.5 for the country [83]. The Rankings and the Cullman assessment draw on the federal provider registry with different definitions of a provider, and the Kids Count profiles print no source or definition. The broadest of them comes with a warning from its own publisher: the registry may include providers who are no longer practicing or accepting new patients, which would overstate supply [150]. On the Rankings measure both counties look better than Alabama; on the hospital's measure Cullman is below the state and far below the nation.

99.title: The shortage, measured three ways · B0100
99.text: The third measure is what people say. A participant in the Cullman assessment wrote that there are "never enough psychiatrists, psychiatric nurses" [83].

100.title: What cannot be staffed · B0101
100.text: The most concrete evidence of shortage in the region is a building. WellStone's pediatric crisis unit opened in September 2024 with 24 beds. On 23 October it could treat six children at a time, and its medical director described the problem as "just finding the right staff that have that passion for working with youth who are in a crisis" [56]. No later report says when, or whether, the unit reached full staffing.

101.title: What cannot be staffed · B0102
101.text: WellStone's strategic plan a year later names "recruiting and retaining a qualified nursing workforce" as one of its three greatest unmet needs, gives no vacancy or turnover figure, and includes an objective to reduce overtime cost [1]. Its chief executive said in 2022 that the field lacks the workforce "locally, statewide, or nationally to absorb the demand," and put the cause on reimbursement rates that leave community providers unable to pay competitive wages [87]. The hospital system across town said much the same of its own nurses in 2023 [151].

102.title: What cannot be staffed · B0103
102.text: The organization has grown regardless. Its chief executive recalled 200 employees in 2011; press reports give 450 in September 2022 and more than 600 by February 2026 [87] [69]. A workforce target in the plan concerns quality, not numbers: 75% of therapists certified in an evidence-based practice by 30 September 2026, with no baseline stated and no result yet published [1].

103.title: The pipeline · B0104
103.text: Huntsville now trains psychiatrists. The University of Alabama at Birmingham runs a four-year psychiatry residency at its Huntsville campus, approved for up to six residents a year, with Huntsville Hospital as its clinical site [152] [153]. Its page listed two classes in October 2026, six first-year and six second-year residents, which suggests the program is new [154]. The curriculum includes eight weeks of community psychiatry and four each of forensic and addiction psychiatry [155]. The American Medical Association's residency database also lists a second four-year psychiatry program in Huntsville under WellStone's own name, with six first-year positions. The entry shows 24 current residents, a figure that equals four full classes of six and may describe approved positions; whether it has residents in training could not be established [156].

104.title: The pipeline · B0105
104.text: The other professions have local programs too. The University of Alabama in Huntsville offers a psychiatric mental health nurse practitioner track requiring 720 clinical hours [157]. Alabama A&M University offers bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees in social work and a master's in counseling [158] [159]. In Cullman County, Wallace State in Hanceville trains practical and associate-degree nurses and says its numbers are limited by faculty and clinical placements [160]. None of these pages publishes how many graduates it produces or where they go to work.

105.title: The pipeline · B0106
105.text: Two parts of the workforce are trained outside the academic system. Peer specialists are certified by the Department, whose trainings as listed in autumn 2026 are virtual or held in Columbiana, with none listed in either county [161]. Police crisis intervention training is organized regionally, with Huntsville Police as the hub for an eighteen-county region [11]. The city said in 2020 that officers must take 16 hours of it, with WellStone teaching several modules [162].

106.title: The pipeline · B0107
106.text: Federal loan repayment is tied to the shortage score of the site where a clinician works, which favors sites in Cullman County; in Madison County only a site with its own facility designation would qualify, and whether WellStone's sites hold one was not established [163] [52].

107.title: Well-being and retention · B0108
107.text: Almost nothing is published locally on the well-being of the people who do this work. The fire department's page and the ambulance service's home page describe staffing and equipment and say nothing about peer support or behavioral health for their own crews; the police department's directives sit in a portal the reader could not search [164] [165] [166]. Absence from a web page is not absence of a program. It does mean that a resident, or a job applicant, cannot find out.

108.title: Key actors · B0109
108.text: Actor Role in the workforce WellStone Community mental health center with more than 600 employees; names nursing as an unmet need [69] [1] UAB Huntsville Regional Medical Campus; Huntsville Hospital Psychiatry residency and its clinical site [152] [153] University of Alabama in Huntsville Psychiatric nurse practitioner track [157] Alabama A&M University Social work and counseling degrees [158] [159] Wallace State Community College (Hanceville) Practical and associate-degree nursing [160] Alabama Department of Mental Health Peer specialist certification [161] Huntsville Police Department; NAMI Alabama Regional crisis intervention training hub [11] Alabama Department of Public Health Explains shortage designations and federal loan repayment [146] [163]

109.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0110
109.text: The official measure gives Madison County no area shortage designation, and a 24-bed unit there could staff six beds a month after opening [52] [56]. The designation was not built to see the kind of shortage the region has.

110.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0111
110.text: Nursing is the named bottleneck, and no number describes it. No vacancy or turnover figure for behavioral health nursing was found for WellStone or the hospital system [1] [151].

111.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0112
111.text: The pipeline is new and its output is unknown. A psychiatry residency listed two classes in training in October 2026; whether its graduates stay is the question that matters, and none of the program pages read publishes retention [154].

112.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0113
112.text: No peer training is listed locally, in a region where WellStone's Cullman mobile crisis team was designed in 2020 to pair a clinician with a peer or a case manager [161] [31].

113.title: Scope · B0114
113.text: This section covers the physical and technical base of the local system: the buildings, the record systems, the medicines, and the means of getting a person from where they are to where the care is. The last of these turns out to be the weakest.

114.title: Facilities · B0115
114.text: The region's crisis buildings stand together on South Memorial Parkway in Huntsville. The Department lists WellStone Emergency Services and WellStone Pediatric Crisis Care at one address, 4020 Memorial Parkway SW, and WellStone's Huntsville outpatient clinic is next door at 4040 [3] [5]. The adult center is a 25,000-square-foot building; the pediatric unit beside it is 12,000 square feet with 24 beds, and can hold a child for up to 14 days [88] [91] [167]. WellStone's website names eight service locations in all, including a Madison campus, the Nova Center for children, the River Crossing detox unit and a recovery center, though the pages that would give their addresses did not open [168].

115.title: Facilities · B0116
115.text: WellStone's Cullman campus is at 1909 Commerce Avenue NW. It was renovated and enlarged by about 3,000 square feet in April 2024, and it houses the county's mobile crisis teams, outreach and primary care [41] [145]. There is no crisis facility in the county. WellStone's chief operating officer said as much at a town hall in October 2024: Cullman has crisis response teams and no local crisis center, so a resident who needs one goes to Huntsville [169].

116.title: Facilities · B0117
116.text: Hospital capacity is large in total and small for psychiatry. Huntsville Hospital has 881 authorized beds and state approval, granted in November 2024, for a $150 million tower that will take it to 931 [170] [171]. Cullman Regional became a 175-bed hospital in January 2024 after a $30 million expansion, and employs a psychiatrist in an outpatient clinic with counselors there and in the emergency room [172] [84]. The health system that owns Huntsville Hospital describes Decatur Morgan West, in Morgan County, as north Alabama's only behavioral health hospital, with 64 licensed beds used mainly for children and adolescents [151]. Domain 3 sets out what is known about psychiatric beds; the short answer is that no public source read gives a full count by facility.

117.title: Information systems · B0118
117.text: Little is published about how local providers keep and share records. The state requires every Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic to connect its electronic health record to Alabama's health information exchange, which reported more than 5.5 million hospital discharge messages from 46 hospitals in 2025 and has a Huntsville Hospital representative in its governance [173] [174]. No document confirms that WellStone's connection is live. The homeless services system runs on its own database, and the coalition that manages it was rebuilding its website in October 2026 and published no data [175]. The Department's 988 page says nothing about a registry of open crisis beds [4].

118.title: Information systems · B0119
118.text: One public directory a resident might consult is unreliable. A state family services directory lists WellStone's service area as "Cullman and Decatur Counties," and another entry in the same directory still describes the crisis center as due to open in the summer of 2022 [176] [177].

119.title: Telehealth and broadband · B0120
119.text: Census figures show 92.3% of Madison County households and 87.3% of Cullman's with a broadband subscription [52]. The state's clinic manual expects telehealth to be used as far as possible to support access [57]. What is actually delivered that way locally is not documented. The one account found dates from the school closures of spring 2020, when WellStone moved school-based therapy to phone and video [178]. Cullman Regional's mental health plan does not mention telehealth [84].

120.title: Medicines · B0121
120.text: Another of the three greatest unmet needs named in WellStone's strategic plan is "funding for medications for our adult clients with no third-party reimbursement" [1]. The plan does not say how many clients that covers or how large the shortfall is. Around it sits a patchwork. The Community Free Clinic in Huntsville fills prescriptions for uninsured Madison County residents from its own dispensary; in Cullman, United Way's 2022–23 funding list describes the Good Samaritan Health Clinic as providing health care and prescriptions for uninsured, low-income residents; and Huntsville Hospital's community grants list medication assistance among the needs they address [179] [180] [181]. WellStone's mobile unit, announced in November 2025, was described as dispensing psychiatric medication as well as offering therapy [47].

121.title: Medicines · B0122
121.text: For opioid use disorder the picture is clearer. Both counties are among the sixteen in Alabama with a certified opioid treatment program [182]. Huntsville has two clinics dispensing methadone and buprenorphine, both accepting Medicaid and Medicare, and Cullman has one, on the same street as WellStone's campus [183] [184] [185]. WellStone is the certified provider of outpatient substance use treatment inside both county jails [186] [187].

122.title: Medicines · B0123
122.text: A naloxone figure was found for one county only. The state's opioid council reports 2,344 doses distributed in Madison County between November 2024 and October 2025, placing it among the highest counties, and the text of its report does not mention Cullman, which may appear only on the report's map [188]. Huntsville's ambulance service was reported to have given the drug about 380 times in the first half of 2024 [189].

123.title: Transportation · B0124
123.text: Getting to care is easier in Huntsville than anywhere else in the region, and even there it has limits. City buses run until 9 p.m. on weekdays and 5 p.m. on Saturdays, with no Sunday service listed [190]. The city's paratransit service has carried the mental health center's clients since the 1990s and now provides up to 10,000 rides a year to WellStone's adult day treatment program, with three operators assigned to it [191]. Outside the city limits, Madison County's rural service runs on weekdays only and must be booked a day ahead [192].

124.title: Transportation · B0125
124.text: Cullman County's only public transit is a demand-response service [398]. With 37 vehicles, it runs Monday to Friday from 6:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m., and a ride must be scheduled by 2:30 the afternoon before [193] [192]. A person in Cullman who needs the crisis center in Huntsville on a weekday evening has no public way to get there.

125.title: Transportation · B0126
125.text: That leaves ambulances and patrol cars. The Department itself says many rural residents cannot easily reach a crisis center, and offers mobile crisis teams as its answer [120]. For people under commitment, state law has the probate judge order "one or more persons or law enforcement officers" to take the person to hospital, with the expense taxed as a cost of the proceeding; another section has the state general fund pay such costs unless the party liable is not indigent [194] [195]. In Madison County the judge orders the sheriff to serve notice, and in 2020 he appointed deputies with more than 80 hours of crisis training as community mental health officers [196] [197]. For adults committed to a state bed the destination is Bryce Hospital in Tuscaloosa; no source read describes how often local deputies make that trip or what it costs them [198]. Before the pediatric unit opened, Huntsville's ambulance service was reported to be carrying about 800 children a year out of the county for mental health care [91].

126.title: Key actors · B0127
126.text: Actor Role WellStone Operates the crisis, pediatric and outpatient facilities; its website also lists a withdrawal management unit [3] [41] [168] Huntsville Hospital; Cullman Regional Medical Center Hospital capacity [170] [172] Decatur Morgan West The region's behavioral health hospital, in Morgan County [151] Alabama One Health Record State health information exchange [174] Huntsville Transit (Orbit and Access); TRAM; CARTS Public and rural transport [191] [192] Sheriffs' offices Serve commitment notices in Madison County; state law lets the judge order law enforcement officers to convey a committed person [196] [194] Opioid treatment clinics Methadone and buprenorphine in both counties [183] [184] [185] Community Free Clinic; Good Samaritan Health Clinic Prescriptions for uninsured residents [179] [180]

127.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0128
127.text: The buildings are in one place and the catchment is fifteen counties wide. WellStone has said its Cullman crisis team can take a person to the Huntsville center; beyond that, no source read describes how a person without a car, or a family without a free day, reaches Memorial Parkway from Cullman, let alone from the ring [3] [192] [41].

128.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0129
128.text: Medication for the uninsured is a named need without a number [1].

129.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0130
129.text: Record sharing is required and unreported. Whether the crisis center, the hospitals and the courts can see one another's information when a person moves between them is not something any public source answers [173].

130.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0131
130.text: A state directory is out of date. A family consulting it in 2026 could be told the crisis center has not yet opened [177].

131.title: Scope · B0132
131.text: Every other section of this report ends on some version of the same sentence: the number is not published. This section gathers those gaps in one place. It sets out what is measured about mental health in the two counties and by whom, what a planner would want that is missing, and what quality reporting the new clinic model will require.

132.title: What is measured, and by whom · B0133
132.text: The most useful local figures come from state and national publishers, not local ones. County Health Rankings gives suicide rates of 15.3 per 100,000 in Madison County and 20.7 in Cullman, drug overdose death rates of 29.1 and 35.6, and 5.4 and 5.7 poor mental health days a month [52]. The Kids Count profiles add a figure found nowhere else in this review: 2,294 children with serious emotional disturbance received mental health services in Madison County in 2024, and 444 in Cullman [148] [149]. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention publish estimates below county level, down to the census tract, which is what makes the map in this edition possible [199].
132.section: What is measured, and by whom

133.title: What is measured, and by whom · B0134
133.text: About WellStone, the Department's annual report is the main source: counts for it as a center and as a clinic, and for the crisis center and the pediatric unit [64]. The only access times ever published are the four numbers in the Department's January 2026 budget presentation, which are not divided by county or by age [50]. WellStone's own statements add totals and monthly admissions, in round numbers [1].
133.section: What is measured, and by whom

134.title: What is measured, and by whom · B0135
134.text: Locally produced assessments exist for one county in a usable form. Cullman Regional has published a community health needs assessment every three years since 2013, the latest in 2025, and it includes rates, a survey and a ranking of needs [200] [83]. Madison County's equivalent is the United Way assessment of 2024. Its executive summary carries one sentence on mental health and no percentages, and the full report is a file of more than 31 megabytes that the reader could not open [86] [201]. Huntsville Hospital's request for proposals for its community grants names no priority health areas and cites no needs assessment [202]. A state health department listening session in Huntsville in 2023 recorded knowledge about resources, an aging community and chronic disease as its three biggest concerns [203].
134.section: What is measured, and by whom

135.title: What is measured, and by whom · B0136
135.text: Deaths are the hardest thing to find. The Madison County coroner's website publishes no statistics [204]. His counts reach the public through interviews: a projection of 16 fatal overdoses in one month of 2021, or a WellStone spokesperson relaying an average of one suicide every six days in 2022 [205] [206]. Cullman's coroner counted 17 suicides in 2022 and 22 in 2021, according to the local paper [207]. The state health department publishes deaths by county, cause, race and sex only inside statewide documents of several hundred pages and through an online query tool [208]. Those documents could not be read for either county, so this report has no local death counts by race or sex.
135.section: What is measured, and by whom

136.title: What is not published · B0137
136.text: The table below lists what this review looked for and did not find. Each row records what could not be located as of 4 October 2026, with a partial figure where one exists; no row is a claim that the number does not exist.

137.title: What is not published · B0138
137.text: What a planner would want What the public record offers People served by WellStone in each county Organization-wide totals with no county split [64] Crisis center lengths of stay, drop-offs by law enforcement, diversions from jail or emergency rooms None; the state's evaluation gives none for Huntsville [62] County of residence of people admitted to the crisis center or pediatric unit None [64] Results of the police co-responder program since 2022 None; the police page publishes no figures [209] Commitment petitions, hearings and orders by year Press figures only, in different units: 309 petitions in 2019 and 414 in 2021; 589 involuntary commitments in 2023, all for Madison County [80] [51] How many commitments begin each way, and how long people wait at each stage None; one report lists the three ways a commitment can start, without counts [51] Psychiatric beds by hospital Not obtained; the state health plan prints no inventory and refers readers to the planning agency, whose site could not be reached [129] Emergency department boarding of psychiatric patients None found [399] Jail mental health caseload in either county None found [65] [400] Staff vacancies and turnover at WellStone No rate found; an undated television report said its website listed more than 50 openings in Huntsville [50] [404] WellStone's revenue by source, or any return after FY2021 No Form 990 data after FY2021; audits for FY2022 to FY2025 are listed and could not be read [66] The capital campaign's goal and total None on the campaign's page; a press report at the opening in 2022 gave close to $550,000 raised toward about $5 million, and no later total was found [89] [88] [87] Suicides and overdose deaths by year, race and sex No local publication found; coroners' totals for some years reach the press, without race or sex [204] [207] Counties answered by the Huntsville 988 center No list found; WellStone has said Cullman callers reach it [4] [41] A homelessness count for Cullman County None; only a 37-county total [210] Clinic quality measures under the CCBHC model Promised by the Department; not yet published [173]

138.title: Where the numbers disagree · B0139
138.text: Where figures do exist they often come in pairs. WellStone's FY2025 count is 11,659, 13,700, "over 12,000" or "more than 13,500," depending on the document; the first two are the Department's, from tables whose column headings were not captured, so their unit is unconfirmed [64] [1] [48]. The pediatric unit's count is 520 for fiscal year 2025 in the Department's report and 400 individuals in its first year in WellStone's account [64] [69]. The children once sent out of the county number "about 800" a year in one account and "over 600," with no period given, in another [112] [69]. Cullman's drug overdose death rate is 26.4 per 100,000 in its hospital's assessment and 35.6 in County Health Rankings, for different years [83] [52].

139.title: Where the numbers disagree · B0140
139.text: Most of these differences have innocent explanations: different periods, different definitions, a fiscal year against a calendar year. The trouble is that no source says which explanation applies. The state's own evaluators made the same point about the crisis centers in September 2025, finding inconsistencies in the centers' monthly reports that suggested a lack of quality control and calling for a consistent method of judging their effectiveness [62].

140.title: Quality improvement · B0141
140.text: The clinic model brings reporting duties that should close part of this gap. As a Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic, WellStone must report five measures it collects itself, including time to services, depression remission at six months and screening for social drivers of health, and the Department has bought a software platform to report clinic outcomes [173] [42]. The Department's quality manual says it "will also develop an annual CCBHC Quality Report" [173]. None had appeared by the date of this report.

141.title: Quality improvement · B0142
141.text: WellStone's own plan sets objectives to improve satisfaction scores and cut missed calls, with no baseline for either [1]. Cullman Regional says it has joined a suicide prevention initiative, Project Zero Suicide, and has not yet reported results [84].

142.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0143
