142.text: The region is described mostly by people outside it. The figures that can be compared across counties come from national projects and state agencies; the local institutions that hold the operational data publish little of it [52] [204] [209].

143.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0144
143.text: A county split would cost nothing to produce. The Department publishes WellStone's figures without a county split, so no public figure shows how many Cullman residents it serves [64].

144.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0145
144.text: Madison County's needs assessment could not be read in full for this report, because the full version is a file of more than 31 megabytes; the smaller county has published one every three years since 2013 [201] [200].

145.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0146
145.text: The first clinic quality report, when it appears, would be the first published quality and outcome measures for WellStone beyond its access times [173].

146.title: Scope · B0147
146.text: Part I set out who lives in the two counties. This section asks whether the system reaches them evenly: what the data show about differences between and within the counties, which groups have services built for them, and which do not appear in the record at all. The honest summary is that the region can describe its inequities by place and hardly at all by race, language or income, because the data needed for the second kind of description have not been published locally.

147.title: What the data show · B0148
147.text: By every measure this review found, Cullman County carries the heavier burden. Federal estimates put adult depression at 26.5% in Cullman and 22.0% in Madison in 2023, and frequent mental distress at 18.9% and 16.0% [211]. The suicide rate in County Health Rankings is 20.7 per 100,000 in Cullman and 15.3 in Madison; Cullman's own hospital assessment gives 20.6 for 2018–2022, against 16.5 for Alabama and 14.5 for the country [52] [83]. Drug overdose deaths run at 35.6 per 100,000 in Cullman and 29.1 in Madison [52]. Cullman has the federal shortage designation, fewer mental health providers for its population (568 residents per provider against Madison's 474), the higher uninsured rate and the higher share of residents with a disability [52] [16].

148.title: What the data show · B0149
148.text: The people Cullman Regional surveyed described the consequences in their own words. One wrote of "few resources for mental health treatment other than incarceration," and others named stigma and lack of insurance among the reasons people go without care [83]. Their assessment rests on 47 community representatives and secondary data, and does not break its mental health findings down by income, age, sex or Hispanic origin [83].

149.title: What the data show · B0150
149.text: Madison County's averages are better, and its volumes are larger. The county coroner's figure for 2022, as relayed in a television report, was one suicide every six days [206]. WellStone's emergency services director said in late 2023 that 55% of people who walked into the crisis center that year were experiencing suicidal thoughts [206]. And as Part I showed, the county's averages conceal a spread between Huntsville and the city of Madison that is wider than the gap between Madison and Cullman counties [18] [17].

150.title: What the data show · B0151
150.text: What cannot be said is how any of this differs by race. Madison County is a quarter Black and Huntsville nearly 30% [15] [17]. The state health department counted 834 suicides among Alabama residents in 2024 and publishes them by race and sex for every county, in a document whose Madison and Cullman pages the reader could not reach [212]. No local body publishes service use, crisis admissions, commitments or jail mental health caseloads by race.

151.title: Programs built for specific communities · B0152
151.text: Veterans and military families are the best served group, at least in Huntsville. The VA clinic offers individual and group therapy and the Vet Center counsels without requiring VA enrollment; the Vet Center's page lists no access point in Cullman, where 4,727 veterans live [143] [144] [15] [16]. A firearm-storage initiative for veterans and first responders runs with a Huntsville partner and reports that 86.4% of Alabama veteran suicides involve a firearm, against 73.5% nationally [213].

152.title: Programs built for specific communities · B0153
152.text: People with intellectual and developmental disabilities have a separate and larger provider network than people with mental illness. The Department's directory lists 26 developmental disability entries in Madison County out of 43 of all kinds, and three in Cullman [130] [131]. The Arc of Madison County serves more than 315 people and runs an autism clinic [214]. The University of Alabama in Huntsville hosts the autism information hub for thirteen north Alabama counties [215]. Statewide, the waiting list for the Department's disability waivers stood at 1,800 people in May 2025, with no county figure [42].

153.title: Programs built for specific communities · B0154
153.text: Older adults have dedicated inpatient care in Huntsville: a separate program for people 65 and over at Huntsville Hospital and 20 beds at Unity Psychiatric Care for people 55 and over [124] [126]. The two counties are served by different aging agencies [395]. Cullman's, based in Decatur, helps Medicare beneficiaries apply for benefits that cover premiums and prescription costs, and United Way of Cullman County's 2022–23 funded list included no behavioral health service for older people [216] [180].

154.title: Programs built for specific communities · B0155
154.text: LGBTQ+ residents lost a dedicated counseling organization in Huntsville, Free2Be, which closed suddenly some years ago [217]. Thrive Alabama lists LGBTQ+ health care among its services in Huntsville [218]. Rocket City Pride's resource page names one counseling provider, a private practice, and does not list WellStone, Crisis Services of North Alabama or 988; a local television station's resource list has nothing in Cullman County [219] [220].

155.title: Programs built for specific communities · B0156
155.text: Hispanic residents are 7.6% of Madison County and 5.8% of Cullman, and almost invisible in the service record [15] [16]. The statewide Hispanic services nonprofit lists one office, in Birmingham [221]. The state's clinic manual requires WellStone to have interpretation and translation available in proportion to its population with limited English, and nothing read says how it does so [57]. No local source describes Hispanic residents' use of, or barriers to, mental health care in either county.

156.title: Programs built for specific communities · B0157
156.text: Deaf residents are served through regional clinicians of the Department's Office of Deaf Services, whose page names no Huntsville staff [222]. Students have counseling centers at the University of Alabama in Huntsville and Alabama A&M, the latter with an on-call counselor after hours [223] [224].

157.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0158
157.text: The burden is heavier where the services are thinner. Cullman has the higher rates of depression, suicide and overdose and the fewer providers, with no inpatient unit at its hospital and no VA site or peer recovery center listed there [211] [52] [53] [142] [231].

158.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0159
158.text: Nothing local is published by race. In a county that is a quarter Black, no public figure shows who uses the crisis center, who is committed or who is jailed with a mental illness [15].

159.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0160
159.text: Language access is a rule without a report [57].

160.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0161
160.text: Community resource lists do not point to the public system. The pride organization's list omits the crisis center and 988, which suggests the system's front door is not known, or not trusted, by everyone it is meant for [219].

161.title: Scope · B0162
161.text: This section describes who speaks for mental health in the two counties, how the public is educated about it, what local advocacy has won, and whether people who have lived with mental illness or addiction have a formal voice in how services are run. Little Orange Fish, the publisher of this report, is the backbone organization of one of the bodies described here, the North Alabama Mental Health Coalition; the coalition is described only from public web pages, its own and its founding organization's, and none of its meeting records were used as sources.

162.title: Who engages · B0163
162.text: Madison County has a dense advocacy network. The North Alabama Mental Health Coalition was formed in 2015 by a committee of the Society of St. Vincent de Paul to improve the situation of people with serious mental illness, many of them homeless or in jail [25]. It describes itself as stakeholders who pool knowledge and resources to find and close gaps in access to care, and lists as core partners WellStone, Huntsville Hospital and Decatur West, the sheriff, the Huntsville and Madison police, the ambulance service, the VA, First Stop, the city, the county and the probate judges [225] [226].

163.title: Who engages · B0164
163.text: NAMI Madison County runs family and peer support groups, one of which meets in Athens in the next county, and an eight-week course for families [135] [227]. Crisis Services of North Alabama operates the HELPline, a domestic violence shelter and forensic nursing across four counties, with sexual assault response in Cullman and Winston as well [136]. Not One More Alabama, founded in 2016, offers family, grief and recovery support to people affected by addiction, and the Partnership for a Drug-Free Community runs prevention education, drug take-back and a recovery hub [228] [229]. The Alabama chapter of the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention holds its north Alabama walk in Huntsville [230].

164.title: Who engages · B0165
164.text: Cullman County has almost none of this. NAMI Alabama lists eleven affiliates and none in Cullman [55]. The Department's directory shows a peer-run recovery center in Huntsville and none in Cullman [231]. United Way of Cullman County names seventeen partner agencies, and no mental health treatment provider is among them; the closest in its 2022–23 funding list were a victim services agency, a sober living program and 2-1-1 [232] [180]. The organizations that do the work in Cullman are the hospital's partners: WellStone, Lighthouse Inc., The Link of Cullman County, and the police and sheriff [84].

165.title: Public education · B0166
165.text: The best documented form of public education in the region is police training. An undated television feature describes Huntsville Police's crisis intervention certification as a 40-hour course of about 26 training blocks, taught by volunteers from NAMI and WellStone among others, with a 16-hour introduction for other personnel; the department is the training hub for an eighteen-county region [233] [234]. Mental Health First Aid is an eight-hour course that, the Department says, more than 90 certified instructors offer in Alabama; the Department publishes no count of people trained [235]. WellStone was announced to teach it free at the Cullman County library in July 2022 on a state grant [236]. A Huntsville television station has run a recurring "Mental Health Monday" segment, and the University of Alabama in Huntsville announced a suicide prevention campus walk for April 2025 [233] [237].

166.title: What advocacy has achieved · B0167
166.text: The region's recent gains can be dated, and several of them began locally. The probate court's assisted outpatient treatment program was launched publicly in February 2020, first paid for from the court's own passport fees [30]. The state named Huntsville one of three pilot crisis centers on 28 October 2020 [32]. The city council funded police co-responders in May 2021 [63]. A mental health court opened in Cullman in May 2022 [82]. A federal grant for outpatient commitment began in 2022, and the ribbon was cut on the pediatric crisis unit in September 2024 [80] [91]. The coalition claims a part in other changes, saying it spearheaded crisis intervention training locally and successfully pressed for mental health caseworkers in the Madison County jail [226]. Those are its own statements and were not independently confirmed.

167.title: What advocacy has achieved · B0168
167.text: The region also has unusual weight in Montgomery. The chair of the House General Fund budget committee, Rep. Rex Reynolds, is a Huntsville-area legislator, the same one who sponsored the 2022 commitment bill [238] [81]. In February 2025 he said that expanding mental health beds and crisis services would have to wait until prison construction costs were covered [238].

168.title: What advocacy has achieved · B0169
168.text: A Cullman attempt to raise local money, a third of it for mental health, went to the voters and lost. Before the November 2024 referendum on a medical cannabis tax, Wallace State hosted a town hall at which WellStone's chief operating officer said his priorities, if the measure passed, would be residential and crisis care in Cullman, and a sheriff's captain said, "We don't have services here that we need" [169]. The measure failed by about 1,100 votes [44].

169.title: The voice of lived experience · B0170
169.text: Peers lead much of the region's mutual support. NAMI's Connection groups are run by trained peers, the recovery center in Huntsville is staffed by people in recovery, and the Partnership's hub by certified peer specialists [227] [239] [229].

170.title: The voice of lived experience · B0171
170.text: Whether people with lived experience help govern the public system is harder to establish. Alabama's clinic manual requires that they and their families take a meaningful part in a clinic's governance, through a board at least 51% made up of such people or through another arrangement, and a clinic that uses the alternative must support the posting of an annual summary of that body's recommendations on its website [57]. WellStone's board is appointed by four local governments [1]. It has a Community Advisory Committee, known to this review only because the Madison County probate judge's biography says he sits on it; no membership list, remit or count of consumer and family seats was found [240].

171.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0172
171.text: Cullman has services, and no organized advocacy group was found there. It has a WellStone campus and a hospital that ranks mental health first; no NAMI affiliate or peer recovery center is listed there, and no coalition of its own was found [242] [55] [231] [83].

172.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0173
172.text: The coalition's partner list is a Madison County list [226]. The two counties share a mental health center and, as far as its public pages show, not a table.

173.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0174
173.text: A governance requirement that can be checked. If WellStone meets the lived-experience rule through an advisory body, an annual summary of that body's recommendations should be on its website [57]. Its site was not checked for such a summary in this review.

174.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0175
174.text: No count of public education was found. Apart from about 100 university staff, no figure was found for how many residents have had Mental Health First Aid [235] [134].

175.title: Scope and frame · B0176
175.text: A child's mental health care is delivered through more doors than an adult's: the school, the pediatrician, the child welfare agency, the juvenile court. The statewide report reads Alabama against the principles of a system of care, in which those doors open onto the same hallway. This section describes each door in Madison and Cullman counties and what is known about how many children pass through it.

176.title: Where the area stands · B0177
176.text: About a quarter of each county's residents are children: 102,878 in Madison and 22,458 in Cullman in 2024 [148] [149]. Their circumstances differ in the way the adult figures would predict. In Madison County 13.1% of children lived in poverty in 2019–2023, the third-best rank in the state; in Cullman it was 18.5% [148] [149]. In Cullman 11.1% of teenagers were neither in school nor working, three times Madison's 3.7% [149].

177.title: Where the area stands · B0178
177.text: On the measures closest to mental health the picture is less tidy. Kids Count reports that 2,294 Madison County children and 444 Cullman children with serious emotional disturbance received mental health services in 2024, which this report calculates as roughly 2% of children in each county [148] [149]. Madison's schools suspended 11.1% of students in 2024–25 against Cullman's 3.3%, and recorded more of them as homeless [148] [149]. Preventable teen death rates were close, 70.9 and 73.0 per 100,000 in 2023, though Cullman's rests on four deaths [148] [149]. No county-level figure for youth suicide or self-harm is published.

178.title: The public children's system · B0179
178.text: WellStone's children's services run through the Nova Center for Youth & Family in Huntsville and its Cullman campus [1] [241]. The Department's directory lists case management, outpatient care, a juvenile court liaison, an in-home intervention program and school-based services at the Cullman site [242]. Child and adolescent mobile crisis teams, funded by the state with the Department of Human Resources, cover both counties and saw 498 young people in FY2025 [120] [64]. No source gives the number of children WellStone serves in total.

179.title: The public children's system · B0180
179.text: The pediatric crisis unit is the largest change in children's services in the region for many years. Until it opened, WellStone said, Madison County had "no inpatient psychiatric options for youth" [91]. The nearest psychiatric hospital for adolescents was Decatur Morgan West in the next county, and the ambulance service was reported to be taking about 800 young people a year out of Madison County for stabilization, half to Decatur and half to Birmingham, Mobile, Dothan, Nashville or Chattanooga [112]. One family described waiting 24 hours in the emergency room and then traveling four hours for a bed [243].

180.title: The public children's system · B0181
180.text: The ribbon was cut in September 2024 on a unit of 24 beds, with stays planned from under a day to two weeks, for ages 12 to 18 at first and from eight by early 2026 [91] [112] [69]. How much it has changed the flow of children out of the county cannot be measured from what is published. The Department's count for FY2025 is 520. A press report of February 2026 said the unit had served 400 individuals since opening, and WellStone's chief executive said it had passed its goal of reaching half of the "over 600" children formerly sent away [64] [69]. No source read for this report says how many children still leave.

181.title: The public children's system · B0182
181.text: What the unit is not is a hospital. It is a crisis service with a two-week ceiling, and no inpatient psychiatric unit for children was found in either county. Two residential programs appear in state lists: a 42-bed facility in Madison County on a 2022 education department list, and a 110-day program for boys aged 12 to 18 that the youth services department lists as serving Cullman among sixteen counties. Neither list describes a psychiatric role, and their current status was not checked [112] [405] [279] [267].

182.title: Schools · B0183
182.text: Five school systems serve the two counties, and they have made different arrangements. Madison County Schools, with more than 20,500 students, names a mental health services coordinator, describes a three-tiered model with social workers and counselors, and lists three outside partners: WellStone's Nova Center, a Huntsville nonprofit called The Enrichment Center, and a grief program [244] [245]. Madison City Schools uses The Enrichment Center, not WellStone, for therapy on school grounds [246]. That nonprofit reports 35 school-based therapists, 1,290 students and 14,166 sessions in 2025–26 across three districts, at no cost to families and without billing insurance [247]. WellStone's therapists were reported to have seen Madison County students more than 1,700 times in FY2024 [248].

183.title: Schools · B0184
183.text: Huntsville City Schools, which says it serves more than 23,000 students, could not be described: its counseling and student support pages returned only menus to the reader [249] [250]. In Cullman, the city schools employ a district mental health specialist and list three outside prevention programs, and the county schools had four full-time social workers and a coordinator in 2022 [251] [252] [253]. The Department lists WellStone's Cullman site as part of the state's school-based mental health collaboration without saying which district [242].

184.title: Schools · B0185
184.text: Two details show how unevenly information travels. State law raised the age below which a student needs a parent's written consent for ongoing counseling from 14 to 16 in October 2025; Cullman City's page states the new rule and Madison County's still gives the old one [251] [254]. And the Department's list of which school systems partner with which mental health center returned an error on the day it was checked [255].

185.title: Child welfare · B0186
185.text: Child welfare is where the two counties diverge most. Kids Count recorded 338 Cullman children with an indication of abuse or neglect in 2024, a rate of 16.4 per 1,000 that ranks 53rd of Alabama's 67 counties. Madison's rate was 3.6 per 1,000, the best in the state, against 10.1 statewide [149] [148] [256]. Foster care moved the other way: Madison County's count rose from 252 in 2014 to 411 in 2025, while Cullman's fell from 159 to 112 [148] [149].

186.title: Child welfare · B0187
186.text: Huntsville is home to the National Children's Advocacy Center, which opened there in 1985 and provides services for Huntsville and Madison County [22] [401]. Its 2024 report gives 488 forensic interviews, 991 team case reviews and 129 forensic medical exams; its therapy figures for that year could not be read reliably and are left out [257]. It offers trauma therapy to children up to 18 regardless of a family's finances [258]. Cullman's center, Brooks' Place, provides forensic interviews, counseling and medical exams with five staff and says all its funding comes from local donations [259] [260]. Residential and foster care providers include Kids to Love in Madison, which also runs a trauma therapy center, and Childhaven in Cullman, with capacity for 32 [261] [262] [263].

187.title: Juvenile justice · B0188
187.text: Madison County's juvenile court runs three specialty dockets: a drug court, a truancy court and an Alternative Court, which the circuit's website describes as founded by a judge to address the mental health needs of juveniles and as the first of its kind in Alabama [264] [265]. Its detention center, Neaves-Davis, has 48 beds; the county's page says nothing about mental health screening or services for the young people held there [266]. The state's youth services agency funds a 47-slot diversion program in the county with in-home crisis intervention and family counseling [267].

188.title: Juvenile justice · B0189
188.text: Cullman County has a short-term juvenile detention facility of its own, renamed in October 2024, which does not appear on the state's list of eleven detention centers [268] [269] [270]. Its diversion grant has eight slots, and WellStone runs a 15-slot after-school program there [267]. Youth incarcerations have fallen in both counties: from 519 to 229 in Madison and from 116 to 78 in Cullman between the decade ending 2009 and the decade ending 2024 [148] [149].

189.title: Early childhood and pediatric medicine · B0190
189.text: The earliest years are covered by programs whose reach is counted and whose mental health content is not. Madison County had 1,563 children in First Class Pre-K and 766 in early intervention; Cullman had 314 in pre-K [148] [149]. The children's advocacy center made 397 home visits to first-time parents in 2024 [257]. The Department's infant and early childhood mental health page does not say which consultants serve either county [271]. One figure stands out: only 64.5% of Madison County births in 2023 followed adequate prenatal care, ranking it 62nd of 67, against 75.4% in Cullman [148]. Huntsville Hospital for Women & Children lists no postpartum or perinatal mood group among its support groups [272].

190.title: Early childhood and pediatric medicine · B0191
190.text: Child psychiatry is scarce and its scarcity is undocumented. Huntsville Hospital for Women & Children says it runs the only dedicated pediatric emergency department in north Alabama, seeing more than 36,000 children a year; the system's pediatric page lists no pediatric psychiatry service [273] [274]. A university clinic in Huntsville that sees children as well as adults lists four psychiatrists, without saying which of them treat children [275]. One private child psychiatry practice states that it is at capacity and is not adding names to its waiting list [276]. The state's telephone consultation service for pediatricians said in 2024 that it can take three to six months to see a therapist or psychiatrist, a statewide statement [277]. For autism, a Huntsville clinic for children aged two to five gives a wait of three to four months, and the Department's guide lists 21 diagnostic providers for north Alabama families, none of them in Cullman County [278] [279].

191.title: Key actors · B0192
191.text: Actor Role for children and families WellStone (Nova Center; pediatric crisis unit; child mobile crisis) Public outpatient, crisis and school-based care [1] [242] [120] [91] The Enrichment Center School-based therapy in Madison City and Madison County schools [247] [245] Five school systems Counselors, social workers and coordinators where described; Huntsville City's pages could not be read [245] [251] Madison and Cullman County Departments of Human Resources County offices in Huntsville and Cullman [280] National Children's Advocacy Center; Brooks' Place Forensic interviews, trauma therapy [257] [258] [259] Madison County Juvenile Court; Neaves-Davis Center Specialty dockets; detention [264] [266] Huntsville Hospital for Women & Children Pediatric emergency department [273] UAB Medicine Huntsville Child and adult psychiatry clinic [275] Kids to Love; Childhaven Foster care, residential care, trauma therapy [261] [262] [263]

192.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0193
192.text: A crisis unit is not a continuum. The region now has somewhere to take a child in crisis; no local inpatient option was found for the child who needs more than two weeks, and no measure was found of how many still travel [112] [69].

193.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0194
193.text: Cullman's child welfare numbers call for attention that its services do not show. A rate of indicated abuse or neglect more than four times Madison's sits beside an advocacy center funded entirely by donations [149] [260].

194.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0195
194.text: School-based care is split among providers, and nobody adds it up. WellStone counts contacts, The Enrichment Center counts students and sessions, and Huntsville City Schools' pages could not be read by the tool used for this review [248] [247] [250].

195.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0196
195.text: Child psychiatry capacity is unknown. The evidence is a full private practice and a statewide estimate of months-long waits [276] [277].

196.title: Scope and frame · B0197
196.text: The statewide report organizes the meeting points between mental illness and the justice system by the Sequential Intercept Model: community and crisis services, law enforcement, initial detention and court, jails and courts, reentry, and community supervision. This section walks the same six intercepts in Madison and Cullman counties. It deals with deaths and lawsuits as well as programs. People who died or were charged are not named; cases are given by their captions, and what was alleged is kept apart from what a court found.

197.title: Intercept 0: community and crisis response · B0198
197.text: Diversion was the stated purpose of the crisis center from the start. WellStone's chief executive described the beds in 2022 as a way to keep people out of jails and emergency departments, and the permanent building was designed with a rear entrance for people brought by ambulance or police [88]. The Department lists it as the place to which law enforcement and first responders in fifteen counties can bring a person in crisis at any hour [3].

198.title: Intercept 0: community and crisis response · B0199
198.text: How many people it has diverted is unknown. WellStone's chief executive said in March 2024 that its jail diversion program was saving about $300,000 of taxpayer money a year "the last time we measured," and that the crisis center had produced savings for the emergency departments at Huntsville Hospital and Crestwood [112]. No method, year or count accompanies either statement. The only published inputs date from 2018, when the jail diversion program was a few months old: it had moved 20 people out of the jail, and the cost of holding an inmate with mental illness was put at $70 a day [27]. The state's own evaluation of the crisis centers in 2025 publishes no counts of jail or emergency room avoidance for any single center, found the centers' monthly reports inconsistent, and noted that one center, not named in the passages read, has always reported zero for jail avoidance [62].

199.title: Intercept 0: community and crisis response · B0200
199.text: In Cullman the path to the crisis center runs through a phone line. As WellStone described it in 2024, a Cullman caller to 988 reaches the Huntsville center, which connects them to a local crisis team that can take them to Huntsville if needed [41].

200.title: Intercept 1: law enforcement · B0201
200.text: Huntsville Police have the region's most developed response. In May 2021 the department had 75 officers certified through the 40-hour crisis intervention course, and a later briefing gave 94 certified and 190 trained in the 16-hour version; the department's page publishes no current figure [34] [281] [209]. The co-responder program approved that month was planned for two clinicians working 2 p.m. to midnight, and WellStone's chief executive said a federal grant later added two more positions [34] [281]. The city's review of the department's 2025 does not mention co-responders, crisis intervention or mental health, and no count of calls attended, arrests avoided or transports was found on the City's or the department's pages in the program's five years [282] [63].

201.title: Intercept 1: law enforcement · B0202
201.text: Any account of how Huntsville police respond to people in crisis has to include one case. In 2018 a Huntsville officer shot and killed a man who was holding a gun to his own head [283]. The officer was convicted of murder in May 2021 and sentenced to 25 years that August [283]. On 24 March 2023 the Alabama Court of Criminal Appeals reversed the conviction over the jury instruction on self-defense, and on 13 October 2023 the former officer pleaded guilty to manslaughter, with three years' probation and a 20-year split sentence to take effect only on a probation violation, and there was no retrial [284] [283].

202.title: Intercept 1: law enforcement · B0203
202.text: Outside Huntsville the record thins. The Madison County Sheriff's Office, with 194 sworn deputy positions, lists mental commitments among the calls its patrol deputies handle and mentions no crisis intervention team [285]. In 2020 the probate judge appointed deputies with more than 80 hours of crisis training as community mental health officers [197]. Nothing on the Cullman County Sheriff's website shows crisis-trained officers or a co-responder, and the district attorney told a town hall in 2024 that the Sheriff's Office had handled hundreds of mental health calls in the previous year [286] [169].

203.title: Intercept 2: initial detention and first court appearance · B0204
203.text: Detention for Huntsville Police is run by the Madison County Sheriff's Office at the county jail, which makes the jail the booking point for the county's largest police department [287]. The county's Office of Alternative Sentencing and Release runs a Mental Health Pre-Trial Release Program there that interviews, evaluates and supervises detainees who show or have a diagnosis of mental illness; it publishes no numbers [288].
203.section: Intercept 2: initial detention and first court appearance

204.title: Intercept 2: initial detention and first court appearance · B0205
204.text: The civil side of this intercept is the probate court, described in Domain 1. Its assisted outpatient treatment program is court-ordered care for people who can live safely in the community with treatment and have not stayed in it voluntarily [30]. The federal grant that has paid for it since 2022 set targets of 275 people enrolled over four years and a 75% decrease in participants needing inpatient care or incarceration; no results against those targets have been published, and the grant period ended in July 2026 [37].
204.section: Intercept 2: initial detention and first court appearance

205.title: Intercept 2: initial detention and first court appearance · B0206
205.text: Huntsville's Municipal Court, which handles 45,000 to 50,000 cases a year with three judges, runs its own mental health court and a pretrial diversion program [289]. Its mental health docket requires defendants to attend counseling and see a psychologist and a psychiatrist [289]. For people without housing, the city's account is a judge's statement that the court tries to find them a place to live and the skills to stay there [289].
205.section: Intercept 2: initial detention and first court appearance

206.title: Intercept 2: initial detention and first court appearance · B0207
206.text: In Cullman, as of the state's 2020–21 evaluation, WellStone staff evaluated people in the hospital emergency room on a probate judge's order or the hospital's request [290]. A 2019 arrangement let a judge order a mental health evaluation, adopted after voluntary screening in the jail failed: of 98 inmates the jail referred that year, four agreed to be screened [291] [28].
206.section: Intercept 2: initial detention and first court appearance

207.title: Intercept 3: jails and courts · B0208
207.text: Neither county publishes its jail's population or mental health caseload. The Madison County Sheriff's pages give no capacity or screening figures; the most recent capacity statement found is from 2010, when the then sheriff said the jail could hold about 1,200 [65] [292]. The health care contract approved in September 2026 covers up to 1,235 inmates at about $3.74 million a year and adds a mental health nurse paid from opioid settlement funds [75]. Cullman's detention center has 553 beds and a medical staff that includes a physician and nurses, with no mental health staff named; its contract with the same company, Southern Health Partners, is $849,156.24 for FY2027 [293] [294]. WellStone is the certified provider of outpatient substance use treatment inside both jails [186] [187].

208.title: Intercept 3: jails and courts · B0209
208.text: The Madison County jail's history includes three deaths in 2013 that led to federal lawsuits. The families' complaints, reported in October 2014, alleged that officers and medical staff failed to act as each person died of a treatable condition, and that the county and its then health contractor delayed hospital transfers to save money; the defendants denied breaching the standard of care [295]. The three cases, numbered 5:14-cv-01964, 5:14-cv-01959 and 5:14-cv-01309 in the Northern District of Alabama, were all reported as pending in September 2016 [296]. In the third, the court denied all motions to dismiss on 9 March 2015, a ruling that the complaint stated a claim and could proceed, not a finding that the allegations were proved [297]. How the three cases ended could not be established from any source that would open. The contractor named in the suits is no longer the jail's provider [298].

209.title: Intercept 3: jails and courts · B0210
209.text: Madison County has an Adult Mental Health Court. The circuit's site says a district judge has presided over it since 2015, and a circuit judge's biography says she has presided over it since taking the bench; the same circuit judge established a veterans court for veterans with mental illness or substance problems [299] [265]. The adult drug court is run from the county's alternative sentencing office [300]. None publishes its capacity or how many people have completed it. Cullman County's courts added a veterans court in May 2019 and a mental health court in May 2022, the latter with state funding and a federal grant and with WellStone providing services regardless of ability to pay [29] [35]. By October 2026 the circuit's web page named neither the judge who launched the mental health court nor any of the specialty dockets [301].

210.title: Intercept 3: jails and courts · B0211
210.text: Both counties were early sites for Stepping Up, the national initiative to reduce the number of people with mental illness in jails, and the results show how hard jail screening is to sustain. In the first year, 2018–19, Madison's site screened 82 inmates and found 35 positive, and the state's report said the county had no plan to sustain the work [28]. In 2020–21 the Madison jail referred 63 people, of whom 57 were confirmed as having a serious mental illness, 35 were referred on, and 12 people received case management, a figure that includes people carried over from earlier years; the state's report says no site summary was completed because of staff turnover and inconsistent data [290]. Cullman's numbers that year were 11 referred and three confirmed [290]. Whether either county is a current Stepping Up site could not be read from the Department's 2026 map [302].

211.title: Intercept 3: jails and courts · B0212
211.text: Competency to stand trial is the last piece. Jail-based restoration runs in seven Alabama counties, and neither Madison nor Cullman is one of them, so defendants found incompetent wait for the state's forensic hospital along with everyone else in a queue that stood at 273 men in August 2025 [64] [303]. No county-level wait is published.

212.title: Intercepts 4 and 5: reentry and community supervision · B0213
212.text: Reentry support is better documented in the smaller county. The Link of Cullman County won a $500,000 federal Second Chance Act grant in 2020 for a reentry program of case management and follow-up, working with the sheriff and taking referrals from the state parole bureau [304] [305]. In Madison County, WellStone's jail diversion staff work to get people held because of mental health problems out of jail, into housing and to their follow-up appointments [112]. The parole bureau runs one of its five day reporting centers in Huntsville, for high-risk probationers and parolees, with mental health among the needs it addresses [306].
212.section: Intercepts 4 and 5: reentry and community supervision

213.title: Intercepts 4 and 5: reentry and community supervision · B0214
213.text: Supervision in Madison County is concentrated in one office. Pretrial release, community corrections, misdemeanor probation, court referral and the drug court all sit in the Office of Alternative Sentencing and Release [288]. Cullman's community corrections program is a nonprofit based in the courthouse [307] [308]. Neither publishes how many of the people it supervises have a mental illness or what treatment conditions they carry.
213.section: Intercepts 4 and 5: reentry and community supervision

214.title: Victims and violence · B0215
214.text: The trauma side of the interface has its own agencies. Crisis Services of North Alabama serves victims of domestic and sexual violence in Madison and three neighboring counties, with a shelter and forensic exams, and provides sexual assault response in Cullman [136]. Cullman's domestic violence agency, renamed The Willow Path in September 2025, takes 600 to 800 crisis calls a year and has a 24-bed shelter [309] [310].

215.title: The area against the intercepts · B0216
215.text: Intercept Madison County Cullman County 0. Law enforcement Crisis-trained officers and co-responders in Huntsville; no outcomes published [34] [63] No crisis-trained officers shown on the sheriff's site [286] 2. Initial detention and court Mental health pretrial release; municipal mental health court [288] [289] Court-ordered evaluation arranged in 2019 after voluntary screening failed; current status not confirmed [291] [28] 3. Jails and courts Adult Mental Health Court; no jail figures [299] [65] Mental Health Court announced in 2022; current status not confirmed [35] Competency restoration No jail-based program [64] No jail-based program [64] 4. 216.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0217
216.text: The most-cited success is the least measured. Diversion is the reason the crisis center was built, and after four years there is no published count of people diverted, by either county's jail or either hospital [62] [112].

217.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0218
217.text: Programs are known by their launch dates. The co-responders, Cullman's mental health and veterans courts and assisted outpatient treatment have a funding or launch date on the public record; the Madison County and municipal courts have not even that; none has an annual report [63] [299] [35] [29] [30].

218.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0219
218.text: What officials say is missing is a place to hold and treat. The probate judge describes people who have "exhausted their circle of support"; the Cullman sheriff says the county has no facility for evaluations; WellStone's plan puts stabilization for committed adults first [36] [78] [1].

219.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0220
219.text: The jails are the system's least visible part. Neither county publishes how many people in its jail have a mental illness, and the one state program that counted them recorded data problems in Madison and near-total refusal in Cullman [65] [290] [28].

220.title: Scope and frame · B0221
220.text: The statewide report reads Alabama against the five domains of social determinants used in Healthy People 2030: neighborhood and built environment, economic stability, health care access, education access, and social and community context. This section does the same for the two counties. It gives most of its length to housing, because housing is a need WellStone's own plan names twice and the one for which the public record is richest.

221.title: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness · B0222
221.text: The first fact to know is that WellStone's two counties belong to different homelessness systems. Madison County is one of three counties, with Limestone and Morgan, in the continuum of care run by the North Alabama Coalition for the Homeless [311]. Cullman County is one of 37 in the Alabama Balance of State continuum, coordinated from Montgomery [312]. Federal counts, funding and housing inventories follow those lines, so almost everything below describes Madison's three-county continuum, and almost nothing can be said about Cullman.
221.section: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness

222.title: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness · B0223
222.text: The count in the Huntsville continuum has risen. The federal report of the January 2025 count gives 718 people: 416 in emergency shelter, 37 in transitional housing and 265 unsheltered [60]. The figures for the three years before were 549, 646 and 621 [59] [313] [314]. On the night of the 2025 count the continuum had 421 year-round emergency shelter beds, nearly all of them full, and 265 people outside [61] [60]. No 2026 count had been published by either the federal department or the coalition by October 2026 [315].
222.section: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness

223.title: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness · B0224
223.text: How many of those people have a serious mental illness is uncertain, because the published figure jumps about: 71 in 2022, 24 in 2023, 40 in 2024 and 49 in 2025 [313] [60]. In 2023 the report shows none of the people counted as severely mentally ill as unsheltered, which says more about how the count was taken than about who was outside [313]. The count of people with chronic substance use problems fell from 117 to 41 over the same four reports [60].
223.section: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness

224.title: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness · B0225
224.text: The housing that is meant to end homelessness for people with disabilities has shrunk. Permanent supportive housing in the continuum stood at 334 beds in the 2022 inventory, 154 in 2023, 153 in 2024 and 190 in 2025 [61]. In 2022 most of those beds, 268 of 334, were in a veterans' voucher project; the 2025 list has no project under that name, though the housing authority's 166-bed project, labelled "- V" in the list, may be the same program; that could not be confirmed [316] [61]. The 2025 inventory names two projects: the Huntsville Housing Authority's, with 166 beds, and WellStone's Shelter Plus Care, with 24 [61]. That month the count found 128 chronically homeless people [60]. Federal continuum funding for FY2024 came to $945,663 in four grants, the largest of them $615,231 to the housing authority for supportive housing [317].
224.section: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness

225.title: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness · B0226
225.text: Huntsville's city government leads the local response through its Community Development department [73]. It manages a sanctioned camp on South Derrick Street, rebuilt after a fire with marked spaces and a fence; the city's release of April 2025 says 84 spaces, while press reports in 2026 give a capacity of about 58 and some 30 to 35 residents [318] [319] [320]. People staying there must now take part in case management, and the city said in June 2026 that its Homeless Services Team had helped 22 former residents into stable housing in six months [320] [321]. First Stop, the day services provider, was tracking about 20 encampments across the county in March 2026 and thought that was about half of them [319]. The Downtown Rescue Mission supplies 200 of the continuum's emergency shelter beds and hosts its coordinated entry [61] [322].
225.section: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness

226.title: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness · B0227
226.text: For Cullman there is no count. The Balance of State continuum reported 636 people across its 37 counties in January 2026, 72.3% of them unsheltered, with no county breakdown [210]. The only project with Cullman in its name in the 2025 federal housing inventory is a domestic violence shelter listed with 21 beds; the agency that runs it was reported in August 2026 to have 24 [323] [310]. Emergency shelter in the county is weather-triggered: the city's warming center may open when the forecast is 28 degrees or below [324]. The Cullman Housing Authority's voucher waiting list is closed and, it says, rarely opens [325].
226.section: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness

227.title: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness · B0228
227.text: Behind all of this is the cost of ordinary housing. A two-bedroom apartment at fair market rent takes an hourly wage of $25.19 in the Huntsville area and $17.94 in Cullman County [326]. The Huntsville Housing Authority, with more than 1,500 rental units and close to 1,800 voucher families, reports a wait of six to twelve months for public housing [327] [328]. WellStone's plan names "adequate housing options to meet our clients' needs" and supervised housing for adult clients among its unmet needs [1].
227.section: Neighborhood and built environment: housing and homelessness

228.title: Economic stability · B0229
228.text: Work is plentiful in both counties by the usual measure: unemployment was 3.4% in Madison and 3.6% in Cullman in June 2026, after annual averages near 2.5% in 2025 [329] [330]. Income is another matter. County Health Rankings puts children in poverty at 13.5% in Madison and 21.3% in Cullman [20]. In 2023, 34,783 Madison County residents and 8,554 Cullman residents received food assistance through SNAP [331] [332]. In December 2024, 6,140 people in Madison and 2,241 in Cullman received Supplemental Security Income, nearly all on grounds of disability [333]. Set against population, Cullman's SSI count is proportionally the larger, which fits its higher disability rate [333] [334].

229.title: Economic stability · B0230
229.text: Employment support for people with serious mental illness is thin. None of the five mental health centers the Department named in February 2025 as offering Individual Placement and Support, the evidence-based supported employment model, is in north Alabama [335]. State vocational rehabilitation serves Madison County from Huntsville and Cullman County from Decatur [336].

230.title: Health care access · B0231
230.text: Primary care is easier to find in Madison County: one physician for every 1,140 residents, against one for every 2,159 in Cullman [20]. The safety net is concentrated there too. A federally designated health center, HAPPI Health, lists four sites, all in Huntsville, with a sliding fee and its own behavioral health service of therapy, evaluations and crisis intervention [337] [338]. Thrive Alabama runs primary care, a behavioral health clinic and a pharmacy in Huntsville [339]. The Community Free Clinic has served uninsured Madison County residents since 1999 [340].

231.title: Health care access · B0232
231.text: Cullman has a free clinic. The Good Samaritan Health Clinic sees uninsured adults, provides most medications free through a patient assistance program, and offers mental health counseling through a partnership with a memorial fund; the page does not say who provides it [341] [342]. Neither county's health department lists a behavioral health service [343].

232.title: Education access · B0233
232.text: School systems in both counties score above the state on Alabama's report card. In 2024–25 Cullman City scored 96 and Cullman County 91, with graduation rates of 96.83% and 96.96%; Madison City's campuses averaged 95, Madison County scored 91 and Huntsville City 89, against a state score of 87 [344] [345] [346] [403]. The gap opens after high school: 46.4% of Madison County adults hold a bachelor's degree and 19.7% of Cullman's [15].

233.title: Social and community context · B0234
233.text: The two counties look alike on measures of social connection, with about a third of adults in each reporting loneliness [20]. They differ in the infrastructure around those adults. Madison County's 2-1-1 calls are answered in Huntsville and Cullman's from Birmingham [13]. The regional council that holds Madison County's aging agency lists mental health services among the things older people most need, and Cullman's commission on aging runs ten senior centers and delivers meals to almost 250 homebound people a day [347] [348]. Huntsville has a bus system and Cullman a demand-response service that averaged 190 rides per operating day in July 2026 [190] [398] [349].

234.title: Social and community context · B0235
234.text: Community organizations carry much of the non-clinical load. In Madison County the public library keeps a guide to social services whose mental health page lists eight resources, and congregations coordinate emergency food through a shared line [350] [402] [351]. In Cullman, The Link's food pantry serves 800 households a month, Cullman Caring for Kids runs the United Way food bank, and The Link became an accredited family resource center in September 2026 [352] [180] [353].

235.title: The area against the five domains · B0236
235.text: Domain Madison County Cullman County Housing and homelessness 718 counted in a three-county continuum (2025); 190 supportive housing beds [60] [61] No county count; voucher list closed [210] [325] Economic stability Unemployment 3.4% (June 2026) [329] Unemployment 3.6% (June 2026) [330] Employment support No supported employment site named by the Department in north Alabama (February 2025) [335] Same [335] Health care access Health center with four sites; free clinic [337] [340] A free clinic [341] Education access 46.4% of adults with a bachelor's degree [15] 19.7% [15] Social and community context 2-1-1 answered locally; city bus system [13] [190] 2-1-1 answered from Birmingham; demand-response transit [13] [398]
235.section: The area against the five domains

236.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0237
236.text: Two counties, two homelessness systems. WellStone's clients in Cullman fall under a 37-county continuum with no county count and no supportive housing project in its inventory [312] [323].

237.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0238
237.text: Supportive housing fell by more than two-fifths in three years in the Huntsville continuum while the count of homeless people rose by almost a third [61] [60] [59].

238.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0239
238.text: The mental illness figures in the homelessness count cannot be trusted as a series [313].

239.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0240
239.text: None of the five centers the Department named in February 2025 as offering supported employment is in north Alabama [335].

240.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0241
240.text: The safety net stops at the county line. Health center sites and the 2-1-1 center are in Huntsville; Cullman's equivalents are a free clinic and a family resource center, and its 2-1-1 calls are answered in Birmingham [337] [13] [341] [353].

241.title: Scope · B0242
241.text: Who pays shapes who is served. This section sets out how residents of the two counties are covered, how Medicaid pays for mental health care here, what the move to the Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic model has changed, and where the commercial and hospital markets stand. The statewide report explains the rules; this section applies them.

242.title: The coverage picture · B0243
242.text: Madison County relies more on employer coverage than Cullman, where public programs cover a larger share. Census survey estimates for 2024 put 53.2% of Madison residents on employer plans, against 41.9% in Cullman; Medicaid covers 9.77% in Madison and 15.9% in Cullman, and Medicare 10.4% and 15% [354] [355]. Madison County is also home to 34,400 veterans [356]. The uninsured share was 7.72% in Madison and 10.9% in Cullman on those all-ages estimates, and 8.3% and 11.9% among people under 65 [354] [355] [356] [357].

243.title: The coverage picture · B0244
243.text: Administrative counts tell the same story from the other side. Alabama Medicaid counted 54,803 eligible people in Madison County and 15,922 in Cullman in April 2026, both down from a year earlier [358]. The agency reports that 18% of Madison's population was eligible at some point in FY2024, one of the five lowest shares in the state [58]. Medicare had 78,966 beneficiaries in Madison and 21,317 in Cullman in 2025; 9,547 and 4,141 of them were also eligible for Medicaid [359] [360]. The children's insurance program covered 12,741 children in Madison and 4,757 in Cullman in July 2026, up from 11,337 and 4,462 a year before [361] [362].

244.title: The coverage picture · B0245
244.text: One part of the picture changed sharply in 2026. After the enhanced marketplace tax credits expired at the end of 2025, about 95,000 Alabamians, some 23% of the state's enrollees, left the marketplace [363]. A hospital president in the Huntsville system had estimated beforehand that about 19,500 of those expected to lose coverage lived in the system's north Alabama territory [364]. The federal government publishes county-level marketplace plan selections for 2026, but the file could not be opened for this report, and no local estimate of the coverage gap in a state that has not expanded Medicaid could be found [365] [366].

245.title: How Medicaid pays for mental health here · B0246
245.text: Under Alabama Medicaid's rule a provider of rehabilitative mental health services must be certified by the Department as a 310-board community mental health center, which in these two counties means WellStone [367]. Care coordination for Medicaid recipients is organized by region; Madison and Cullman share the Northeast region with Jackson, Limestone, Marshall and Morgan [368].
245.section: How Medicaid pays for mental health here

246.title: How Medicaid pays for mental health here · B0247
246.text: Coverage of stays in psychiatric institutions has a hole for working-age adults; how Medicaid pays for stays in general-hospital psychiatric units was not read for this report. Medicaid's psychiatric facility rule covers inpatient psychiatric care for recipients under 21 [369]. For those aged 21 to 64, Alabama's federal waiver pays for stays in institutions for mental disease only in Baldwin and Mobile counties, and no north Alabama facility is covered [370]. Statewide, Medicaid spent $703 million on mental health in FY2025, 7% of its total; no breakdown of that spending by county was found in the agency's documents as read [58] [358].
246.section: How Medicaid pays for mental health here

247.title: The CCBHC transition · B0248
247.text: WellStone was one of the first two clinics in Alabama to enter the federal demonstration, certified by the state effective July 2024 [119] [42]. It had been preparing since 2022 on a federal implementation grant of $3,974,261, whose abstract set targets of 1,700 economically disadvantaged adults served in Madison County, 1,200 mobile crisis responses and 500 primary care screenings by September 2026 [39]. By June 2024 it said it had added primary care and an adult mobile crisis team [119].

248.title: The CCBHC transition · B0249
248.text: The payment works like this. For each day on which a Medicaid enrollee receives at least one qualifying service, the clinic is paid a single daily rate that covers everything delivered that day; each clinic's rate is rebuilt from its actual costs after its second demonstration year [371] [372]. WellStone's rate is not published.

249.title: The CCBHC transition · B0250
249.text: The model's central tension is written into the state's own manuals. A clinic must provide the full range of services to anyone who seeks care, regardless of ability to pay or place of residence [373] [374]. The provider manual says the daily rate "will not be paid for services provided to populations outside of those enrolled in Medicaid" [57]. In Madison County, where fewer than one resident in five was eligible for Medicaid at some point in FY2024 [58], and in a state without expansion, that leaves every adult who is not enrolled in Medicaid outside the new payment; how many of WellStone's clients that is could not be established from the documents read. WellStone states that no one is turned away for inability to pay, reports nearly $3.4 million in uncompensated care for FY2025, and names medication for adults with no payer as an unmet need [48] [1].

250.title: The CCBHC transition · B0251
250.text: What has the model produced? The Department's answer to legislators was two access measures: days to first evaluation down from 18 to under one, and days to first therapy from 33 to eight, over 2025 [50]. Its annual report counts 13,700 people served by WellStone as a clinic in FY2025 [64]. No other measured result was found. The demonstration requires 15 to 17 outcome measures, and no results for its first year, which ended in mid-2025, were found in any document read [42].

251.title: The CCBHC transition · B0252
251.text: The model is spreading around WellStone. Mountain Lakes, which serves Jackson and Marshall counties in the ring, received federal approval in October 2025, and the Department's board was told that five more centers would convert in 2026 [46] [115]. The centers for Morgan, Lawrence and Limestone and for the Shoals were not among the five clinics in the Department's directory as read for the statewide report, and are not among the six centers a September 2026 press report listed as receiving grants to pursue certification; one ring center, Northwest Alabama Mental Health Center, is on that list [375].

252.title: Commercial insurance and the hospital market · B0253
252.text: The commercial market has one dominant insurer and, since 2026, one dominant hospital system. Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Alabama held 82% of the commercial health insurance market in the Huntsville metropolitan area at the start of 2024, by the American Medical Association's measure [376]. On 31 March 2026 the Huntsville Hospital Health System completed its purchase of Crestwood Medical Center from a for-profit chain, which put Huntsville Hospital and Crestwood in one system [49]. A news report at the time recorded concerns about competition and cost and no action by a regulator [377].
252.section: Commercial insurance and the hospital market

253.title: Commercial insurance and the hospital market · B0254
253.text: The system's finances bear on mental health mainly through what it absorbs. Its audit puts uncompensated care at about $144.4 million for the year ended June 2025, down from $171.4 million the year before, a fall it attributes mainly to higher Medicaid access payments [125]. In December 2025 the system expected the figure to rise by $10 million to $15 million in 2026 if marketplace subsidies expired; no later figure was found [364]. The audit, as read, contains no figure for behavioral health revenue, cost or volume [125]. The system's chief executive said in April 2026 that over half its reimbursement comes from Medicare and Medicaid at below-cost rates [49].
253.section: Commercial insurance and the hospital market

254.title: Key actors · B0255
254.text: Actor Role Alabama Medicaid Agency Pays for rehabilitative services through certified centers; sets coordination regions [367] [368] Alabama Department of Mental Health Certifies clinics and issues the CCBHC billing manual [42] [371] WellStone The certified center for both counties and a CCBHC since July 2024; reports nearly $3.4 million a year in uncompensated care [367] [42] [48] Medicare; children's health insurance (ALL Kids and its Medicaid expansion group) Cover 100,283 beneficiaries (2025) and 17,498 children (July 2026) across the two counties [359] [360] [361] Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Alabama 82% of the Huntsville commercial market [376] Huntsville Hospital Health System Owner of Huntsville Hospital and, since 31 March 2026, Crestwood Medical Center [49] VA Outpatient mental health care for veterans at its Huntsville clinic [143]

255.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0256
255.text: The clinic model pays for Medicaid patients in a county with few of them. The duty to serve everyone and the rule that pays only for Medicaid enrollees meet in WellStone's uncompensated care line [57] [48].

256.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0257
256.text: Working-age adults on Medicaid have no covered psychiatric hospital in north Alabama under the state's waiver [370].

257.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0258
257.text: Coverage losses in 2026 are known for the state; the county file could not be read for this report [363] [365].

258.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0259
258.text: One insurer and one hospital system now face each other across the Huntsville market, and the system's audit, as read, gives no behavioral health revenue, cost or volume [376] [49] [125].

259.title: Gaps and opportunities · B0260
259.text: The payer mix of the public mental health center could not be read: its plan lists funding sources without amounts, and its audits could not be opened [1].

260.title: Scope · B0261
260.text: This section has no counterpart in the statewide report. It describes, in outline only, the thirteen counties beyond Madison and Cullman whose crises the state routes to Huntsville, and the four community mental health centers that serve them for everything else. It does not examine their courts, schools, hospitals or housing. Its purpose is to show what the crisis center's wider catchment looks like and how much of that catchment's use of the center is known.

261.title: Four centers · B0262
261.text: The Department assigns the thirteen ring counties to four centers: Mountain Lakes Behavioral Healthcare for Jackson and Marshall; the Mental Health Center of North Central Alabama for Lawrence, Limestone and Morgan; CED Mental Health Center for Cherokee, DeKalb and Etowah; and Northwest Alabama Mental Health Center for Fayette, Lamar, Marion, Walker and Winston [2]. Its FY2025 report counts 3,129 people served by Mountain Lakes, 2,694 by North Central, 2,558 by CED and 3,306 by Northwest, against WellStone's 11,659 [64]. The centers' own figures run higher: Northwest's plan reports 10,317 consumers in 2023, a count that includes substance use and disability services, and no source reconciles the two [378].

262.title: Four centers · B0263
262.text: Mountain Lakes is the only other Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic in the fifteen counties, approved in October 2025 [46]. It says it runs its own mobile crisis team in both of its counties around the clock, pairing a clinician with a peer specialist or case manager; its crisis page says the team may arrange inpatient admission and does not mention the Huntsville center [379].

263.title: Four centers · B0264
263.text: North Central Alabama, based in Decatur, says it treated over 3,525 people in 2023 with about 140 staff across sites in Decatur, Athens and Moulton [380] [381]. It broke ground in December 2024 on a 16-bed crisis residential unit in Decatur for people under commitment, due for completion in October 2025 [382]. In October 2026 it was advertising for nurses for the unit, and no source confirmed that it had opened [383] [384]. Its chief executive said at the groundbreaking that crisis residential facilities in the region had existed only in Huntsville, Cullman, Jasper and Anniston for a decade [382].

264.title: Four centers · B0265
264.text: CED has one office in each of its three northeastern counties. Its published crisis service is a 24-hour telephone line; the parts of its plan and website that were read name no mobile crisis team or crisis residential unit of its own, and its plan lists transportation as a continuing need [385] [386] [387].

265.title: Four centers · B0266
265.text: Northwest covers five counties: Fayette, Lamar, Marion, Walker and Winston. It runs mobile crisis in two of them, Marion and Winston, a 16-bed crisis residential unit for adults at Townley in Walker County that takes referrals statewide, and by contract a 24-bed behavioral unit at the Jasper hospital [378].

266.title: What the ring looks like · B0267
266.text: The ring is more rural, poorer and thinner in providers than the core. Six of the thirteen counties are classed as entirely rural [20]. Median household income runs from $49,488 in Fayette to $83,629 in Limestone, and the uninsured share of people under 65 from 8.4% in Limestone to 14.6% in DeKalb [6]. Residents per mental health provider range from 339 in Marshall to 4,774 in Winston [20]. Walker County's drug overdose death rate, 69.1 per 100,000, is the highest of the thirteen counties with a published rate and nearly twice Cullman's [20]. Every ring county carries a federal mental health shortage designation [52]. Appendix A gives the figures county by county.

267.title: What the ring looks like · B0268
267.text: The ring holds inpatient psychiatric beds. Decatur Morgan West has 64 beds, Mountain View Hospital in Gadsden 68, and hospitals in Boaz, Guntersville, Gadsden and Jasper list psychiatric services without bed counts [388] [389] [390] [391] [392] [393]. Several ring hospitals belong to or are affiliated with the Huntsville Hospital system, among them Athens-Limestone Hospital, Decatur Morgan Hospital, the Marshall Medical Centers, Highlands Medical Center and DeKalb Regional Medical Center [394].

268.title: How much the ring uses Huntsville · B0269
268.text: No source read for this report says where the crisis center's patients come from. The Department's report gives 1,879 served at the adult unit and 520 at the pediatric unit with no county of residence, and WellStone's plan gives a monthly total with none [64] [1]. The Department's crisis pages say nothing about distance or transport from the thirteen counties; the only ways in they describe are walking in and being brought by a first responder [7].
268.section: How much the ring uses Huntsville

269.title: How much the ring uses Huntsville · B0270
269.text: The state's evaluators offered the one piece of evidence there is, and it is indirect. Crisis centers, they reported in 2025, may serve fewer people from communities outside the metropolitan areas where they sit, and peer staff said they wished they saw more people from farther away [62]. They also recorded that people face transport barriers when they leave [62]. Taken with the ring centers' own mobile teams and residential units, this suggests that the ring's dependence on Huntsville is smaller than the catchment map implies, and that for the counties nearest the Birmingham and Tuscaloosa catchments the assignment may exist mostly on paper [3]. No number in the sources read for this report can confirm or refute that.
269.section: How much the ring uses Huntsville

270.title: Overlapping boundaries · B0271
270.text: The fifteen counties share a crisis center and little else. They are divided among six area agencies on aging, four homelessness continuums and three Medicaid care coordination regions [395] [311] [396]. The Department's Region I Community Services office is in Decatur and lists thirteen counties, not the same thirteen; its page does not say which division's regions these are [10]. For a planner this means that none of the regional bodies, data series or funding areas examined here has the catchment as its unit.

271.title: Cross-Domain Dependency Map · B0272
271.text: The statewide report draws a map of how its twelve parts depend on one another. The table below does the same for the region, using the same twelve nodes so that the two can be compared. The links are this report's reading of the evidence in the sections above; the evidence on each link is sourced there.

272.text: From To The link in this region Payers (12) Service continuum (3) The clinic payment covers Medicaid enrollees; WellStone must serve everyone [57] [374] Financing (2) Service continuum (3) Federal grants funded assisted outpatient treatment from 2022 and a clinic grant whose abstract committed WellStone to round-the-clock mobile crisis teams; their periods ended in 2026 [39] [37] Workforce (4) Service continuum (3); Children (9) A 24-bed pediatric unit opened able to staff six beds [56] Service continuum (3) Justice (10) The crisis beds were meant to divert people from jail; the state's evaluation publishes no per-center count of diversion [88] [62] Housing (11) Service continuum (3); Justice (10) Supportive housing beds fell from 334 in 2022 to 190 in 2025; WellStone names housing twice among its unmet needs [61] [1] Service continuum (3) Housing (11) The center asks for stabilization beds and supervised housing; a probate court official asked for more stabilization beds and a step into group homes [1] [51] Infrastructure (5) Equity (7) Cullman's transit ends at 2:30 p.m.; the crisis center is in Huntsville [192] Governance (1) Equity (7); the ring (13) The board is appointed by governments in two counties; its crisis center's catchment is fifteen [1] [3] Data (6) Every other node Access times are the only measured outcome found for the clinic and crisis services [50] [62] Children (9) Service continuum (3) The pediatric unit absorbed children once sent out of the county [69] Engagement (8) Governance (1); Equity (7) NAMI has a Madison County affiliate and lists none for Cullman [55]

273.title: Cross-Domain Dependency Map · B0274
273.text: Reading the map. Three links carry most of the weight. The first runs from payers to services: the new clinic model improved access to a first appointment and pays only for Medicaid patients, in Madison County, where 18% of residents were eligible for Medicaid at some point in FY2024 [50] [57] [58]. The second runs from housing to everything else: supportive housing has fallen and a court official put the wait for a group home at 100 days or more, and the likely result is that people stay longer in crisis beds, hospital beds and jail [61] [51]. The third runs from data to all the rest. Almost every judgment in this report about whether a program works rests on a launch date and a volume figure, because that is all the public record read for this report holds.

279.title: Could not be read · B0280
279.text: WellStone's website. About fifty of its pages, including those on its programs, locations, board, school-based services and psychiatry residency, refused the automated reader. Two pages and two press releases were read. WellStone's audits for fiscal years 2022 to 2025, and Form 990 filings after FY2021. The City of Huntsville's outside agency appropriations books, which hold the annual amount for WellStone. Cullman County Commission minutes and agendas, ten documents. The full report of United Way of Madison County's 2024 needs assessment, a file too large for the reader. State health department death tables for Madison and Cullman by race and sex. Huntsville City Schools' counseling and student support pages, which returned menus only. The 2025 strategic plans of Mountain Lakes and North Central Alabama, which are scanned images. Crisis Services of North Alabama's impact report and audit.

280.title: Needs checking by eye · B0281
280.text: The Department's FY2025 annual report, page 29. WellStone's clinic count is read as 13,700 on the page's layout; one reading attached 6,627, which belongs to the 988 table. The National Children's Advocacy Center's 2024 therapy figures and all of its 2025 figures, where numbers and captions could not be paired reliably. The state health department's shortage-area map for Madison and Cullman. The Department's 2026 Stepping Up map, to see whether either county is a current site. The 2025 federal housing inventory for the Huntsville continuum, for which of two columns holds chronic and which veteran beds. The number of participants in the United Way needs assessment, read as 1,000 once and 1,500 twice.

281.title: Could not be confirmed · B0282
281.text: How the three federal lawsuits over the 2013 deaths in the Madison County jail ended. Whether North Central Alabama's crisis residential unit in Decatur has opened. Whether WellStone's psychiatry residency has residents in training. Whether the peer living room, the veterans program and the mobile crisis targets in WellStone's 2022 federal grant were met. The capacity of the South Derrick Street camp, given as 84 spaces by the city and about 58 people by the press. The exact day North Alabama Regional Hospital closed in 2015. Whether Cullman County's mental health court still sits.

283.title: [1] WellStone Strategic Plan Fiscal Years 2026-2027
283.text: WellStone, Inc. (filed with the Alabama Department of Mental Health). WellStone's two-year strategic plan as submitted to its Board of Directors on 18 November 2025 and posted on the ADMH website in January 2026. It states how many people WellStone served in FY2025, names its three greatest unmet needs (housing, medication funding for adults with no third-party payer, nursing recruitment and retention) and sets a target that 75% of therapists be evidence-based certified by 30 September 2026. The reader found no mention of an electronic health record, telehealth, transportation or CARF/Joint Commission accreditation in it.

289.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. It is the second ADMH statement of the Huntsville center's 15 counties. No date shown to the reader.

290.title: [8] WellStone Emergency Services (provider directory entry)
290.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health (ADMH). ADMH's provider-directory entry for the Huntsville crisis center: services offered, address and the same 15 counties served. A third ADMH statement of the 15-county catchment.

291.title: [9] ADMH Maps
291.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health (ADMH). ADMH's index of map images: CMHC catchment areas, crisis centers (FY26), mental illness service regions, developmental disability service regions, mobile crisis teams, CCBHCs and others. The maps are images; the reader returned titles and file URLs only, so region membership could not be re-read from them today.

292.title: [10] Regional Offices
292.text: Alabama Department of Mental Health. ADMH's list of five 'Community Services' regional offices with address, phone and counties. Region I is in Decatur and lists 13 counties; Fayette, Lamar, Marion, Walker and Winston fall under Region II (Tuscaloosa). The page does not say which division the regions belong to. No date shown.

293.title: [11] NAMI AL CIT Division Strategic Plan 2024-2026
293.text: NAMI Alabama. NAMI Alabama's plan for statewide Crisis Intervention Team training. It names the Region 1 program as WES/Huntsville Police Department/NAMI Huntsville and lists the 18 counties in Region 1, which includes Madison and Cullman. It gives no count of officers trained.

294.title: [12] Public Health Districts roster
294.text: Alabama Department of Public Health. ADPH's list of public health districts with their counties and administrators. It places the 15 counties in three districts.

295.title: [13] Contact Local 2-1-1
295.text: 2-1-1 Connects Alabama (United Ways of Alabama). The state 2-1-1 network's list of regional call centers with the counties each serves. Madison County is answered by the Huntsville HELPline center; Cullman County by 2-1-1 Central Alabama in Birmingham.

296.title: [14] Alabama's 988 crisis lifeline supporters call for more funding amidst growing mental health needs
296.text: Alabama Reflector. Reflector report quoting WellStone's clinical director on 988 staffing. It names the Birmingham and Huntsville call centers but gives no county coverage.

297.title: [15] QuickFacts: Madison County, Alabama (V2025)
297.text: U.S. Census Bureau. Census QuickFacts profile for Madison County, vintage V2025. Gives population, growth since 2020, age, race and Hispanic origin, veterans, foreign-born, language, disability, insurance, income, poverty and density.

298.title: [16] QuickFacts: Cullman County, Alabama (V2025)
298.text: U.S. Census Bureau. Census QuickFacts profile for Cullman County, vintage V2025. Same rows as S01, allowing a side-by-side comparison of the two core counties.

299.title: [17] QuickFacts: Huntsville city, Alabama (V2025)
