751.title: Commercial insurance (employer coverage and Blue Cross)
751.text: employer plans · employer coverage · commercial market · commercial health insurance · Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Alabama · Blue Cross — Private health insurance, most often obtained through a job. Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Alabama held 82% of the Huntsville area's commercial market at the start of 2024.

752.title: Uninsured rate
752.text: uninsured rate · uninsured share · uninsured — The share of people with no health insurance. Two versions appear here: people under 65 (8.3% in Madison, 11.9% in Cullman) and all ages in 2024 (7.72% and 10.9%).

753.title: Medicaid eligibles (people eligible for Medicaid)
753.text: eligible for Medicaid · Medicaid enrollees · enrolled in Medicaid — Alabama Medicaid's count of people eligible for the program. A monthly count and the share eligible at any point in a year are different measures and give different percentages.

754.title: Eight domains
754.text: eight domains — The framework this report shares with the statewide report: eight domains of a mental health system, followed by four sections on systems outside the Department of Mental Health.

755.title: Inpatient psychiatric unit
755.text: inpatient psychiatric unit · inpatient psychiatric — A hospital unit where people are admitted for psychiatric care. Huntsville Hospital describes units for adults and seniors; Cullman County's hospital lists outpatient psychiatry only.

756.title: Nova Center for Youth & Family
756.text: Nova Center for Youth & Family · Nova Center — WellStone's service for children and adolescents in Huntsville, offering individual, group and family counseling. A similar name, NOVA-Huntsville, belongs to its psychosis program.

757.title: Withdrawal management (residential)
757.text: withdrawal management · residential withdrawal management · withdrawal management unit — Medically supervised withdrawal from alcohol or drugs in a staffed unit, often called detox. WellStone's River Crossing unit in Huntsville has 16 beds.

758.title: First-episode psychosis program (NOVA-Huntsville)
758.text: first episode of psychosis · first-episode psychosis · NOVA-Huntsville — Team-based early treatment for young people having a first psychotic episode. WellStone runs NOVA-Huntsville, one of Alabama's three such programs.

759.title: Mobile mental health clinic
759.text: mobile mental health clinic · mobile unit — A van WellStone announced in November 2025, to offer therapy and dispense psychiatric medication, starting at First Stop and the Downtown Rescue Mission.

760.title: Answer rate (988)
760.text: answer rate — The share of 988 calls from Alabama answered by a counselor in the state instead of rolling over to a national backup center.

761.title: HELPline (Crisis Services of North Alabama)
761.text: HELPline — A confidential 24-hour crisis counseling telephone line run by Crisis Services of North Alabama, separate from the 988 call center at WellStone.

762.title: Observation beds (temporary and extended)
762.text: observation beds · temporary observation beds · extended observation beds — Short-stay beds in a crisis center where a person is watched and treated for hours or a few days without being admitted to a hospital.

763.title: State psychiatric hospital
763.text: state hospital · state hospitals — A psychiatric hospital owned and run by the state. North Alabama's, in Decatur, closed in 2015, which left the state's remaining hospitals in Tuscaloosa.

764.title: Bryce Hospital
764.text: Bryce Hospital — The state's psychiatric hospital for adults, in Tuscaloosa. An adult from north Alabama who is committed to a state bed is sent there.

765.title: Decatur Morgan West
765.text: Decatur Morgan West · Decatur West · behavioral health hospital — A hospital campus in Decatur, Morgan County, licensed for 64 psychiatric beds and used mainly for children and adolescents. It lies outside Madison and Cullman counties.

766.title: Unity Psychiatric Care (Huntsville)
766.text: Unity Psychiatric Care — A 20-bed psychiatric hospital in Huntsville giving inpatient care to people aged 55 and older.

767.title: State Health Plan (psychiatric bed need rule)
767.text: state health plan · health planning rule · bed need · North Region — Alabama's planning rule for inpatient psychiatric beds. It decides by region when more beds may be added; Madison and Cullman fall in a ten-county North Region.

768.title: Crisis residential unit
768.text: crisis residential · crisis residential beds · crisis residential unit — A small staffed residence where a person in crisis can stay for a short period as an alternative to a hospital ward.

769.title: Bradford Health Services (Madison campus)
769.text: Bradford — A private addiction treatment provider whose campus in the city of Madison offers medical detox, residential treatment and medication-assisted treatment.

770.title: Medication-assisted treatment (MAT)
770.text: medication-assisted treatment — Treating opioid addiction with a prescribed medicine, such as buprenorphine or methadone, usually alongside counseling.

771.title: Heads Up (WellStone prevention program)
771.text: Heads Up — WellStone's prevention program, which has taught Mental Health First Aid to faculty and staff at the University of Alabama in Huntsville since 2023.

772.title: Mental Health First Aid
772.text: Mental Health First Aid — An eight-hour course that teaches members of the public to recognize and respond to someone developing a mental health problem or in crisis.

773.title: Our Place (drop-in center)
773.text: Our Place — The one drop-in center for people with mental illness that the Department of Mental Health lists in north Alabama, on Max Luther Drive in Huntsville.

774.title: Recovery Organization of Support Specialists (ROSS)
774.text: Recovery Organization of Support Specialists — A peer-run organization supporting recovery from substance use. The Department of Mental Health lists Huntsville among its locations and none in Cullman.

775.title: Peer living room
775.text: living room · peer living room — A walk-in space where peers offer support. WellStone's 2022 federal grant promised one serving 400 people; no source says whether it opened.

776.title: Follow-up after hospitalization
776.text: follow-up after hospitalization — A measure of continuity: the share of people who see a mental health provider soon after leaving a psychiatric hospital. No result for WellStone is published.

777.title: Time to services (access times)
777.text: time to services · access times — How long a new patient waits: days to an initial evaluation and days to a first therapy session. It is one of the measures a certified clinic must report.

778.title: Fox Army Health Center
778.text: Fox Army Health Center — The military clinic on Redstone Arsenal. Its behavioral health department serves service members, families, retirees and civilian employees on weekdays.

779.title: VA clinic and Vet Center (Huntsville)
779.text: VA · VA clinic · Vet Center — The federal Department of Veterans Affairs' own sites for veterans. Huntsville has an outpatient clinic and a Vet Center; no VA site is listed in Cullman County.

780.title: Mental health professional shortage area (HPSA)
780.text: mental health professional shortage area · shortage area · shortage designation · shortage designations · area designation · facility designation · federal designation · federal designations — A place, population or facility the federal government has designated as short of mental health providers. Cullman County has one; Madison County has no area designation.

781.title: Low-income population designation
781.text: low-income designation — A shortage designation for the low-income people of an area: too few providers serve Medicaid and sliding-fee patients for the size of that population.

782.title: Shortage score (HPSA score)
782.text: shortage score · score of 16 — A number attached to each federal shortage designation. Federal loan repayment for clinicians is tied to the score of the site where they work.

783.title: Provider ratio (residents per mental health provider)
783.text: provider ratio · residents per mental health provider · providers per 100,000 — The number of residents for each mental health provider of any kind. Published figures for Madison and Cullman differ by source and by who is counted.

784.title: Kids Count
784.text: Kids Count — A collection of indicators of child well-being for Alabama and each county, compiled by VOICES for Alabama's Children.

785.title: Federal provider registry (NPPES)
785.text: federal provider registry · provider registry — The national list of health care providers' identifier numbers, used to count mental health providers by county. It can include people no longer practicing.

786.title: Psychiatry residency
786.text: psychiatry residency · residency — The years of supervised training a doctor completes after medical school to become a psychiatrist. A four-year program in Huntsville takes up to six residents a year.

787.title: Psychiatric mental health nurse practitioner (PMHNP)
787.text: psychiatric mental health nurse practitioner · psychiatric nurse practitioner · nurse practitioner — An advanced practice nurse specializing in mental health care. The University of Alabama in Huntsville offers a training track requiring 720 clinical hours.

788.title: Federal loan repayment (National Health Service Corps)
788.text: loan repayment · Federal loan repayment — A federal program that repays clinicians' student loans in return for at least two years of work at an approved site in a shortage area.

789.title: Sliding fee scale
789.text: sliding-fee — A charge that falls with a patient's income, so that people with low incomes pay little or nothing.

790.title: Alabama Department of Public Health (ADPH)
790.text: Alabama Department of Public Health · state health department — The state public health agency, separate from the Department of Mental Health. It keeps the statistics on deaths, including suicides and overdoses.

791.title: Health information exchange (Alabama One Health Record)
791.text: Alabama One Health Record · health information exchange · electronic health record — Alabama's network for sharing patient records electronically between hospitals, clinics and other providers. Certified clinics must connect their record systems to it.

792.title: Telehealth
792.text: telehealth — Care delivered at a distance by video or telephone.

793.title: CCBHC provider manual (the state's clinic manual)
793.text: clinic manual — The Department of Mental Health's rulebook for Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics: what they must provide, how they are paid and how they must be run.

794.title: Community Free Clinic (Huntsville/Madison County)
794.text: Community Free Clinic — A free clinic in Huntsville for uninsured Madison County residents, with an on-site dispensary where prescriptions are filled. It lists no mental health service.

795.title: Opioid treatment program (OTP)
795.text: opioid treatment program · certified opioid treatment program · opioid treatment clinics — A clinic certified to dispense methadone, and often buprenorphine, for opioid use disorder. Huntsville has two and Cullman one.

796.title: Methadone and buprenorphine
796.text: methadone · buprenorphine — Two medicines prescribed to treat opioid addiction. They reduce craving and withdrawal and lower the risk of overdose.

797.title: Naloxone
797.text: naloxone — A medicine that reverses an opioid overdose within minutes, often given as a nasal spray.

798.title: Alabama Opioid Overdose and Addiction Council
798.text: opioid council — The state council that reports each year on opioid overdose and addiction in Alabama, including where naloxone has been distributed.

799.title: Huntsville Transit (Orbit buses and Access paratransit)
799.text: Huntsville Transit · Orbit · paratransit · paratransit service — The City of Huntsville's public transport: Orbit, the fixed-route bus, and Access, a booked service for riders who cannot use the standard bus.

800.title: TRAM (Transportation for Rural Areas of Madison County)
800.text: TRAM · Madison County's rural service — Madison County's rural public transport outside Huntsville: a weekday service on which a ride must be booked a day ahead.

801.title: CARTS (Cullman Area Rural Transportation System)
801.text: CARTS — Cullman County's only public transit: a county-run weekday service, 6:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m., on which a ride must be booked by 2:30 p.m. the day before.

802.title: Demand-response transit
802.text: demand-response · demand-response service — Public transport that runs on booked trips instead of a fixed route: the rider reserves a ride in advance.

803.title: Community mental health officer
803.text: community mental health officers — A sheriff's deputy appointed by the Madison County probate judge, with more than 80 hours of crisis training, to respond to people in a mental health crisis.

804.title: Authorized beds and licensed beds
804.text: authorized beds · licensed beds — Counts of the beds a hospital is permitted to operate. The hospital association's figures cover a whole hospital and do not show how many of its beds are psychiatric.

805.title: Certificate of need (state approval for hospital beds)
805.text: state approval — The state's permission for a hospital to build or add beds. Alabama's review board approved a $150 million tower at Huntsville Hospital in November 2024.

806.title: HEMSI (Huntsville Emergency Medical Services, Inc.)
806.text: ambulance service — Madison County's not-for-profit ambulance service, which reports more than 65,000 calls a year. Its home page publishes nothing on behavioral health transports.

807.title: CCBHC quality measures
807.text: outcome measures · clinic quality measures · quality measures — The results a Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic must report: five measures the clinic collects itself and twelve the state calculates.

808.title: CCBHC Quality Report
808.text: CCBHC Quality Report · quality manual · clinic quality report — An annual report on clinic and state quality measures that the Department of Mental Health's manual says it will produce. None had appeared by 4 October 2026.

809.title: Drug overdose death rate
809.text: drug overdose death rate · drug overdose death rates — Deaths from drug overdose for every 100,000 residents. Two sources give different figures for Cullman County, 35.6 and 26.4, for different periods.

810.title: Poor mental health days
810.text: poor mental health days — A County Health Rankings measure given as a number of days a month: 5.4 in Madison County and 5.7 in Cullman County in the March 2026 figures.

811.title: Serious emotional disturbance (SED)
811.text: serious emotional disturbance — The children's counterpart of serious mental illness: a diagnosable disorder in someone under 18 that seriously limits life at home, at school or with others.

812.title: Census tract
812.text: census tract — A small area within a county for which statistics are published. The federal PLACES estimates of local health go down to this level.

813.title: County coroner
813.text: coroner — The county official whose office investigates deaths. Local counts of suicides and overdoses come from coroners and reach the public mainly through news interviews.

814.title: Emergency department boarding
814.text: Emergency department boarding · boarding — Holding a psychiatric patient in an emergency room, sometimes for days, because no inpatient bed or placement is available.

815.title: Project Zero Suicide
815.text: Project Zero Suicide — A suicide prevention initiative that Cullman Regional Medical Center says it has joined. No results have been reported.

816.title: Frequent mental distress
816.text: frequent mental distress — A federal estimate of the share of a county's adults who report frequent mental distress: 18.9% in Cullman County and 16.0% in Madison County in 2023.

817.title: Disability waivers (Medicaid waivers for developmental disabilities)
817.text: disability waivers — Medicaid waivers for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities, run by the Department of Mental Health. The statewide waiting list stood at 1,800 people in May 2025.

818.title: Area agency on aging
818.text: area agencies on aging · aging agencies · aging agency — A regional body designated by the state to plan and run services for older people. Madison and Cullman counties fall under different ones.

819.title: Language access (limited English proficiency)
819.text: Language access · limited English — A health service's duty to offer interpreters and other language help to people who speak little English. Alabama's clinic manual places it on WellStone.

820.title: NAMI Madison County
820.text: NAMI Madison County · Connection groups — The local affiliate of the National Alliance on Mental Illness. It runs peer and family support groups and a course for families. No affiliate is listed for Cullman County.

821.title: Peer recovery center
821.text: peer-run recovery center · peer recovery center · peer center — A community center for people seeking recovery from addiction, staffed by peers who are in recovery themselves. The state lists one in Huntsville and none in Cullman County.

822.title: Lived experience
822.text: lived experience · lived-experience — Personal experience of a mental or substance use disorder, one's own or a family member's. Alabama's clinic manual requires such people to have a part in governing a certified clinic.

823.title: The Link of Cullman County
823.text: The Link of Cullman County · The Link's — A Cullman nonprofit that works against poverty. It runs a food pantry, won a 2020 federal grant for a reentry program for people leaving jail or prison, and is an accredited family resource center.

824.title: System of care (children's mental health framework)
824.text: system of care — A national framework holding that services for children with serious mental health needs should be family-driven, community-based and coordinated across agencies.

825.title: School-based mental health services (School-Based Mental Health Collaboration)
825.text: school-based mental health collaboration · school-based services · School-based care · The Enrichment Center — Therapy and other mental health care delivered on school grounds. In Madison County the providers include WellStone and a nonprofit, The Enrichment Center.

826.title: Department of Human Resources (DHR)
826.text: Department of Human Resources · Departments of Human Resources · child welfare agency — Alabama's child welfare agency, responsible for child protection and foster care, with a county office in each of Madison and Cullman counties.

827.title: Mental health services coordinator
827.text: mental health services coordinator — A school-district employee who links students and families to mental health services but does not provide treatment. State law requires every district to have one.

828.title: Brooks' Place (Cullman's child advocacy center)
828.text: Brooks' Place — Cullman County's child advocacy center. It provides forensic interviews, counseling and medical exams at no cost to families and says it is funded entirely by local donations.

829.title: Forensic interview
829.text: forensic interviews — An interview, by a specialist at a child advocacy center, of a child who may have been abused or may have witnessed a crime or violent incident.

830.title: Foster care (out-of-home care)
830.text: foster care — The placement of a child, by the child welfare agency, away from the family home: with relatives, with foster parents or in a facility.

831.title: Children with an indication of abuse or neglect
831.text: indication of abuse or neglect · indicated abuse or neglect — A Kids Count measure: the number of children in a county with an indication of abuse or neglect in a year, also given as a rate per 1,000.

832.title: Alternative Court (Madison County's juvenile specialty courts)
832.text: Alternative Court · truancy court — Madison County's juvenile mental health docket, one of three specialty courts in its juvenile court alongside a drug court and a truancy court.

833.title: Neaves-Davis Center for Children
833.text: Neaves-Davis Center · Neaves-Davis — Madison County's 48-bed juvenile detention center in Huntsville, which holds young people detained by court order.

834.title: Juvenile detention
834.text: juvenile detention — Secure custody for young people held by court order while they await a hearing. Madison County's center has 48 beds; Cullman County has a short-term facility of its own.

835.title: Alabama Department of Youth Services (DYS)
835.text: youth services department · youth services agency · diversion grant — The state's juvenile justice agency. It holds young people committed by juvenile courts and funds local diversion programs, including grants in Madison and Cullman counties.

836.title: Home visiting
836.text: home visits — Programs that send a trained visitor to the homes of pregnant women and families with young children to support parenting and health.

837.title: Infant and early childhood mental health
837.text: infant and early childhood mental health — Support for the emotional development of children from birth to about five, delivered mainly through the adults who care for them.

838.title: PATHS (the state's telephone consultation service for pediatricians)
838.text: telephone consultation service — A statewide line through which children's doctors can consult child mental health specialists at Children's of Alabama. Families do not call it directly.

839.title: Consent age for school counseling (Act 2025-455)
839.text: parent's written consent — A 2025 Alabama law raised from 14 to 16 the age below which a student needs a parent's written permission for ongoing school counseling.

840.title: Sequential Intercept Model
840.text: Sequential Intercept Model · intercepts · intercept — A map of the six points, numbered 0 to 5, at which a person with mental illness can be turned from the criminal justice system toward treatment.

841.title: Office of Alternative Sentencing and Release (Madison County)
841.text: Office of Alternative Sentencing and Release · alternative sentencing office · alternative sentencing · Mental Health Pre-Trial Release Program · pretrial release — The Madison County department that runs pretrial release, community corrections, misdemeanor probation, court referral and the adult drug court for the county's courts.

842.title: Competency to stand trial
842.text: Competency to stand trial — A defendant's ability to understand the proceedings and help in their own defense. A person found incompetent cannot be tried until competency is restored.

843.title: Competency restoration
843.text: competency restoration · Jail-based restoration — Treatment meant to make a defendant who was found incompetent able to stand trial. It is given at the state forensic hospital or, in seven Alabama counties, inside the jail.

844.title: Taylor Hardin Secure Medical Facility (the state's forensic hospital)
844.text: forensic hospital — Alabama's forensic psychiatric hospital, in Tuscaloosa, which treats defendants sent by the criminal courts. In August 2025, 273 men were waiting for a bed.

845.title: Second Chance Act grant
845.text: Second Chance Act — A federal grant source for programs that help people returning from jail or prison. A $500,000 grant went to The Link of Cullman County in 2020.

846.title: Reentry
846.text: reentry — The return of a person from prison or jail to the community, and the services that support it. It is Intercept 4 of the Sequential Intercept Model.

847.title: Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles (the parole bureau)
847.text: parole bureau — The state agency that supervises people on probation and parole. It runs a day reporting center in Huntsville.

848.title: Day reporting center
848.text: day reporting centers — A facility where people on probation or parole who are judged high-risk report for supervision and treatment while living at home. One of Alabama's five is in Huntsville.

849.title: Community corrections
849.text: community corrections — Locally run programs that supervise people convicted of crimes in the community as an alternative to prison. Madison County's is a public authority; Cullman County's is a nonprofit.

850.title: Probation, parole and community supervision
850.text: probation · community supervision · probationers · parolees — Probation is supervision in the community in place of prison; parole is supervised release after part of a prison sentence. Both carry conditions and can be revoked.

851.title: Healthy People 2030
851.text: Healthy People 2030 — The federal government's set of national health goals for the decade to 2030. This report uses its five-domain grouping of the social conditions that shape health.

852.title: North Alabama Coalition for the Homeless (the Huntsville continuum)
852.text: North Alabama Coalition for the Homeless · three-county continuum — The homelessness continuum of care for Madison, Limestone and Morgan counties. Federal counts and housing inventories for the Huntsville continuum cover all three.

853.title: Alabama Balance of State continuum
853.text: Alabama Balance of State · Balance of State — The homelessness continuum of care that covers 37 Alabama counties, Cullman among them, from Montgomery. It publishes no county-level count.

854.title: Point-in-time count (the homelessness count)
854.text: January 2025 count · homelessness count — A count of everyone found homeless, in shelters and outdoors, on a single night in January. Each homelessness continuum conducts one and the federal housing department publishes it.

855.title: Housing inventory count
855.text: housing inventory · housing inventories — The federal housing department's yearly list of the beds a homelessness continuum has, by type: emergency shelter, transitional housing, permanent supportive housing and rapid re-housing.

856.title: Chronic homelessness
856.text: chronically homeless — A subgroup reported in the federal homelessness count. The Huntsville continuum's January 2025 count listed 128 chronically homeless people.

857.title: Shelter Plus Care (WellStone)
857.text: Shelter Plus Care — WellStone's permanent supportive housing project, with 24 beds in the 2025 federal housing inventory for the Huntsville continuum.

858.title: Huntsville Housing Authority
858.text: Huntsville Housing Authority — The public housing agency for Huntsville, with more than 1,500 rental units and close to 1,800 voucher families. It holds most of the area's permanent supportive housing beds.

859.title: Housing voucher (Housing Choice Voucher, Section 8)
859.text: voucher — Housing assistance, also called Section 8, administered by local housing authorities. Cullman's waiting list is closed; Huntsville's authority assists close to 1,800 families.

860.title: Coordinated entry
860.text: coordinated entry — A homelessness continuum's shared entry process for people seeking help. In the Huntsville continuum it is held in person at the Downtown Rescue Mission.

861.title: South Derrick Street Camp
861.text: South Derrick Street · sanctioned camp — A camp for unsheltered people in Huntsville that the city manages. It was rebuilt after a 2024 fire with marked spaces and a perimeter fence.

862.title: Fair market rent
862.text: fair market rent — A benchmark rent for an area. The report cites the hourly wage needed to afford a two-bedroom home at that rent: $25.19 in the Huntsville area and $17.94 in Cullman County.

863.title: SNAP
863.text: SNAP — The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, the federal food benefit once called food stamps.

864.title: Supplemental Security Income (SSI)
864.text: Supplemental Security Income · SSI — A federal payment for disabled people with very low income, run by the Social Security Administration. It is separate from the disability insurance earned through past work.

865.title: Individual Placement and Support (supported employment)
865.text: Individual Placement and Support · supported employment — The evidence-based model of supported employment for people with serious mental illness: help finding an ordinary paid job, then lasting support in it.

866.title: Vocational rehabilitation
866.text: vocational rehabilitation — The state program that helps people with disabilities prepare for and find work, run by the Alabama Department of Rehabilitation Services.

867.title: Federally designated health center (federally qualified health center)
867.text: federally designated health center · HAPPI Health · health center sites — A federally funded community clinic that provides primary care to anyone, with fees scaled to income. HAPPI Health has four sites, all in Huntsville.

868.title: Family resource center
868.text: family resource center — An organization accredited within the Alabama Network of Family Resource Centers. The Link of Cullman County became the state's 28th in September 2026.

869.title: Mental Health Center of North Central Alabama
869.text: Mental Health Center of North Central Alabama · North Central Alabama · North Central — The community mental health center for Lawrence, Limestone and Morgan counties, based in Decatur. One of the four centers that serve the ring.

870.title: CED Mental Health Center
870.text: CED Mental Health Center · CED — The community mental health center for Cherokee, DeKalb and Etowah counties in northeast Alabama. One of the four centers that serve the ring.

871.title: Northwest Alabama Mental Health Center
871.text: Northwest Alabama Mental Health Center · Northwest — The community mental health center for Fayette, Lamar, Marion, Walker and Winston counties. It runs its own mobile crisis service and crisis residential beds.

872.title: Census QuickFacts
872.text: Census QuickFacts · QuickFacts — The Census Bureau's summary profile of population, income, insurance and other figures for a county or city. Appendix A takes population, income and uninsured rates from it.

873.title: Crisis system
873.text: crisis system — The services for a mental health emergency: a line to call, a team that comes, and a place to go that is neither an emergency room nor a jail.

874.title: American Community Survey (ACS)
874.text: American Community Survey — The Census Bureau's continuous household survey. Its five-year estimates are the only survey figures published for areas as small as a census tract.

875.title: Margin of error
875.text: margin of error · margins of error — The range around a survey estimate within which the true value probably lies. For a small area such as a census tract it is often wide.

876.title: CDC PLACES
876.text: PLACES — A federal dataset of modeled health estimates for counties, cities and census tracts. Its tract values are produced by a model, not by surveying each tract.

877.title: Open items
877.text: Open Items · open items — The list of things this report could not read, confirm or find, each with where it was looked for and what would settle it.

878.title: Claims ledger
878.text: claims ledger — The record behind the report: every claim it makes, the passage that supports it, and whether it is verified, the report's own analysis, or a statement that something was not found.

879.title: CCBHCs and prospective payment
879.text:
A certified clinic must serve everyone who comes and is paid its daily rate only for people enrolled in Medicaid; WellStone has been such a clinic since July 2024. What it is 
 Alabama Medicaid  is a fee-for-service program, which means it pays by the item  [397] . A payer of this kind publishes a price for each billable service and pays that price each time the service is delivered  [397] . Work that has no billing code earns nothing, so outreach, coordination and follow-up tend to go unpaid  [397] . 
 The  Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic , or CCBHC, is a federal clinic model that pairs a list of duties with a different way of being paid  [397] . A certified clinic must provide nine kinds of service, among them round-the-clock crisis response, outpatient mental health and substance use treatment, primary-care screening, targeted case management, peer and family support and services for veterans  [397] . It must serve anyone who seeks help "regardless of their place of residence, ability to pay, or age"  [374] . It may deliver some services through partner organizations, but it must itself provide 51% or more of the service encounters  [373] . 
 The payment is the other half. A clinic's rate is "prospective", meaning fixed ahead of time from the clinic's expected costs and not billed item by item afterwards  [397] . Each clinic's rate is built from a cost report of the total cost of running the clinic, so it can carry work that fee schedules do not pay for, such as care coordination  [397] . Alabama uses the daily version: a clinic receives a single payment for each day on which at least one qualifying service is provided to a Medicaid enrollee  [371] . The rate is rebuilt from actual costs and visits after the clinic's second demonstration year and every three years after that  [372] . 
 One limit is written into the state's own manual. The  daily rate  "will not be paid for services provided to populations outside of those  enrolled in Medicaid "  [57] . 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw two layers, one above the other. The upper layer is headed  who must be served . It is a wide box labeled  anyone who seeks care, regardless of residence, ability to pay or age   [374] . Inside it sits a smaller box labeled  people enrolled in Medicaid , with the note  Madison County: 18% of residents eligible at some point in  FY2024   [58] . 
 The lower layer is headed  what is paid . An arrow drops from the smaller box to a box that reads  a day with at least one qualifying service: one daily payment at the clinic's own rate   [371] . A second arrow drops from the rest of the wide box to a box that reads  no daily rate   [57] , and from there to  other money, or  uncompensated care : nearly $3.4 million at  WellStone  in FY2025, by its own account   [48] . To one side, a small loop shows  cost report, then daily rate, then rate rebuilt from actual costs after the second demonstration year   [372] . 
 How it works in north Alabama 
 WellStone began preparing in 2022 on a four-year federal implementation grant  [118] . The award record shows $3,974,261 paid in four installments and a project period that ended on 29 September 2026  [39] . The grant's abstract set targets of 1,700 economically disadvantaged adults served in Madison County, 1,200  mobile crisis  responses and 500 primary care screenings  [39] . By June 2024 WellStone said it had added primary care and an adult mobile crisis team  [119] . 
 Certification followed. WellStone announced in June 2024 that it and a Mobile center were the first two Alabama clinics in the federal Medicaid demonstration  [119] , and the Department's board minutes record that both were certified by the state effective July 2024  [42] . The Department's directory lists two WellStone sites offering the full range of clinic services, one in Huntsville and one in Cullman  [5] . 
 The measured results so far are about access. The Department told legislators in January 2026 that WellStone's wait for an  initial evaluation  fell from 18 days in January 2025 to less than one day in December, and the wait for a first therapy session from 33 days to eight  [50] . These are two points in time for one clinic, not divided by county or age  [50] . The Department's annual report counts 13,700 people served by WellStone as a certified clinic in FY2025  [64] . The federal demonstration specifies 15 to 17  outcome measures , and no result for WellStone was found in any document read  [42] . 
 The  uninsured  are where the model's two halves pull apart. Alabama Medicaid reports that 18% of Madison County's population was eligible at some point in FY2024, one of the five lowest shares in the state  [58] . Among people under 65, 8.3% in Madison County and 11.9% in Cullman have no health insurance  [6] . WellStone states that no one is turned away for inability to pay and reports nearly $3.4 million in uncompensated care for FY2025  [48] . Its  strategic plan  names "funding for medications for our adult clients with no third-party reimbursement" as an unmet need  [1] . How many of its clients fall outside Medicaid could not be established from the documents read for the report. 
 Other centers are moving to the model.  Mountain Lakes , which serves Jackson and Marshall counties in  the ring , received federal approval in October 2025  [46] , and its two sites are the only other certified clinic sites the Department's directory lists in the fifteen counties  [5] . The Department's board was told in November 2025 that five more centers would become certified clinics in 2026  [115] . A September 2026 press report listed six centers receiving grants to pursue certification;  Northwest Alabama Mental Health Center  is on that list, and the centers for Morgan, Lawrence and Limestone counties and for the Shoals are not  [375] . The Department says the process of becoming a certified clinic can take from six to eighteen months  [46] . 
 How this report uses it 
 Section 12 explains the payment and states the tension between the duty to serve everyone and a rate paid for Medicaid enrollees. The dependency map in Part IV carries the same point as a link from payers to the service continuum. Domain 2 asks what follows the federal grant, and reports that no document read says whether the Medicaid clinic payment, local budgets or nothing at all will pick up the costs the grant carried.  
 Domain 6 looks ahead to what the model's rules require clinics to report. As a certified clinic WellStone must report five measures it collects itself, among them  time to services  and depression remission at six months  [173] . The Department's  quality manual  says it "will also develop an annual CCBHC Quality Report"  [173] , and the report found none published by 4 October 2026. 
 A few cautions help with the numbers. WellStone's rate is not published; the re-base memorandum names no clinic and no rate  [372] . The Department's 13,700 for WellStone as a clinic sits beside 11,659 for it as a  community mental health center  in the same annual report  [64] , and WellStone's own plan says "over 12,000"  [1] . A grant to pursue certification is an award. It does not make a center a certified clinic.

880.title: Civil commitment and assisted outpatient treatment
880.text:
A probate judge decides whether a person can be ordered into treatment; Madison County has built an outpatient program around that power, and neither county's court publishes how often it is used. What it is 
 Civil commitment  is treatment ordered by a court for a person who has not agreed to it, outside the criminal process  [397] . In Alabama the court is the  probate court  of the county where the person is, the same county court that handles wills and estates  [397] . Any person may file the petition  [397] . 
 A judge may order inpatient treatment only on clear and convincing evidence, a standard of proof that sits between the ordinary civil standard and the criminal one  [397] . The evidence must show that the person has a mental illness, poses a real and present threat of substantial harm to self or others, will keep deteriorating without treatment and cannot make a rational decision about it  [397] . An initial order runs for up to 150 days  [397] . 
 The judge must also choose the least restrictive alternative that is necessary and available  [397] . One alternative is  outpatient commitment , an order to follow a treatment plan while living in the community, which a judge may make only where a designated facility has consented to provide the treatment  [397] . Assisted outpatient treatment is the name of Madison County's version: a court-ordered program for people with severe mental illness who can live safely in the community with treatment and have had trouble staying in it voluntarily  [30] . 
 State law changed in 2022, when  House Bill 70  added a ground on which an officer can take a person to a mental health facility to be seen by a physician, namely being unable to meet medical and physical needs  [36] . It also allowed courts to mandate outpatient care after release, and it took effect that July  [36] . The Madison County probate judge helped draft the bill  [81] . 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw a path from left to right. Three arrows enter the first box, labeled "walk-in at the probate office", "emergency room visit" and "911 call"  [51] . Box 1 reads "Petition filed in the probate court of the county where the person is"  [196] . Box 2 reads "Judge orders the sheriff to serve notice; guardian ad litem appointed"  [196] . Box 3 reads "Held on an intent to commit; hearing at about day three or four; by then at  Huntsville Hospital  or  WellStone "  [51] . After Box 3 the path splits. The upper branch ends at "Inpatient commitment, up to 150 days"  [51] . The lower branch ends at "Assisted outpatient treatment: case manager and therapist, reporting every 30 days for up to 150 days"  [79] . A dashed arrow runs from the upper box to the lower one, labeled "moved to outpatient status once stabilized"  [80] . Under the inpatient box add a note, "state bed for adults:  Bryce Hospital , Tuscaloosa"  [198] . Along the foot of the picture write "No annual count published by the court was found in either county"  [79]   [77] . 
 How it works in north Alabama 
 Madison County's court publishes its instructions: a petition is filed in the county where the patient is, the judge orders the sheriff to serve notice of the hearing, and a guardian ad litem is appointed to protect the patient's rights  [196] . In 2020 the probate judge appointed sheriff's deputies with more than 80 hours of crisis training as  community mental health officers   [197] . As the judge described the process in May 2025, a person held on an intent to commit has a hearing at about the third or fourth day and by then is at Huntsville Hospital or WellStone  [51] . Inpatient commitment lasts up to 150 days and can be renewed to 300, which the judge called very rare because of bed availability  [51] . 
 State law has the probate judge order "one or more persons or law enforcement officers" to take the person to the  Department of Mental Health  or a designated facility  [194] . The region once had a  state hospital  of its own:  North Alabama Regional Hospital  in Decatur had 74 beds when the state announced its closure in January 2015  [24] . With that closure, all remaining state hospitals were in Tuscaloosa  [123] . No document read says how often a committed person from Madison or Cullman County is taken there or what the trip costs  [194] . In May 2025 the court's director of mental health programs put the wait for a  group home  at 100 days or more  [51] . WellStone's current plan lists crisis stabilization for adults under civil commitment as a priority for expansion  [1] . 
 The outpatient program began as a local arrangement: the court announced it for 3 February 2020, in partnership with WellStone and paid for from the passport application fees the court collects  [30] . A person enters only after a commitment petition, an assessment, a physician's confirmation that outpatient care is appropriate, a written treatment plan and a hearing  [30] . In 2023 a press account said the $35 passport fee paid for two case managers, one for the patient and one for the family  [80] . 
 A four-year federal award to WellStone, with a project period from 31 July 2022 to 30 July 2026, brought $3,099,656 and named the probate court and Huntsville Hospital as partners  [37] . Its targets were 275 people enrolled and a 75% decrease in participants needing inpatient care or incarceration  [37] . No results against those targets were found  [37] . Whether the program continues at the same scale now that the grant period is over is not established  [37] . 
 How much demand the court faces is known only from press reports  [79] . The probate judge said in February 2020 that over 300 people had been committed the previous year  [79] . A January 2023 report gave 309 petitions in 2019 and 414 in 2021  [80] . A May 2025 television report said involuntary commitments peaked at 589 in 2023 and named no source  [51] . Petitions and commitments are different counts, so these figures are not one series  [51] . One account said about 63 people had been through the program and about 10% had returned to the court, against nearly 50% of people committed in the traditional way  [81] . Another gave repeat cases as 86 of 414 petitions in 2021 against 142 of 309 in 2019  [80] . No independent evaluation was found  [81] . 
 Cullman County's court puts far less on the public record: its page lists commitments among its case types and publishes no procedure, forms or counts  [77] . In late 2023 the sheriff told the state's  opioid settlement  commission that the county no longer had facilities to take people who need mental evaluations  [78] . 
 How this report uses it 
 Domain 1 describes the two courts and the outpatient program, Domains 3 and 5 follow committed people to beds and to transport, Section 10 places the probate court at  Intercept  2, and Domain 6 lists commitment counts among the things not published.  
 Read each figure with its unit. The 309 and the 414 are petitions and the 589 is given as commitments, all for Madison County and all from press reports  [80]   [51] . The return rates were given to reporters, and the 2023 article does not define what counts as a return  [80] . The grant's 275 and 75% are targets written into an application, so they describe an intention  [37] . 
 One report lists the three ways a commitment can start, and no public source gives how many start each way or how long people wait at each stage  [51] . When the state spent opioid settlement money on civil commitment and  crisis residential beds , none of those beds was in Madison or Cullman  [45] .

881.title: Counting homelessness and housing
881.text:
Federal homelessness figures are collected by continuum of care, so the Huntsville numbers describe three counties together and Cullman County has no count of its own. What it is 
 A  Continuum of Care  is a regional body, recognized by the federal housing department, that plans the local response to homelessness  [397] . Despite the name it is an organization and not a range of services, and it should not be confused with the continuum of mental health care described in Domain 3  [397] . Each continuum coordinates housing and services for homeless people in its area, runs the point-in-time count and sets priorities for federal Continuum of Care grants  [397] . Alabama has nine, which together cover the state  [397] . 
 The point-in-time count is a count of everyone found homeless, in shelters and outside, on a single night in January  [397] . The federal report of each count sorts people by where they were that night (emergency shelter, transitional housing or unsheltered) and adds lines for subgroups, such as people recorded as severely mentally ill or as  chronically homeless   [60] . It is a snapshot  [397] . People who are homeless at other times of year, or who are staying with friends, are not in it, and the result depends on the weather and on how many volunteers search  [397] . 
 The  housing inventory  is the companion document: a list of the beds in the continuum, with a summary table and a project-by-project list  [61] . It groups year-round beds as emergency shelter, transitional housing,  permanent supportive housing  and rapid re-housing  [61] . Permanent supportive housing is the housing agencies' term for an ordinary home paired with visiting support services, when it is aimed at people leaving homelessness  [397] . 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw two boxes side by side. The left box is labeled  Huntsville continuum: Madison, Limestone and Morgan counties   [311] . The right box is labeled  Balance of State  continuum: 37 counties, Cullman among them   [312] . Between the boxes write  one  mental health center ,  WellStone , for Madison and Cullman counties   [2] . In the left box draw two short lines over the years 2022 to 2025. The first, rising, is  people counted: 549, 646, 621, 718   [59]   [313]   [314]   [60] . The second, falling, is  permanent supportive housing beds: 334, 154, 153, 190   [61] . In the right box put a single figure,  636 people in 37 counties, January 2026 , and beside it an empty outline of Cullman County labeled  no county count published   [210] . 
 How it works in north Alabama 
 WellStone's two counties belong to different homelessness systems  [311]   [312] . Madison County is one of three counties, with Limestone and Morgan, in the continuum run by the  North Alabama Coalition for the Homeless , numbered AL-503  [311] . Cullman County is one of 37 in the Alabama Balance of State continuum, coordinated from Montgomery  [312] . Federal counts, inventories and grants follow those lines, so each Huntsville figure below covers three counties  [311] . The fifteen counties of the  crisis catchment  are split among four continuums  [311] . 
 The federal reports give 549 people in the Huntsville continuum in 2022, 646 in 2023, 621 in 2024 and 718 in 2025  [59]   [313]   [314]   [60] . The 2022 count was taken on 22 February; the other three were taken in late January  [59]   [313]   [314]   [60] . Of the 718 people counted in January 2025, 416 were in emergency shelter, 37 in transitional housing and 265 unsheltered  [60] . The inventory for the same month lists 421 year-round emergency shelter beds  [61] . No 2026 count had been published by the federal department or the coalition by October 2026  [315] . 
 The inventory tells the other half of the story. Permanent supportive housing stood at 334 beds in 2022, 154 in 2023, 153 in 2024 and 190 in 2025  [61] . In 2022, 268 of the 334 beds were in a veterans'  voucher  project  [316] . The 2025 inventory names two projects: the  Huntsville Housing Authority 's, with 166 beds, and WellStone's  Shelter Plus Care , with 24  [61] . That January the count found 128 chronically homeless people  [60] . The inventory lists beds; the rows read for this edition do not say how many were free  [61] . Federal continuum grants for  FY2024  came to $945,663, the largest of them $615,231 to the housing authority for supportive housing  [317] . 
 The subgroup lines are less steady than the totals. The number recorded as severely mentally ill was 71 in 2022, 24 in 2023, 40 in 2024 and 49 in 2025  [313]   [60] . In 2023 none of the people recorded as severely mentally ill was listed as unsheltered  [313] . The chronically homeless line ran 118, 218, 71 and 128 over the four reports, and the line for chronic substance use fell from 117 to 41  [59]   [60] . The report reads the 2023 figure as saying more about how the count was taken than about who was outside  [313] . 
 For Cullman County there is no count  [210] . The Balance of State continuum reported 636 people across its 37 counties on 27 January 2026, 72.3% of them unsheltered, with no county breakdown  [210] . The only project with Cullman in its name in the 2025 federal inventory for that continuum is a 21-bed domestic violence shelter  [323] . Emergency shelter in the county depends on the weather: the city's warming center may open when the forecast is 28 degrees or below  [324] . 
 How this report uses it 
 Section 11 gives most of its length to housing, and the same figures reappear in the summary in Part I, in the dependency map and in Domain 6's table of what is not published. From them the report computes that supportive housing in the Huntsville continuum fell by more than two-fifths in three years while the count of homeless people rose by almost a third  [61]   [60]   [59] . 
 Three cautions apply when reading those figures. The first is geography: a Huntsville figure is a three-county figure, and no count for Madison County alone or for Cullman County was found  [311]   [210] . The second is the nature of a one-night count, which the statewide report describes as better for rough scale than for year-to-year change  [397] . The third is the reading of the tables. In the 2025 inventory the supportive housing row shows 24 beds in one subgroup column and 166 in the next, and readings disagreed on which column holds beds for chronically homeless people and which holds veterans' beds  [61] . The year-round totals agreed on every reading  [61] . The table is on the list of items that need a check by eye, and the  open items  add a second question: whether the housing authority's 166-bed project is the veterans' voucher program that held 268 beds in 2022  [61]   [316] . 
 The report also declines to treat the mental illness line of the count as a series  [313] . For Cullman County it can say only that no county count was found  [210] .

882.title: The crisis system
882.text:
Someone to contact, someone to respond and a safe place for help all now exist in Huntsville, and no published count shows how many people they have kept out of a jail or an emergency room. What it is 
 Federal guidance describes a  crisis system  as three essential elements: someone to contact, someone to respond, and a safe place for help  [397] . The first is a phone line, and since July 2022 the national number for it has been  988   [397] . The second is a  mobile crisis team , clinicians who travel to a person in crisis at home or elsewhere in the community  [397] . The third is a  crisis center , a walk-in place open at all hours where a person can be assessed and stabilized instead of going to an emergency room or a jail  [397] . 
 The parts depend on each other. A call line with nowhere to send people, or a center nobody is brought to, does little  [397] . A Huntsville business paper, writing in 2022 while the local center was being built, named the two places where a person in crisis might otherwise end up: "The local hospital emergency room or jail"  [33] . 
 Steering a person away from those two places and into care is called  diversion   [397] . It is hard to count, because counting a diversion requires a judgment about what would have happened to the person otherwise  [397] . 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw three boxes in a row. The first is labeled  Someone to contact: the 988 call center at  WellStone , one of four in Alabama   [4] . The second is labeled  Someone to respond  and holds three smaller boxes:  adult mobile crisis teams, Cullman and Huntsville   [31]   [119] ,  child and adolescent mobile crisis teams, both counties   [120] , and  police co-responders , Huntsville   [63] . The third is labeled  A safe place for help:  WellStone Emergency Services  and  WellStone Pediatric Crisis Care , one address in Huntsville, serving fifteen counties   [3] . 
 An arrow from the first box to the second reads  a Cullman caller is connected to a local crisis team , and an arrow from the second to the third reads  the team can take the person to Huntsville   [41] . Two arrows enter the third box from outside the row:  walk-in  and  brought by law enforcement, first responders or ambulance crews   [3] . Below the row, two boxes with dashed outlines are labeled  emergency room  and  jail , under the heading  what the crisis beds are meant to divert people from   [88] . The line joining them to the third box carries the label  diversions: no count published for Huntsville   [62] . 
 How it works in north Alabama 
 Someone to contact.  One of Alabama's four in-state 988 call centers is at WellStone  [4] . The Department's  FY2025  table gives it 6,627 of the 35,118 recorded for the four centers, without saying whether the unit is calls or people  [64] . The Department's board was told in November 2025 that the state  answer rate  had been above 90% since July, and no rate is published for Huntsville alone  [115] . State  opioid settlement money  has gone to the line as well: the Department gave WellStone $660,000 of a $3,000,000  appropriation  to expand staffing and hours at the north Alabama call center  [45] .  Crisis Services of North Alabama  runs a separate 24-hour  HELPline   [116] . 
 Someone to respond.  Mobile crisis began in Cullman, where a state-funded adult team was announced as a pilot in June 2020  [31] . A team member said in September 2022 that it had intervened in more than 150 crises in the county that summer  [117] . Huntsville's adult team came later, with a federal grant awarded in 2022  [118]   [119] . WellStone's child and adolescent teams cover both counties and served 498 young people in FY2025  [120]   [64] . In Huntsville the City Council voted on 13 May 2021 to support a plan for two master's-level clinicians to work alongside crisis-trained police officers, and two were riding with officers by February 2022  [34]   [63] . 
 A safe place for help.  The state named WellStone one of its first three crisis center awardees on 28 October 2020  [32] . A temporary center opened in May 2021  [33] . The permanent building, WellStone Emergency Services, had its ribbon cut on 19 September 2022 and was built for up to 15  temporary observation beds  and up to 24 extended observation beds, starting with 16  [38]   [88] . At the temporary site the center had averaged 45 to 50 people a month  [88] . By September 2024 the adult unit was admitting 175 a month, and WellStone's plan of November 2025 says "over 150"  [121]   [1] . The Department counts 1,879 people served there in FY2025, a figure that covers all fifteen counties of the  catchment   [64] . 
 The pediatric unit opened next door in late September 2024 with 24 beds for ages 12 to 18  [43] . A month later a staffing shortage meant it could treat six patients at a time  [56] . The Department counts 520 served in FY2025  [64] . WellStone, for its part, reported 400 individuals served in the unit's first year and said it had begun taking children as young as eight  [69] . 
 Cullman County has the first two parts and not the third. WellStone said in 2024 that Cullman callers to 988 reach the Huntsville center, and its chief operating officer told a town hall in October 2024 that it has crisis response teams in Cullman and no local crisis facility  [41]   [169] . 
 How this report uses it 
 Domain 3 takes the three parts in order. Domain 2 follows the money and Domain 5 the buildings and the transport to them. Section 10 meets the same services again as  Intercept  0, the point before any arrest, and Section 13 asks how much the thirteen  ring counties  use a center that stands in Huntsville.  
 What the report can show is that the parts exist and are used. What it cannot show is diversion. WellStone's chief executive said in 2022 that the main purpose of the crisis beds "is to divert individuals from our jails and our emergency departments"  [88] . The state  evaluation office 's 2025 report gives no admissions, lengths of stay, law enforcement drop-offs or diversion figures for Huntsville  [62] . It found the centers' monthly reports inconsistent and noted that one center, not named in the passages read, has always reported zero for jail avoidance  [62] . The police co-responder program is in the same position: the City's 2022 account gives no call or outcome counts  [63] . 
 The savings claimed locally come without their workings. The chief executive said in March 2024 that the jail diversion program was saving about $300,000 of taxpayer money a year "the last time we measured", and no method, year or count accompanies the statement  [112] . The only published inputs date from 2018, when the program had moved 20 people out of the jail and the cost of holding an inmate with mental illness was put at $70 a day  [27] . 
 Two habits help when reading the figures. A count of people served or admitted shows that the door was open; it carries no county of residence, so it says nothing about where people came from  [64] . And the fifteen-county list is an assignment  [3] . The state's evaluators reported that crisis centers may serve fewer people from communities outside the metropolitan areas where they sit  [62] .

883.title: The eight domains
883.text:
The report asks of Madison and Cullman counties the same questions the statewide report asks of Alabama, in eight domains and four cross-sector sections, and adds one section of its own on the ring. What it is 
 The statewide  Alabama Mental Health Systems Report  describes a mental health system by the jobs it has to do. Its list of jobs follows the World Health Organization's six building blocks, a description of what any health system needs: service delivery, a health workforce, health information systems, access to essential medicines, financing, and leadership and governance  [397] . To those six it adds two domains of its own, on equity and on community engagement  [397] . Four further sections cover systems outside the  Department of Mental Health , which are children, justice, social determinants and payers  [397] . 
 The statewide report called itself a baseline for "a planned North Alabama regional edition built on the same template"  [397] . This report is that edition. It keeps the  eight domains  and the four sections and narrows the view to two counties. 
 In this region one organization holds several roles at once.  WellStone  is the  community mental health center  for both counties  [2] . It runs the  crisis center  that the Department assigns to fifteen counties  [3] , and one of Alabama's four in-state  988  call centers is at WellStone  [4] . A report organized around that one provider would leave out much of what the domains bring in, such as a city council that voted to fund  police co-responders   [63]  or a Cullman hospital whose  needs assessment  ranks mental health first  [83] . 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw three columns of boxes inside one frame. The left column of six holds the World Health Organization's building blocks  [397] . The middle column of eight holds Domain 1 to Domain 8. Six arrows cross to it: leadership and governance to Domain 1, financing to Domain 2, service delivery to Domain 3, health workforce to Domain 4, access to essential medicines to Domain 5, which the report widens to technology and infrastructure, and health information systems to Domain 6  [397] . Domain 7, on equity, and Domain 8, on community engagement, receive no arrow and carry the label  added by the statewide report   [397] . On the right, four boxes hold Section 9 (children, youth and families), Section 10 (justice), Section 11 (housing and social determinants) and Section 12 (payers), under the heading  systems beyond the Department   [397] . 
 Label the frame around all twelve boxes  the core : Madison and Cullman counties, 527,525 residents   [6] . Outside the frame, draw a band labeled  Section 13,  the ring : thirteen counties, four other centers, 792,981 residents   [2]   [6] . One arrow runs from the band to Domain 3 and is labeled  crisis center only , because the fifteen-county list applies to  WellStone Emergency Services  and the  pediatric unit   [3] . 
 How it works in north Alabama 
 Each part keeps its statewide name and puts its question to local institutions. The table gives the question and one thing the report found.  
 
 
 
 Part 
 What it asks here 
 One finding 
 
 
 
 
 Domain 1. Governance 
 Who decides locally, and to whom each body answers 
 WellStone's board has eighteen members, appointed by four local governments in the two counties  [1] 
 
 
 Domain 2. Financing 
 What money reaches the two counties, and how much of it a resident could trace 
 The last  Form 990  data on the public record for WellStone are for the year ending September 2021  [66] 
 
 
 Domain 3. Service continuum 
 What exists at each step from prevention to recovery supports 
 The wait for an  initial evaluation  at WellStone fell from 18 days in January 2025 to less than one day in December  [50] 
 
 
 Domain 4. Workforce 
 Whether there are enough trained people 
 A month after it opened, the 24-bed pediatric unit could treat six patients at a time  [56] 
 
 
 Domain 5. Medicines, technology and infrastructure 
 Buildings, record systems, medicines and transport 
 Cullman County's rural transit runs Monday to Friday, from 6:30 in the morning to 2:30 in the afternoon  [193] 
 
 
 Domain 6. Information and data 
 What is measured, by whom, and what is missing 
 The Department's  FY2025  counts for WellStone are not split by county  [64] 
 
 
 Domain 7. Equity 
 Whether the system reaches people evenly 
 The  suicide rate  is 20.7 per 100,000 in Cullman County and 15.3 in Madison  [52] 
 
 
 Domain 8. Community engagement 
 Who speaks for mental health, and who has a formal voice 
 NAMI Alabama  lists eleven affiliates, one in Madison County and none in Cullman  [55] 
 
 
 Section 9. Children, youth and families 
 What is known about each door a child's care passes through 
 In 2024, 2,294 Madison County children and 444 Cullman children with  serious emotional disturbance  received mental health services  [148]   [149] 
 
 
 Section 10. Justice 
 What happens at each of six points between crisis and  community supervision 
 The state's 2025 evaluation publishes no count of jail or emergency room avoidance for any single crisis center  [62] 
 
 
 Section 11. Housing and social determinants 
 How housing, income and other conditions of daily life differ between the counties 
 Permanent supportive housing  in the  Huntsville continuum  went from 334 beds in 2022 to 190 in 2025  [61] 
 
 
 Section 12. Payers 
 How residents are covered and how care is paid for 
 18% of Madison County's population was  eligible for Medicaid  at some point in FY2024  [58] 
 
 
 Section 13. The ring 
 What the crisis center's wider  catchment  looks like, in outline 
 The thirteen ring counties are assigned to four other community mental health centers  [2] 
 
 
 
 Following one service through the report shows the design. In Domain 2 the pediatric crisis unit is a $9 million building, credited by WellStone to the Legislature, the Department and campaign donors without the share of each  [91] . In Domain 3 it is a service that opened in late September 2024 with 24 beds, where the Department counts 520 people served in FY2025  [43]   [64] . Domain 4 treats it as evidence of a staffing shortage  [56] . Domain 6 sets the Department's 520 beside WellStone's own figure of 400 individuals in the unit's first year  [64]   [69] . Section 9 places it among children's services as a crisis unit that can hold a patient for up to 14 days  [167] . 
 Putting each question to two counties also turns every domain into a comparison.  County Health Rankings  counts 17.1% of Madison County's population as rural and 75.6% of Cullman's  [20] . 
 How this report uses it 
 The domains work as an index of questions: who holds a decision is a matter for Domain 1, and whether a number exists is one for Domain 6. Each domain and section closes with "Gaps and opportunities". Those bullets are the report's own reading of the evidence, marked as analysis, and should be quoted that way.  
 The dependency map in Part IV uses the same twelve parts as the statewide map. One of its links runs from payers to services: the state requires a  certified clinic  to serve anyone who seeks care and pays the clinic's  daily rate  only for people enrolled in Medicaid  [374]   [57] . 
 Two cautions apply to the frame at this scale. The figures in Parts II and III mostly describe the core, with standing exceptions: counts for the crisis center cover all fifteen counties of its catchment  [64] , and the homelessness counts in Section 11 cover the three counties of the Huntsville continuum  [311] . And a tool built for comparing counties can miss what is happening inside one. The federal shortage measure gives Madison County no  area designation , which makes it the only Alabama county without one  [52] , and that is the county where, a month after it opened, the pediatric unit could staff six of its 24 beds  [56] .

884.title: How local mental health is funded
884.text:
The public system in Madison and Cullman counties is paid for by state appropriations, Medicaid, federal grants, local governments, settlement money and gifts, and only some of those streams can be read to the dollar. What it is 
 No single budget pays for public mental health care in the two counties:  WellStone 's plan lists its sources as federal and state funds, local government  appropriations ,  Medicaid , commercial insurance, private pay, and other grants and contracts, and gives no amounts  [1] . 
 Each kind of money behaves differently. An appropriation is a legislature's permission to spend a set amount in a given year, and because appropriations are made a year at a time, a program funded once has no claim on the next year's budget  [397] . Medicaid is public health insurance for low-income people, paid for jointly by the federal government and the state, and it pays only for people who are enrolled  [397] . A federal grant pays for a named project over a stated period, and the federal government publishes each award  [96] .  Opioid settlement funds  come from legal settlements with companies that made and distributed opioid painkillers, and nothing they pay for recurs unless it is later written into a regular budget  [397] . 
 One more distinction runs through Domain 2: capital money builds a building once, and operating money pays staff every year. The state's  evaluation office  shows the shift for WellStone's  crisis center : capital was 74.5% of its spending in  FY2021 , and by FY2024 operations and administration were 87.3%  [62] . 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw WellStone as a box in the middle and six arrows pointing into it. Give an arrow a solid line where an amount can be read and a dashed line where it cannot. Arrow 1, solid: "State appropriations through the  Department of Mental Health : $7,000,000 a year for each crisis center, by the evaluation office's account"  [62] . Arrow 2, dashed: "Medicaid: a daily clinic rate for enrollees; WellStone's rate is not published"  [57] . Arrow 3, solid: "Federal grants: three awards, $9,575,938, fiscal years 2021 to 2025"  [96] . Arrow 4, part solid and part dashed: "Local governments: Huntsville allotted $900,000 for FY2026; most other amounts not found"  [98] . Arrow 5, solid: "Opioid settlement: $750,000 from Huntsville in 2023; $660,000 from the state for the  988  call center"  [40]   [45] . Arrow 6, dashed: " Capital campaign : close to $550,000 raised when the crisis center opened; no later total"  [88] . Under the box write "Revenue by source last published for FY2021"  [95] . 
 How it works in north Alabama 
 State money.   Act 310  provides for public corporations, of which WellStone is one, to contract with the Department of Mental Health in operating mental health programs  [21]   [1] . The crisis center also began with a state decision: on 28 October 2020 the Department named WellStone one of the first three crisis center awardees, funded from an $18 million appropriation in the FY2021 General Fund budget  [32] . The evaluation office says the state funds each of its six centers at $7,000,000 a year  [62] . The enacted FY2027 budget carries $36,000,000 for the "Existing Six Crisis Diversion Centers" and has no line naming WellStone or Huntsville  [93] . That would be $6,000,000 apiece if divided evenly, and neither document reconciles the two figures  [62] . 
 Buildings.  The permanent crisis center cost a reported $10 million: $3 million from the state, $2 million from the Madison County Commission and the cities of Huntsville and Madison together, and about $5 million left to a capital campaign called Be the Rock  [87] . The campaign had raised close to $550,000 when the doors opened  [88] . Its page publishes no goal, no total and no donor list  [89] . The  pediatric unit  cost $9 million, which WellStone credits to the Legislature, the Department and campaign donors without giving shares  [91] . 
 Medicaid.  Since July 2024 WellStone has been a  Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic   [42] . For each day on which a Medicaid enrollee receives a qualifying service, the clinic is paid a  single daily rate   [371] . The rate is not paid for people outside Medicaid, and WellStone's own rate is not published  [57] . Statewide, Medicaid spent $703 million on mental health in FY2025, and no breakdown by county was found in the agency's documents as read  [58] . 
 Federal grants.  The federal grants database shows three awards to WellStone between fiscal years 2021 and 2025, totaling $9,575,938  [96] . A two-year  community mental health center  grant awarded in 2021 at $4,288,700 was later reduced to $2,502,021  [97] . A four-year grant to implement the clinic model, with a project period ending 29 September 2026, brought $3,974,261  [39] . The third award, $3,099,656 over a project period ending 30 July 2026, paid for  assisted outpatient treatment   [37] . 
 Local governments.  Huntsville's FY2026 budget allotted WellStone $900,000, from which the council moved $36,000 to another agency  [98] . The city's FY2025 and FY2027 releases name no amount for WellStone  [99]   [74] . The City of Madison had a $45,000 appropriation for FY2024 on a council agenda in October 2023  [68] . Madison County's pandemic recovery plan lists a $1,000,000 grant to WellStone  [92] . In Cullman, the city's FY2027 budget authorizes a community service contract with WellStone and the amount was not reported  [100] . The press account of the county's FY2027 budget mentions no appropriation to WellStone or for mental health  [101] . 
 Settlement money.  Huntsville's first allocations, in 2023, gave $850,000 to the  Huntsville Hospital  Foundation, $810,000 to  First Stop  and $750,000 to WellStone  [40] . Madison County is using settlement funds for a mental health nurse in its jail  [75] . Cullman County gave a one-time $250,000 to the Good Samaritan Health Clinic and $150,000 over three years to the district attorney's  drug court   [105]   [106] . From a $3,000,000 state settlement appropriation, the Department gave WellStone $660,000 to expand staffing and hours at the 988 call center  [45] . WellStone was not among the grantees in the third round of state settlement grants  [108] . 
 WellStone's own filings.  The most recent year with  Form 990  data on the public record ended in September 2021, with revenue of $25,940,539 and expenses of $20,991,369  [66] . For fiscal years 2022 through 2025 the database lists single audits and no Form 990 data, and the audits could not be opened  [66] . WellStone's FY2021 annual report is the only place found where it breaks revenue down by source: $9,882,565 from state government, $8,654,700 from patient fees, $2,639,254 from local government and $1,026,303 from the federal government  [95] . It reports nearly $3.4 million in  uncompensated care  for fiscal year 2025  [48] . 
 How this report uses it 
 Domain 2 does the accounting and Section 12 explains the clinic payment. The gaps at the end of Domain 2 follow from one observation: capital was raised in public, and operating support sits in budget lines that are hard to find.  
 Three cautions apply when reading the amounts. FY2021 included local capital contributions to the crisis center, so its local government figure may not describe a normal year  [95] . The City of Madison's $45,000 comes from an agenda packet, and the vote itself was not read  [68] . The report's own benchmark, about $49 of WellStone revenue for each resident of the two counties, sets a 2021 figure over a 2025 population and is an order of magnitude only  [66] . 
 The grants raise a question the report cannot answer. On their stated periods the awards for the clinic model and for outpatient commitment ended in September and July 2026  [39]   [37] . The record for the outpatient award leaves open whether that program continues at the same scale  [37] .

885.title: How this report was made
885.text:
Facts were recorded with their supporting passages before any prose was written, and every block of the report was then read back against those passages by checkers that did not write it. What it is 
 This report was researched and written with Claude, an AI model, on 4 October 2026, working only from public sources: agency pages and documents, budgets, court records, organizations' own published reports and data, and local press where no primary document could be opened. The method has three steps, and each leaves a record a reader can inspect.  
 The first step is research. The scope file lists 199 web search queries, run before and during two sweeps of research, and the pages they led to were read through an automated page reader. Each statement of fact was recorded as a finding: a claim together with the passage from the source that supports it. The publisher's own document was used wherever it could be read, and the press only where no primary document was reachable. In all, 1,375 findings were recorded and 759 were used.  
 The second step is writing. Prose was written only after the findings were recorded, and the bracketed numbers in the text lead to the sources behind them. Values are shown as published, and anything the report computed is labeled as its own. Figures recalled from memory or estimated were excluded. Sentences marked as analysis are the report's own reading of the evidence.  
 The third step is checking. Every block of the report was read against the source passages attached to it by independent checkers that did not write it. There was a first check of all 283 blocks, a second check of the blocks changed after the first, a third check of the blocks changed after the second, and a final consistency pass against the list of  open items .  
 The method follows the statewide companion, which was checked claim by claim against its sources on 3 October 2026  [397] . That report supplies the frame used here and the checked county data behind the maps and Appendix A  [397] . 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw five boxes in a row joined by arrows:  public source ,  finding (claim and passage) ,  sentence with a bracketed number ,  check (three rounds and a consistency pass) ,  claims ledger . Under the last box hang four smaller boxes for the kinds of entry:  verified, 978 ;  the report's own analysis, 234 ;  not found, 180 ;  about the report itself, 105 . From the first box draw a side arrow labeled  would not open , and from the check box one labeled  could not be settled . Both lead to a box labeled  open items, 129 , divided into four groups:  could not be read, 20 ;  needs a human eye, 13 ;  could not be confirmed, 17 ;  not published, as far as this review found, 79 .  
 How it works in north Alabama 
 The record of the checking is the claims ledger. It breaks the 283 blocks into 1,497 entries, and each entry is one of four kinds. A verified entry, of which there are 978, is a statement matched to a passage in a cited source. An analysis entry (234) is the report's own reading of the evidence, including its arithmetic. A not-found entry (180) says that something was looked for and not located in the sources read. The remaining 105 are statements about the report itself, such as what a section covers.
