 The checks changed the text. The verification record counts 215 problems found and fixed in the first check, 41 in the second, 5 in the third, 11 in the consistency pass and 9 in a second consistency pass made after the glossary and primers were written.  
 What could not be settled went to the open items, which Appendix C prints in short form. There are 129, in four groups. Twenty are sources that could not be read, such as  WellStone 's audits for  fiscal years  2022 to 2025. Eleven need a human eye; tables the reader returned inconsistently are listed there. Seventeen could not be confirmed, among them whether Cullman County's  mental health court  still sits. The largest group, 79, is headed "Not published, as far as this review found." Each item says what is missing, why it matters, where the review looked and how the item could be closed.  
 The wording of that last heading is deliberate. Domain 6 says of its own table that each row "records what could not be located as of 4 October 2026" and that "no row is a claim that the number does not exist." Pages the reader could not open were recorded and never worked around, and archive or mirror copies of blocked pages were not used. Across the two sweeps 390 page reads failed, most of them refused by a site's request limit or its robots rule.  
 The limits follow from that. About fifty pages of WellStone's website refused the reader, so much of what the report says about WellStone's programs rests on the  Department of Mental Health 's documents and on press reports. WellStone's audits for fiscal years 2022 to 2025 could not be opened. The reader returns extracts, so quoted passages are its rendering of a document and a few tables need checking by eye.  
 County figures were not fetched afresh; they come from the checked county table assembled for the statewide report  [52] . The tract values on the regional map were retrieved separately on 4 October 2026 from the Census Bureau and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and they are not used in the report's text  [406]   [407] . 
 The report is a draft for review. It has not been approved by  Little Orange Fish , whose review it awaits, and it has not been peer reviewed. It is independent of WellStone and of every other organization it describes: none of them supplied material, saw the text or endorsed it. It was prepared for Little Orange Fish, which its statewide report names as the backbone organization for the  North Alabama Mental Health Coalition   [397] . The coalition is described only from public web pages, and none of its meeting records were used as sources. 
 How this report uses it 
 Every bracketed number leads to an entry on the References page, which gives the publisher, the date, a summary of what the source establishes and a note on whether it was read in full or in part. Of the 405 references cited when the checks were run, 336 were read in full and 68 in part; 92 are press reports. Where an organization is the only source for a statement about itself, the reference says so.  
 Three habits help when reading with the method in mind. A verified sentence matches the passage recorded for it, which is a narrower thing than the source being right. A sentence marked as analysis is the report's reading and can be argued with. And a statement that something was not found is dated 4 October 2026 and limited to what was read, so the Open Items page is the place to see what a browser, a phone call or the next review might still turn up.  
 The report invites the organizations it describes to correct it, and its figures are dated so that a later edition can show what changed.

886.title: Medicaid and the coverage gap
886.text:
Alabama has not expanded Medicaid, so many low-income adults cannot enroll, and a clinic that is paid its daily rate only for Medicaid enrollees must still serve everyone who comes. What it is 
 Medicaid  is the public health insurance program for low-income people, run by each state within federal rules and paid for jointly by the federal government and the state  [397] . The Affordable Care Act let states extend Medicaid to adults with incomes up to 138 percent of the federal poverty level, and Alabama is one of ten states that have not done so  [397] . Its income limit for parents is about 18 percent of the poverty level, and adults without children or a disability are not eligible at any income  [397] . 
 The other route to coverage for people without a job-based plan is the health insurance  marketplace , where individuals buy private plans with tax credits that lower the premium  [397] . Those subsidies start at the poverty line  [397] . An adult whose income is above the state's Medicaid limit and below the poverty line therefore falls between the two programs, and that space is called the  coverage gap   [397] . 
 About half of the people Alabama Medicaid enrolls are children  [397] . The agency says more than 50 percent of the state's children are covered, and about 25 percent of all residents at some point in a year  [58] . Children in families with somewhat higher incomes are covered by a separate  children's insurance program   [361] . 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw two horizontal bars of equal length, one for each county, each standing for all residents in 2024. On the Madison bar mark off " employer plans , 53.2%", "Medicaid, 9.77%", "Medicare, 10.4%" and " uninsured , 7.72%", and leave the remainder as "other coverage"  [354] . On the Cullman bar mark off "employer plans, 41.9%", "Medicaid, 15.9%", "Medicare, 15%" and "uninsured, 10.9%"  [355] . Above each bar draw a wide bracket spanning the whole bar, labeled "the  certified clinic  must serve everyone"  [374] . Below each bar draw a narrow bracket under the Medicaid segment only, labeled "the  daily rate  is paid only here"  [57] . The space between the two brackets is the point of the picture. 
 How it works in north Alabama 
 Who is covered.  Madison County relies more on employer coverage than Cullman, where public programs cover a larger share: Census survey estimates for 2024 put 53.2% of Madison residents on employer plans against 41.9% in Cullman, and Medicaid at 9.77% in Madison and 15.9% in Cullman  [354]   [355] . The uninsured share on those all-ages estimates was 7.72% in Madison and 10.9% in Cullman  [354]   [355] . Among people under 65 it was 8.3% and 11.9%  [356]   [357] . 
 In April 2026 the Medicaid agency counted 54,803 eligible people in Madison County and 15,922 in Cullman, both down from a year earlier  [358] . It also reports that 18% of Madison's population was eligible at some point in  FY2024 , one of the five lowest shares in the state  [58] . That slide prints only the highest and lowest counties, so Cullman's share is not given  [58] . The children's insurance program covered 12,741 children in Madison and 4,757 in Cullman in July 2026  [361] . 
 No local estimate of the coverage gap could be found: the two statewide studies read give no county figures  [366] . 
 What it means for the clinic.  Under Medicaid's rule a provider of  rehabilitative mental health services  must be certified by the  Department of Mental Health  as a  community mental health center , which in these two counties means  WellStone   [367] . Since July 2024 WellStone has also been a Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic  [42] . A clinic of that kind must serve anyone who seeks help, regardless of place of residence, ability to pay or age  [374] . For each day on which a Medicaid enrollee receives a qualifying service, it is paid a single daily rate  [371] . The state's manual says the rate "will not be paid for services provided to populations outside of those  enrolled in Medicaid "  [57] . WellStone publishes its funding sources as a list of categories with no payer mix, so how many of its clients are outside Medicaid could not be established  [1] . 
 Uncompensated care .  WellStone states that no one is turned away for inability to pay and reports nearly $3.4 million in uncompensated care for fiscal year 2025  [48] . Its plan names funding for medications for adult clients "with no third-party reimbursement" as one of three unmet needs  [1] . Hospitals carry such costs on a larger scale: the  Huntsville Hospital  system's audit puts uncompensated care at about $144.4 million for the year ended June 2025, down from $171.4 million, a fall it attributes mainly to higher Medicaid access payments  [125] . 
 Hospital stays.  Medicaid's psychiatric facility rule covers  inpatient psychiatric  care for recipients under 21  [369] . For enrollees aged 21 to 64, Alabama's  federal waiver  pays for stays in institutions for mental disease only in Baldwin and Mobile counties, and no north Alabama facility is covered  [370] . 
 Marketplace and commercial coverage.  After the enhanced marketplace tax credits expired at the end of 2025, about 95,000 Alabamians, some 23% of the state's enrollees, left the marketplace  [363] . A hospital president in the Huntsville system had estimated beforehand that about 19,500 of those expected to lose coverage lived in the system's north Alabama territory  [364] . The federal county-level file for 2026 could not be opened  [365] . In the commercial market, Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Alabama held 82% of the Huntsville metropolitan area at the start of 2024  [376] . 
 How this report uses it 
 Section 12 sets out the coverage picture and the clinic payment. The seventh finding in Part I states the tension in two sentences, and the dependency map makes the link from payers to services the first of the three it says carry most weight. Domain 2 reports the uncompensated care and Domain 5 the medication need.  
 Three Medicaid figures for Madison County measure different things, and the reader should keep them apart. The 9.77% is a survey estimate of people covered in 2024  [354] . The 54,803 is the agency's count of eligibles in one month  [358] . The 18% counts anyone eligible at some point during the fiscal year, which is higher than a single month's count  [58] . That 18% has nothing to do with the 18 percent of the poverty level that is Alabama's income limit for parents  [397] . The children's program should not be added to the agency's county count, because neither table says whether the two overlap  [361] . 
 What the report cannot show is the size of the gap locally. No county estimate of the coverage gap was found  [366] . The 2026 marketplace losses are known for the state, and the 19,500 is a hospital executive's estimate made before the subsidies expired  [363]   [364] . The Huntsville system's audit, as read, contains no figure for behavioral health revenue, cost or volume  [125] .

887.title: Reading the numbers
887.text:
Before comparing two figures in this report, check what each one counts, who published it, which period it covers and how many events lie behind it. What it is 
 An indicator is a number that stands in for something that cannot be seen directly, and it is only as good as the choices packed inside it: who was counted, out of whom, over which months, and by whom  [397] . Two figures can be compared only when those choices match. In a regional report they often do not, because the figures come from a state agency, a provider, a hospital, a national project and the local press, each with its own habits. 
 Four checks cover most cases. The first is the unit: a person served, an admission, an evaluation and a court petition are different things. The second is the source: an organization's own round figure, an official table and a press report may each count differently. The third is scale: a rate answers how common something is, where a count answers how many, and a rate built on few events will swing from year to year  [397] . The fourth is the period: Alabama's  fiscal year  runs from 1 October to 30 September, so FY2025 means October 2024 to September 2025, and other figures use calendar years  [397] . 
 The regional map adds a fifth matter, which is how an estimate for a small area was made. Its tract layers come from two federal sources: sample estimates from the Census Bureau, published with  margins of error , and model-based estimates from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention  [406]   [407] . 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw four cards in a row under the heading  People  WellStone  served, fiscal year 2025 . Card 1 reads  11,659:  Department of Mental Health , table of  community mental health centers ; adult  mobile crisis  included   [64] . Card 2 reads  13,700: Department of Mental Health, table of certified clinics   [64] . Card 3 reads  over 12,000: WellStone's  strategic plan   [1] . Card 4 reads  more than 13,500: press account, May 2026   [48] . Under each card put the same four blanks to fill in:  unit ,  source ,  period ,  checked by eye . On cards 1 and 2 the first blank is filled with  column heading not captured , and an arrow from card 2 points to a note:  one reading attached 6,627, the  988  call center figure, to this row   [64] . 
 How it works in north Alabama 
 Start with the unit. One person admitted twice in a year is one person and two admissions. WellStone's plan says its  crisis center  has "over 150 admissions per month," and the Department's FY2025 table gives 1,879 for the adult center  [1]   [64] . The Department's report gives a count for each provider in its tables and crisis-center evaluations in its narrative, and the  pediatric unit 's 520 has been read both as people served and as evaluations  [64] .  Commitment  figures for Madison County show the same problem: over 300 people committed in 2019 by the  probate judge 's account, 309 petitions in 2019 and 414 in 2021 in one press report, and a peak of 589 involuntary commitments in 2023 in another  [79]   [80]   [51] . Those are people, petitions and commitments, and the report does not read them as one series. 
 Next, ask who produced the figure. For fiscal year 2025 there are four figures for the people WellStone served. The Department's annual report gives 11,659 in its table of community mental health centers, with a footnote saying adult mobile crisis services are included, and 13,700 in its table of  Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics   [64] . WellStone's own plan says "over 12,000" and a May 2026 press account says "more than 13,500"  [1]   [48] . The column headings of the Department's tables were not captured, so the unit of its two figures is unconfirmed  [64] . None of these sources divides its count between the two counties  [64]   [1] . The pediatric unit has two figures of its own: 520 for fiscal year 2025 in the Department's report, and 400 individuals in its first year in WellStone's account as relayed by the press  [64]   [69] . Figures the centers report to the state are not settled either: the state's evaluators found in September 2025 that the crisis centers' monthly reports contained inconsistencies that suggested a lack of quality control  [62] . 
 Rates need a look at the count behind them. Cullman County's preventable teen death rate for 2023, 73.0 per 100,000, rests on four deaths, beside Madison's 70.9  [149]   [148] . The Cullman  coroner  counted 17 suicides in 2022 and 22 in 2021, according to the local paper, a difference of five deaths in a county that had 94,009 residents in July 2025  [207]   [6] . Appendix A leaves a cell empty where the publisher suppressed or did not publish a value, and notes that its rates are not comparable with single-year state rates. 
 Then check the period. Cullman's  drug overdose death rate  is 26.4 per 100,000 in its hospital's assessment, an average for 2018 to 2022, and 35.6 in  County Health Rankings , for a different period  [83]   [52] . The provider ratios also come in pairs: 474 and 568 residents per provider in County Health Rankings' March 2026 figures, and 500 and 609 for 2024 in the  Kids Count  profiles, which print no source or definition  [52]   [148]   [149] . The report's own figure of about $49 of WellStone revenue for each resident sets FY2021 revenue over a 2025 population, and the report says to read it as an order of magnitude  [66] . 
 The regional map shades 117 census tracts, 95 in Madison County and 22 in Cullman  [406] . One set of layers comes from the Census Bureau's  American Community Survey  for 2020 to 2024: eighteen estimates for each tract, taken with their published margins of error  [406] . These are sample estimates for small areas, so many tract values have wide margins of error, and one cell is suppressed by the Bureau  [406] . The other set comes from the 2025 release of  CDC PLACES : ten measures for adults, among them depression,  frequent mental distress  and loneliness  [407] . The dataset's own description says the estimates are model-based and draw on the 2023 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (2022 for five measures), 2020 census population counts and American Community Survey estimates  [407] . They are modeled values, not counts or survey results for each tract  [407] . Even at county level the PLACES estimates carry confidence limits: 26.5% of Cullman adults with depression in 2023, with limits of 22.5% and 30.7%, and 22.0% in Madison, with limits of 18.7% and 25.3%  [211] . The two ranges overlap  [211] . 
 How this report uses it 
 Domain 6 collects the pairs of figures that disagree, and its table of what is not published shows what was looked for and not found, with a partial figure where one exists. Where the report computes a number it says so: the share of the two counties' residents that WellStone reached in FY2025, between 2.2% and 2.6% depending on which count is used, is labeled as the report's own calculation  [64] . 
 Appendix C lists the tables that need a check by eye. On page 29 of the Department's FY2025 report each heading is printed beneath its table, and one reading attached 6,627, the 988 call center figure, to WellStone's clinic row  [64] . The report prints 13,700 for the clinic and keeps the page on its list until someone has looked at it  [64] . 
 On the map, read a tract's shade as an estimate of one of the two kinds described above. Because many tract values have wide margins of error, a darker tract is a higher estimate and not necessarily a real difference from its neighbor  [406] . Neither set of tract values is used in the report's text, so a tract figure on the map cannot be traced to a sentence in a section  [406]   [407] .

888.title: The Sequential Intercept Model
888.text:
Six points between a crisis and community supervision at which a person with mental illness can be turned toward care; in Madison and Cullman counties most of what stands at each point is known by its launch date and by little else. What it is 
 The  Sequential Intercept Model  is a map of the points at which a person with mental illness can be turned from the criminal justice system toward treatment  [397] . It lists six of them, numbered 0 to 5: community services, law enforcement, initial detention and first court hearings, jails and courts,  reentry , and  community corrections   [397] . Communities use it to find gaps and opportunities at each point  [397] . The earlier the intercept, the less time a person spends in the justice system  [397] . 
 The purpose at every point is  diversion , which means steering a person away from a jail or an emergency room and into care  [397] . Diversion is hard to measure, because counting one requires a judgment about what would have happened otherwise  [397] . 
 A few terms recur. A  Crisis Intervention Team  is a partnership of law enforcement, mental health providers and families, built around a 40-hour training course for officers  [397] . A  co-responder program  pairs officers with clinicians  [397] . A specialty court is a docket within an ordinary court in which a judge supervises a defendant through treatment and regular hearings  [397] .  Stepping Up  is a national initiative to reduce the number of people with mental illness in county jails, and counties that join commit to steps such as screening everyone booked  [397] . 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw six boxes in a row, joined left to right by arrows and numbered 0 to 5. Under each box put two cells, the upper for Madison County and the lower for Cullman County. Box 0, "Community and crisis": " crisis center  on site" above, and below it "local crisis team reached through  988 ; crisis center in Huntsville"  [3]   [41] . Box 1, "Law enforcement": "crisis-trained officers and co-responders in Huntsville", and "none shown on the sheriff's site"  [34]   [286] . Box 2, "Initial detention and court": "mental health  pretrial release ; municipal  mental health court ", and "court-ordered evaluation arranged in 2019"  [288]   [289]   [291] . Box 3, "Jails and courts": "Adult Mental Health Court; veterans court", and "veterans court, 2019; mental health court, 2022"  [299]   [265]   [29]   [35] . Box 4, "Reentry": "jail diversion staff", and "reentry program on a 2020 federal grant"  [112]   [304] . Box 5, " Community supervision ": "one county office", and "nonprofit community corrections"  [288]   [307] . Beneath the whole row draw a single band reading "no count of people diverted published for the Huntsville center"  [62] . 
 How it works in north Alabama 
 Intercept 0.  The  Department of Mental Health  lists the Huntsville crisis center as a place to which law enforcement and first responders in fifteen counties can bring a person in crisis at any hour  [3] .  WellStone 's chief executive described its beds in 2022 as a way to divert people from jails and emergency departments  [88] . As WellStone described it in 2024, a Cullman caller to 988 reaches the Huntsville center, which connects the caller to a local crisis team  [41] . The state's 2025 evaluation publishes no count of jail or emergency room avoidance for any single center and found the centers' monthly reports inconsistent  [62] . 
 Intercept 1.  In May 2021 Huntsville Police had 75 officers certified through the 40-hour course, and the city council voted to pair two WellStone clinicians with crisis-trained officers  [34] . Two clinicians were riding by February 2022  [63] . No count of calls attended, arrests avoided or transports has been published by the city on the pages read  [63] . Nothing on the Cullman County Sheriff's website shows crisis-trained officers or a co-responder  [286] . 
 Intercept 2.  The Madison County jail is the booking point for Huntsville Police  [287] . A county office runs a Mental Health Pre-Trial Release Program there for detainees who show or have a diagnosis of mental illness, and it publishes no numbers  [288] . Huntsville's Municipal Court runs its own mental health court  [289] . On the civil side, the federal grant for the  probate court 's  outpatient commitment program  set a target of 275 people enrolled, and no results were found  [37] . In Cullman, a 2019 arrangement let a judge order a mental health evaluation, adopted after voluntary screening in the jail failed  [291] . Of 98 inmates the jail referred in the first year of Stepping Up, four agreed to be screened  [28] . 
 Intercept 3.  The Madison County Sheriff's pages publish no capacity, population or mental health caseload for the jail  [65] . Its health care contract, renewed in September 2026, covers up to 1,235 inmates and adds a mental health nurse paid from  opioid settlement funds   [75] . Cullman's detention center has 553 beds, and the page describing its staff names no mental health staff  [293] . 
 Three deaths in the Madison County jail in 2013 led to federal lawsuits  [295] . The complaints alleged that officers and medical staff failed to act as each person died of a treatable condition, and the defendants denied breaching the standard of care  [295] . The cases, numbered 5:14-cv-01964, 5:14-cv-01959 and 5:14-cv-01309 in the Northern District of Alabama, were all reported as pending in September 2016  [296] . In the third, the court denied all motions to dismiss on 9 March 2015  [297] . That ruling let the case proceed and was not a finding that the allegations were proved  [297] . How the three cases ended could not be established  [296] . 
 The circuit's site says a district judge has presided over Madison County's Adult Mental Health Court since 2015, and its capacity and completions are not published  [299] . Cullman County announced a mental health court in May 2022, with WellStone providing services regardless of ability to pay  [35] . Both counties were sites in the first year of Stepping Up, 2018–19  [28] . In 2020–21 the state's report completed no site summary for Madison because of staff turnover and inconsistent data  [290] . Jail-based  competency restoration  runs in seven Alabama counties, and neither Madison nor Cullman is among them  [64] . 
 Intercepts 4 and 5.   The Link of Cullman County  won a $500,000 federal grant in 2020 for a reentry program, and no later report of whether it continued was found  [304] . In Madison County, WellStone's jail diversion staff work to get people out of jail, into housing and to their follow-up appointments  [112] . The state  parole bureau  runs one of its five  day reporting centers  in Huntsville  [306] . Pretrial release, community corrections and misdemeanor probation in Madison County sit in one county office, and Cullman's community corrections program is a nonprofit  [288]   [307] . 
 How this report uses it 
 Section 10 takes the intercepts in order and closes with a table that sets Madison beside Cullman at each one. The same services appear elsewhere under other headings: the crisis center is in Domain 3, and the probate court is in Domain 1.  
 The report's main point about this section is that programs are known by when they began. The co-responders have a funding vote in May 2021, Cullman's veterans court a first session in May 2019, its mental health court an announcement in May 2022, and assisted outpatient treatment a start date in February 2020  [63]   [29]   [35]   [30] . None of those sources gives a count of people served since  [63]   [35] . An announcement is not an outcome, and several cells in the table say that current status was not confirmed. 
 The numbers that do exist need care. The savings WellStone's chief executive cited for jail diversion in 2024, about $300,000 a year, came with no method, year or count  [112] . The only published inputs date from 2018, when the program had moved 20 people out of the jail  [27] .

889.title: One service area, three maps
889.text:
WellStone is the mental health center for two counties and the crisis center for fifteen, and "Region 1" names three other areas, so a regional figure means little until its map is known. What it is 
 A  service area , or  catchment , is the set of counties an organization is assigned to serve  [397] . It shows who is responsible for an area and says nothing about how far a resident has to travel  [397] . This report looked for  WellStone 's service area in the public record and found three different answers. 
 The first answer is two counties. The  Department of Mental Health 's county-by-county emergency list assigns Madison and Cullman, and only those two, to WellStone as their  community mental health center   [2] . Centers of this kind are what the Department calls "the designated points of entry" for mental health and substance use services  [21] . WellStone's own  strategic plan  says it "serves the residents of Madison and Cullman Counties"  [1] , and the Department's directory of  Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics  lists full-scope clinic sites at its Huntsville and Cullman campuses  [5] . 
 The second answer is fifteen. The Department's  Crisis Centers  page lists fifteen counties under "Serving" for  WellStone Emergency Services  and  WellStone Pediatric Crisis Care , which share one address in Huntsville  [3] . The list is Madison and Cullman plus Cherokee, DeKalb, Etowah, Fayette, Jackson, Lamar, Lawrence, Limestone, Marion, Marshall, Morgan, Walker and Winston  [3] . Two other Department pages give the same fifteen, and one of them describes the thirteen as "surrounding counties"  [7]   [8] . For routine care those thirteen are assigned to four other community mental health centers  [2] . 
 The third answer is " Region 1 ", a label that sits on three different maps. The Department's mental illness services map draws a Region 1 of twenty counties and seven centers; its county membership is printed only in the map image, and this report relies on the statewide edition's reading of it  [9] . The Department's Regional Offices page lists a Region I Community Services office in Decatur covering thirteen counties  [10] . They include Madison and Cullman and leave Fayette, Lamar, Marion, Walker and Winston to a Region II office in Tuscaloosa  [10] . The  crisis intervention training  program run by  NAMI Alabama  has a Region 1 of its own, with eighteen north Alabama counties  [11] . 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw a county map of the northern part of Alabama. Fill Madison and Cullman in a dark tone and label them  the core : 2 counties, WellStone as community mental health center and certified clinic, 527,525 residents   [2]   [5]   [6] . Fill the thirteen other catchment counties in a light tone and label them  the ring : 13 counties, four other centers for routine care, 792,981 residents   [2]   [6] . Put a heavy outline around all fifteen, labeled  crisis-center catchment , with a marker at Huntsville for the adult and pediatric crisis units  [3] . Hatch Colbert, Franklin and Lauderdale, to the west of the catchment, and label them  no crisis center assigned   [7] . 
 Add three dashed outlines that can be switched on one at a time, each labeled  Region 1 : twenty counties on the Department's mental illness services map  [9] , thirteen for its Region I Community Services office  [10] , and eighteen for crisis intervention training  [11] . The twenty-county outline should carry a note that its membership comes from a map image  [9] . Under the map, a strip of four small bars shows how many pieces each other scheme cuts the fifteen counties into: three public health districts  [12] , six  area agencies on aging   [395] , four  homelessness continuums   [311]  and three  Medicaid  care coordination regions  [396] . 
 How it works in north Alabama 
 The two maps differ most in how many people they hold. Summed from the Census Bureau's July 2025 county estimates, the core had 527,525 residents and the ring 792,981; both totals are this report's arithmetic  [6] . Three of every five residents of the crisis catchment therefore live outside the two counties whose local governments appoint WellStone's board  [6]   [1] . That board has eighteen members, named by the City of Huntsville, the Madison County Commission, the City of Cullman and the Cullman County Commission  [1] . 
 The ring's routine care is divided among four centers. The Department assigns Jackson and Marshall to  Mountain Lakes Behavioral Healthcare ; Lawrence, Limestone and Morgan to the  Mental Health Center of North Central Alabama ; Cherokee, DeKalb and Etowah to  CED Mental Health Center ; and Fayette, Lamar, Marion, Walker and Winston to  Northwest Alabama Mental Health Center   [2] . On its southern side the catchment meets counties assigned to the Birmingham and Tuscaloosa crisis centers  [3] . 
 Other regional schemes cut the same fifteen counties along other lines. They fall into three public health districts and six area agencies on aging  [12]   [395] . Huntsville's  2-1-1  center takes calls from Madison and five ring counties, while Cullman's calls are answered from Birmingham  [13] . Even the two core counties part company. Madison shares a homelessness continuum with Limestone and Morgan  [311] , Cullman belongs to a  Balance of State  continuum of 37 counties  [312] , and the two sit in different councils of governments  [395] . Medicaid's care coordination map does keep them together, in a Northeast region with Jackson, Limestone, Marshall and Morgan  [368] . 
 One map could not be found at all. One of Alabama's four in-state  988  call centers is at WellStone, and the Department's 988 page gives no county coverage for any of them  [4] . No press report read for this edition lists the counties the Huntsville center answers  [14] . WellStone has said that a Cullman caller to 988 is connected to the Huntsville center  [41] . 
 How this report uses it 
 The report settles its vocabulary early. "The core" means Madison and Cullman, and "the ring" means the other thirteen counties. Region 1 is used only as a benchmark, and always with its size stated. Domains 1 to 8 and Sections 9 to 12 describe the core. Section 13 sketches the ring in outline and does not examine its courts, schools, hospitals or housing.  
 Before comparing any two regional figures, a reader can ask four things. The first is which map the figure sits on. The Department counts 1,879 people served at the adult crisis center in  FY2025 , a figure that covers all fifteen counties, and 11,659 served by WellStone as a community mental health center, the role it holds for two  [64]   [2] . The second is whether the figure is split by county, and the Department's FY2025 rows for WellStone are not  [64] . The third is how large the Region 1 behind a benchmark is, since it may hold twenty, thirteen or eighteen counties  [9]   [10]   [11] . The fourth is whether a figure with a familiar name describes the same counties. The 718 homeless people counted in January 2025, for instance, were counted across Madison, Limestone and Morgan together  [60] . 
 A catchment records an assignment, and use is a separate matter. The Department's FY2025 figures for the adult and pediatric units come with no county of residence  [64] , and the state's evaluators reported in 2025 that crisis centers may serve fewer people from communities outside the metropolitan areas where they sit  [62] . Section 13 reads this as a sign that the ring may depend on Huntsville less than the map implies, and it adds that no number in the sources read can confirm or refute that reading.

890.title: Measuring the workforce shortage
890.text:
A federal designation, a provider ratio and a count of beds that cannot be staffed answer different questions, and in Madison and Cullman counties they give different answers. What it is 
 A shortage of mental health workers is measured in several ways, by different bodies and for different purposes, and the measures do not always agree  [397] . This report uses three: a  federal designation , a ratio of residents to providers, and what local employers say they cannot staff. 
 The first is the Health Professional Shortage Area. The federal health workforce agency designates shortage areas for primary, dental and mental health care, and a designation can cover a geographic area, a population within an area, or a facility  [397] . For mental health the designation counts psychiatrists only  [146] . The threshold is a population of at least 30,000 for each psychiatrist, or 20,000 where needs are unusually high  [147] . A designation for a low-income population is narrower: it shows a shortage of providers serving  Medicaid  and  sliding-fee  patients, measured against the low-income population  [146] . The designation is also a gateway, because  federal loan repayment  for clinicians is tied to the  shortage score  of the site where they work  [163] . 
 The second measure is a ratio of residents to mental health providers of all kinds  [397] .  County Health Rankings  counts psychiatrists, psychologists, licensed clinical social workers, counselors, marriage and family therapists, providers who treat alcohol and other drug abuse, and advanced practice nurses specializing in mental health  [150] . It takes them from the national registry of provider identifiers  [150] . The publisher's own caveat is that some providers on the list "may no longer be practicing or accepting new patients," which can overstate supply  [150] . A ratio of this kind counts licensed people, not hours worked, and says nothing about whether they take Medicaid  [397] . 
 The third measure comes from inside the system: the posts and beds an employer cannot fill  [397] . In this region it reaches the public through a  strategic plan , press reports and a hospital's  needs assessment   [1]   [56]   [83] . 
 The key idea in one picture 
 Draw a table with three rows, one for each measure, and a column each for Madison County and Cullman County. Row 1 is labeled  Federal designation (psychiatrists only) : Madison  none ; Cullman  low-income population, score 16   [52]   [146] . Row 2 is labeled  Residents per mental health provider  (all kinds) : Madison  474 , Cullman  568 , with  Alabama 639  in the margin  [52] . Beneath those cells, in smaller type, add the  Kids Count  figures for 2024,  500  and  609   [148]   [149] , and beneath Cullman's a third box reading  132.0 providers per 100,000 (hospital assessment, 2024)   [83] . Row 3 is labeled  What could not be staffed : in the Madison column,  24-bed  pediatric crisis unit  able to treat six children at a time, 23 October 2024   [56] ; across both columns,  nursing named among  WellStone 's three greatest unmet needs, November 2025   [1] . A footnote on row 2 reads  the registry may include providers who are no longer practicing   [150] . 
 How it works in north Alabama 
 Cullman County is a mental health shortage area for its low-income population, with a score of 16  [52] . Madison County has no area designation and is the only county in Alabama without one  [52] . That absence is a statement about psychiatrists, since no other profession is counted  [146] . Sites in Madison County could still hold a facility designation of their own, and whether WellStone's sites do was not established  [163]   [52] . All thirteen  ring counties  carry a designation, three of them (Cherokee, DeKalb and Etowah) flagged as proposed for withdrawal  [52] . 
 For the ratio there are two published numbers for each county and a third for Cullman. County Health Rankings' March 2026 figures give 474 residents per mental health provider in Madison and 568 in Cullman, against 639 for Alabama  [52] . The Kids Count county profiles print 500 and 609 for 2024  [148]   [149] .  Cullman Regional 's needs assessment reports 132.0 providers per 100,000 residents in Cullman County for 2024, against 140.9 for the state and 312.5 for the country  [83] . 
 Part of the difference lies in the counting rules. The hospital's assessment draws on the same federal registry as County Health Rankings and names a shorter list of professions: psychiatrists, psychologists, clinical social workers and counselors  [83]   [150] . The Kids Count profiles print no source or definition for their row  [149] . County Health Rankings also refreshes its registry data between releases, so two ratios for the same county can describe different years  [150] . On the Rankings measure both counties look better than Alabama; on the hospital's measure Cullman is below the state and far below the nation  [52]   [83] . Across the ring the Rankings ratio runs from 339 residents per provider in Marshall to 4,774 in Winston  [20] . 
 The plainest local evidence is a building. WellStone's pediatric crisis unit opened in late September 2024 with 24 beds  [43] . On 23 October it could treat six children at a time because of a staffing shortage  [56] . No later report read for this edition says when, or whether, the unit reached full staffing  [56] . A year later WellStone's strategic plan named "recruiting and retaining a qualified nursing workforce" among its three greatest unmet needs, with no vacancy or turnover figure  [1] . The  Huntsville Hospital  system said in 2023 that recruiting and retaining employees, "especially nurses," was its top priority  [151] . A participant in Cullman Regional's assessment wrote that there are "never enough psychiatrists, psychiatric nurses"  [83] . 
 Training is the longer route. Doctors tend to settle near where they train, which is why  residency  places matter to the supply of psychiatrists  [397] . The University of Alabama at Birmingham runs a four-year psychiatry residency at its Huntsville campus, approved for up to six residents a year, with Huntsville Hospital as its clinical site  [152]   [153] . Its page listed six first-year and six second-year residents in October 2026  [154] . The American Medical Association's residency database lists a second four-year program in Huntsville under WellStone's name, with six first-year positions  [156] . That entry shows 24 current residents, a figure that may describe approved positions, and whether the program has residents in training could not be established  [156] . 
 How this report uses it 
 Domain 4 sets the three measures side by side and then leans on the third, because designations and national ratios work poorly at county scale. Domain 7 uses the designation and the ratio to compare the two counties, and Appendix A prints both for each of the fifteen counties  [52]   [20] . 
 What the report cannot give is a number for the shortage itself. No vacancy or turnover figure for behavioral health nursing was found for WellStone or for the hospital system  [1]   [151] . The  state health department  publishes its mental health shortage designations only as a map, dated May 2024, which could not be read reliably for the two counties; the report takes its designations from the federal file  [146]   [52] . 
 When a workforce figure appears, check which measure it is, who is counted and which year it describes. The two forms of the ratio also run in opposite directions: 474 residents per provider is better than 568, while 132.0 providers per 100,000 is worse than 140.9  [52]   [83] . And a ratio built from a registry describes people who hold an identifier, some of whom may no longer be practicing  [150] .

891.title: Figure 1. Madison and Cullman counties side by side, with Alabama
891.text: Twelve published indicators for the two counties of the core beside the state value from the same source. Values are as published in Census QuickFacts, County Health Rankings and the federal shortage-area file, taken from the county table checked for the statewide report.

892.title: Figure 2. What has been said in public about commitments in Madison County
892.text: The four figures on involuntary commitment in Madison County found in the sources read. All come from press reports; the probate court publishes no count.

893.title: Figure 3. Days a new patient waited at WellStone, January and December 2025
893.text: The two access measures the Department of Mental Health gave legislators for WellStone in January 2026. They are the only measured change in access found for the region.

894.title: Figure 4. Four published figures for WellStone in fiscal year 2025
894.text: How many people WellStone served in FY2025, according to four published statements. Two are the Department's table figures, whose unit could not be confirmed because the column headings did not come through; two are lower bounds ("over 12,000", "more than 13,500") and are drawn at the bound.

895.title: Figure 5. People counted as homeless and supportive housing beds, Huntsville continuum, 2022 to 2025
895.text: The January point-in-time count and the permanent supportive housing beds in the federal housing inventory for the three-county Huntsville continuum (Madison, Limestone and Morgan). No figure exists for Cullman County, which belongs to a different continuum.

896.title: Figure 6. How the parts of the regional system depend on one another
896.text: The statewide report's twelve nodes and the ring, joined by the eleven links in this report's dependency table. Each link carries the evidence the report gives for it.

897.title: OI-001 · Could not be read
897.text: About fifty pages of WellStone's website could not be read, including those on its programs, locations, board, school-based services and psychiatry residency. Two pages and two press releases were read. Much of what the report says about WellStone's programs rests on the Department of Mental Health's documents and on press reports and not on WellStone's own account.

898.title: OI-002 · Could not be read
898.text: WellStone's single audits for fiscal years 2022 to 2025 could not be opened, and no Form 990 data for any year after FY2021 appeared in the public database used. They would show WellStone's revenue by source, its federal awards and the significant deficiency flagged on the FY2025 audit, none of which the report can state.

899.title: OI-003 · Could not be read
899.text: The City of Huntsville's outside agency appropriations books, which hold the annual amount for WellStone and other agencies, could not be opened. Only the FY2026 amount ($900,000, less $36,000 moved by amendment) is known, from a city release. They would give the city's appropriation to WellStone for FY2024, FY2025 and FY2027 and show which agencies share the outside-agency totals.

900.title: OI-004 · Could not be read
900.text: Ten Cullman County Commission documents (agendas and minutes for 2025 and 2026) could not be read when first requested. Two agendas were read later; the minutes turned out to be scanned images with no text. They would show any county appropriation to WellStone, its appointments to WellStone's board, its opioid settlement decisions and the FY2027 budget.

901.title: OI-005 · Could not be read
901.text: The full report of United Way of Madison County's 2024 community needs assessment could not be opened. Only the executive summary was read, and it carries one sentence on mental health and no percentages. It is the nearest thing Madison County has to a needs assessment, and any mental health results by rank, race, income or area would be in the full report.

902.title: OI-006 · Could not be read
902.text: The state health department's death tables for Madison and Cullman counties by cause, race and sex could not be read. The documents run to several hundred pages and the text returned stopped before either county's page; an older county profiles document returned numbers that belonged to other counties. They would give local counts of suicides and drug poisonings by race and sex, which the report cannot state for either county.

903.title: OI-007 · Could not be read
903.text: Huntsville City Schools' pages on prevention and support, school counseling and student welfare returned only menus, so the district's counselors, social workers and mental health partners could not be described. It is the largest of the five school systems, and without it the report cannot say how school-based care is arranged for more than 23,000 students.

904.title: OI-008 · Could not be read
904.text: The current strategic plans of Mountain Lakes Behavioral Healthcare and the Mental Health Center of North Central Alabama (printed in Appendix C as the 2025 plans; filed with the Department in January 2026) are scanned images and could not be read. They would give each center's own count of people served, its crisis services and unmet needs, and any reference to the Huntsville crisis center.

905.title: OI-009 · Could not be read
905.text: Crisis Services of North Alabama's 2025 impact report and 2024 audit could not be opened, and its HELPline page could not be read. They would give the agency's service numbers (calls, shelter nights, forensic exams) and say how its HELPline relates to 988.

906.title: OI-010 · Needs a human eye
906.text: On page 29 of the Department's FY2025 annual report, WellStone's count as a Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic was read as 13,700 on some readings and as 6,627 on others. The page prints each heading beneath its table, and 6,627 appears to belong to the 988 call center table. The report prints 13,700 as WellStone's clinic count and 6,627 as its 988 figure, and both rest on an inference from the order of the text.

907.title: OI-011 · Needs a human eye
907.text: The National Children's Advocacy Center's therapy figures for 2024 and all of its 2025 figures could not be paired with their captions. The 2024 report gave 270 and 1,664 on one reading and 1,311, 83, 3,007 and 1,664 on another; the 2025 page is six numbers followed by five captions. The report leaves the 2024 therapy figures out and uses no 2025 figure, so the center's therapy volume is missing from the section on child welfare.

908.title: OI-012 · Needs a human eye
908.text: The state health department's May 2024 map of mental health shortage areas could not be read for Madison or Cullman County. Its text holds 67 county names and 66 numbers in separate lists, so every pairing returned (18 for Madison; 17 and 18 for Cullman) is unreliable. The report takes the two counties' designations from the federal file (none for Madison; low-income population, score 16, for Cullman), and the state's own map neither confirms nor contradicts that as read.

909.title: OI-013 · Needs a human eye
909.text: The Department's April 2026 Stepping Up map could not be read to say whether Madison or Cullman County is a current site. Both counties were sites in 2018–19 and 2020–21 and appear on the Department's list to September 2023. It would settle whether jail screening under Stepping Up continues in either county, including the arrangement the Cullman County Commission backed in 2018.

910.title: OI-014 · Needs a human eye
910.text: In the 2025 federal housing inventory for the Huntsville continuum, the permanent supportive housing row shows 24 beds in one subset column and 166 in the next, and readings disagreed on which column holds chronic and which veteran beds. It also could not be confirmed that the housing authority's 166-bed project, labeled "- V" in the list, is the veterans' voucher program. It decides whether WellStone's 24 Shelter Plus Care beds can be described as the only ones dedicated to chronically homeless people.

911.title: OI-015 · Needs a human eye
911.text: The number of people who took part in United Way of Madison County's 2024 needs assessment was read as "nearly 1,000" once and as "nearly 1,500" twice, in the same sentence of the executive summary. The figure is the assessment's sample size and should not be printed until it is settled.

912.title: OI-016 · Could not be confirmed
912.text: How the three federal lawsuits over the 2013 deaths in the Madison County jail ended could not be established. All three were reported as pending in September 2016, and in one of them the court denied the motions to dismiss on 9 March 2015. The report describes the allegations and cannot say whether the cases ended in judgment, dismissal or settlement.

913.title: OI-017 · Could not be confirmed
913.text: Whether the Mental Health Center of North Central Alabama's 16-bed crisis residential unit in Decatur has opened could not be confirmed. Ground was broken on 10 December 2024 with completion expected in October 2025, and in October 2026 the center was advertising for nurses for the unit. It would be new bed capacity for committed patients inside the ring and would change how far families and officers from Morgan, Lawrence and Limestone counties travel.

914.title: OI-018 · Could not be confirmed
914.text: Whether WellStone's psychiatry residency has residents in training could not be established. A national residency database lists the program with six first-year positions and shows 24 current residents, a figure that equals four full classes and may describe approved positions. It would show whether Huntsville has one psychiatry residency producing graduates or two.

915.title: OI-019 · Could not be confirmed
915.text: Whether WellStone met the targets in its 2022 federal clinic grant could not be confirmed: a peer "living room" giving walk-in support to 400 people, intensive community care for 50 service members and veterans by 29 September 2023, and at least 1,200 mobile crisis responses by 29 September 2026. WellStone has said it added an adult mobile crisis team; no count against any target was found in the sources read. The report can state what was promised under a $3,974,261 grant and cannot state what was delivered.

916.title: OI-020 · Could not be confirmed
916.text: The capacity of the South Derrick Street camp is given as 84 marked spaces in the city's release of 16 April 2025 and as about 58 people in two press reports of 2026. No source read reconciles the two, gives the day the camp reopened or prints its community standards. The report prints both figures and cannot say which describes the camp today.

917.title: OI-021 · Could not be confirmed
917.text: The exact day North Alabama Regional Hospital closed in 2015 was not found. The closure was announced on 13 January 2015 with a target of 30 June 2015, and admissions stopped on 1 March 2015. The report can date the closure only to mid-2015.

918.title: OI-022 · Could not be confirmed
918.text: Whether Cullman County's mental health court, launched in May 2022, still sits could not be confirmed. By October 2026 the circuit's web page named neither the judge who launched it nor any of the specialty dockets. The report lists the court as launched in 2022 with its current status unconfirmed.

919.title: OI-023 · Not published, as far as this review found
919.text: A count of the people WellStone serves in each county was not found in the sources read. The totals found, from the Department and from WellStone, are organization-wide. It would show how many Cullman County residents the center reaches and let each county be set against its population.

920.title: OI-024 · Not published, as far as this review found
920.text: Lengths of stay, drop-offs by law enforcement, where people went next, readmissions and diversions from jail or emergency rooms at the Huntsville crisis center were not found in the sources read, and neither were admissions and lengths of stay at the pediatric unit. Capacity at opening, monthly admissions and yearly counts of people served were found. Diversion is the stated purpose of the crisis center, and the report cannot say how many people it has diverted.

921.title: OI-025 · Not published, as far as this review found
921.text: The county of residence of people admitted to the crisis center or the pediatric unit was not found in the sources read. It is the only way to tell how much the thirteen ring counties use the Huntsville center.

922.title: OI-026 · Not published, as far as this review found
922.text: Results of the Huntsville Police co-responder program since 2022 (calls attended, arrests avoided, transports to the crisis center) and its current staffing and hours were not found in the sources read. The program has run for five years and the report can describe only its launch.

923.title: OI-027 · Not published, as far as this review found
923.text: An official yearly count of commitment petitions, hearings and orders was not found for either probate court, and neither was a list of designated facilities or a yearly count of people sent to state beds. The only figures are from press reports about Madison County, in different units (309 petitions in 2019, 414 in 2021 and 589 involuntary commitments in 2023); nothing was found for Cullman County. It would show how much demand each court faces and whether Madison County's outpatient program has changed it.

924.title: OI-028 · Not published, as far as this review found
924.text: How many commitments begin each way (a walk-in at the probate office, an emergency room visit or a 911 call) and how long people wait at each stage were not found in the sources read. One press report lists the three routes without counts. It would show where people are held before a hearing and for how long.

925.title: OI-029 · Not published, as far as this review found
925.text: A count of psychiatric beds by hospital was not obtained. Two counts were found (20 beds at Unity Psychiatric Care and 64 licensed beds at Decatur Morgan West); none was found for Huntsville Hospital's adult and senior units, for adolescent beds at Decatur Morgan West, or for the ring hospitals that list psychiatric services, and whether Crestwood runs an inpatient unit was not established. It would settle how many inpatient beds the two counties and the ring have, and which sixty beds a 2025 press report meant.

926.title: OI-030 · Not published, as far as this review found
926.text: A measure of how long psychiatric patients wait in emergency departments was not found for either county. The only accounts are of children waiting up to 24 hours before the pediatric unit opened. It would show whether the crisis center and the pediatric unit have relieved the hospitals.

927.title: OI-031 · Not published, as far as this review found
927.text: The number of people with a mental illness held in either county's jail, the jails' average populations and their screening practice at booking were not found in the sources read. The most recent capacity statement found for the Madison County jail dates from 2010; the Cullman County detention center gives 553 beds. The jails are where the report can say least about people with mental illness.

928.title: OI-032 · Not published, as far as this review found
928.text: Staff vacancy and turnover figures for WellStone were not found in the sources read. Its plan names nursing recruitment as an unmet need without numbers. Nursing is the named bottleneck and no number describes it.

929.title: OI-033 · Not published, as far as this review found
929.text: The goal of WellStone's Be the Rock capital campaign and the total it raised were not found. A press report at the crisis center's opening in 2022 gave close to $550,000 raised toward about $5 million; no later total, donor list or separate WellStone foundation was found. About half the cost of the crisis center was left to the campaign, and the report cannot say whether it was raised.

930.title: OI-034 · Not published, as far as this review found
930.text: Yearly counts of suicides and overdose deaths by race and sex were not found in any local publication, and no county count of veteran suicides was found. The Madison County coroner's website carries no statistics as read; coroners' counts reach the public through interviews, such as overdose deaths for 2016 to 2019 in Madison County and suicides for 2021 and 2022 in Cullman County. Deaths are the plainest measure of the burden, and the report has no local series by year, race or sex.

931.title: OI-035 · Not published, as far as this review found
931.text: Which counties the Huntsville 988 call center answers was not found in the sources read, and neither was an answer rate for that center alone. A Department presentation calls WellStone the call center for Region I, northern Alabama, and WellStone has said that Cullman County callers reach the Huntsville center. It is the fourth map of WellStone's service area and the one the report cannot draw.

932.title: OI-036 · Not published, as far as this review found
932.text: A homelessness count for Cullman County was not found. The county is counted within a 37-county continuum whose figures as read are a total only (636 people in January 2026), and the only shelter with Cullman in its name in the federal inventory is a 21-bed domestic violence shelter. The report cannot say how many people are homeless in one of WellStone's two counties.

933.title: OI-037 · Not published, as far as this review found
933.text: Quality and outcome measures for WellStone under the clinic model were not found: the Department's promised annual quality report, first-year results of the demonstration, follow-up after hospitalization, the clinic count for FY2024 and any access time after December 2025. The two access times reported for 2025 are the only measured results found. The first quality report would be the first published outcome measures for WellStone.

934.title: OI-038 · Could not be read
934.text: The City of Madison's council documents on WellStone could not be read. The only amount known is the $45,000 proposed for FY2024; its appropriations for FY2025 to FY2027 and its agreement with WellStone for first-responder mental health services were not found. The City of Madison pays toward WellStone and appoints no one to its board, and the report can cite one year's amount.

935.title: OI-039 · Could not be read
935.text: Several other City of Huntsville documents could not be opened: the police department's 2025 annual report, its 2021 written response on policy, its directives portal, the FY2027 council budget presentation, the city's record of its appointments to WellStone's board, and files linked from the Homeless Resources page. They may hold current counts of crisis-trained officers, any policy change after the 2018 shooting, directives on staff support and the camp's rules.

936.title: OI-040 · Could not be read
936.text: Several Madison County government pages returned an error and could not be read: the probate court's mental health page, the sub-pages of the juvenile detention center, the community corrections and department index pages and the rural transit page. They may hold the court's own account of its commitment and outpatient programs, services for detained youth and current transit hours.

937.title: OI-041 · Could not be read
937.text: Most of the Alabama Medicaid Agency's website could not be read: its pages on the coordinated health networks, the network chapter of its provider manual, its statistics page with later county files and an FY2022 county map, and its sheet of network regions. They would confirm the care coordination regions and may give Medicaid spending by county.

938.title: OI-042 · Could not be read
938.text: Huntsville Hospital Health System's own website, Decatur Morgan Hospital's psychiatric services pages and Crestwood Medical Center's behavioral health page could not be read. They would give the system's own count of hospitals and beds, how its affiliates in the ring are owned or managed, and the adolescent beds and ages admitted at Decatur Morgan West.

939.title: OI-043 · Could not be read
939.text: About forty requests for local press articles and site searches failed (some articles were tried in both rounds of research), from three Huntsville television stations, a state news site, a web portal's copies of local reports, a national magazine, and the search pages of the Cullman Times, the Cullman Tribune, 256 Today and the Redstone Rocket. Among them are reports on crisis intervention training counts, the Madison County drug court, the jail health contract, a later settled lawsuit against the sheriff, the camp's reopening and school counseling numbers.

940.title: OI-044 · Could not be read
940.text: The websites of several local nonprofits and one regional council could not be read: The Link of Cullman County, two community action agencies, Family Services Center's programs page, Harris Home for Children, The Pathfinder, the Salvation Army in Huntsville, Cullman's domestic violence agency and the North Central Alabama Regional Council of Governments. Their own program descriptions and service numbers are missing; what the report says about them comes from funders' lists, the federal housing inventory and the press.

941.title: OI-045 · Could not be read
941.text: Several public data tools load by script and returned no data: County Health Rankings' county pages, the federal shortage-area search and health center finder, the Kids Count data center and the state's drug use data repository. As a result it was not established whether any WellStone site holds its own facility shortage designation or whether a federally qualified health center has a site in Cullman County. A facility designation decides whether clinicians at WellStone's Madison County sites qualify for federal loan repayment, and the health center question bears on the report's account of Cullman's safety net.

942.title: OI-046 · Could not be read
942.text: County figures on household hardship and schooling could not be read or were not reached: the ALICE county tables and data sheet, the food insecurity map, eviction filings, the state report card's graduation and absenteeism rates for the three Madison County school districts, official enrollment by district, and monthly unemployment and food assistance figures later than those printed. They would fill out the report's account of economic stability and education in the two counties.

943.title: OI-047 · Could not be read
943.text: The federal county-level file of 2026 marketplace plan selections could not be opened, and Census estimates of uninsured adults aged 19 to 64 by county could not be read. Coverage losses in 2026 are known for the state and not for Madison or Cullman County.

944.title: OI-048 · Could not be read
944.text: United Way of Madison County's 2024 annual summary is an image with no readable text, and the state's 2-1-1 dashboard refused the page reader, so United Way's allocations to behavioral health agencies, its list of partner agencies, and 2-1-1 call volumes and top needs for either county could not be recorded. They would show what residents ask for help with and how much local philanthropy goes to mental health.

945.title: OI-049 · Needs a human eye
945.text: In the state evaluation office's table of crisis center spending, WellStone's FY2022 row (21.8% operations, 78.6% capital) agreed on every reading. The FY2021, FY2023 and FY2024 rows were returned once only in one round of research, and the FY2024 row as returned does not sum to 100. The report prints the FY2021 and FY2024 shares.

946.title: OI-050 · Needs a human eye
946.text: The Department's map of mental illness service regions is an image, so the membership of its Region 1 (twenty counties and seven centers) could not be read again for this report, which relies on the statewide edition's reading of it. The Department's regional offices page lists a different, thirteen-county Region I and does not say which division's regions it describes. Region 1 is used in the report as a benchmark, and its county list has been read by eye only once.

947.title: OI-051 · Needs a human eye
947.text: The State Health Plan's psychiatric rule prints its two regions in side-by-side columns, which were returned interleaved. The ten-county North Region list is a reconstruction, and one reading placed a county from another part of the state in it. The report says Madison, Morgan and Cullman sit in a ten-county North Region for psychiatric bed need.

948.title: OI-052 · Needs a human eye
948.text: A naloxone distribution figure for Cullman County could not be read from the state opioid council's 2025 report. The report's text gives 2,344 doses for Madison County and does not mention Cullman, which may appear only on the report's map. The report has a naloxone figure for one county only.

949.title: OI-053 · Needs a human eye
949.text: Several official maps could not be read for the two counties because county assignments are shown only by symbols or shading: the court administration's maps of mental health, veterans and drug courts and of court referral officers, the Department's map of prevention funding sources and the state health department's map of telehealth sites. They would confirm from a state source which specialty courts sit in each county and whether the county health departments are telehealth sites.

950.title: OI-054 · Could not be confirmed
950.text: Whether the pediatric crisis unit reached full staffing could not be confirmed. On 23 October 2024 it could treat six children at a time in its 24 beds; no later count of staffed beds was found. It is the report's most concrete evidence of the workforce shortage.

951.title: OI-055 · Could not be confirmed
951.text: Whether WellStone met its target of 75% of therapists certified in an evidence-based practice by 30 September 2026 could not be confirmed, and the plan gives no baseline. It is the one workforce target in WellStone's plan, and its date fell four days before this report.

952.title: OI-056 · Could not be confirmed
952.text: Results of Madison County's assisted outpatient treatment program against its federal grant targets (275 people enrolled over four years; a 75% decrease in participants needing inpatient care or incarceration) were not found, and no independent evaluation was found. Press reports give return rates of about 10% and of under 20%. The program is the court's main innovation and the report can cite only press figures for its results.

953.title: OI-057 · Could not be confirmed
953.text: What pays for the programs built on WellStone's federal grants now that their periods have ended (30 July 2026 for assisted outpatient treatment, 29 September 2026 for the clinic grant) could not be established, and whether the outpatient commitment program continues at the same scale was not confirmed. The report notes the grants' end dates and cannot say whether Medicaid's clinic payment, local budgets or nothing has replaced them.

954.title: OI-058 · Could not be confirmed
954.text: Whether WellStone's electronic health record is connected to the state health information exchange could not be confirmed. WellStone does not name its record system on any page read, and nothing was found on a registry of open crisis beds. The clinic model requires the connection, and the report cannot say whether the crisis center, the hospitals and the courts can see one another's information.

955.title: OI-059 · Could not be confirmed
955.text: Whether WellStone's mobile clinic is in service could not be confirmed. It was announced on 7 November 2025 as due to be deployed in the coming weeks. The report describes the van as a way round transport barriers in Madison County.

956.title: OI-060 · Could not be confirmed
956.text: Whether a Defense Department plan to limit Fox Army Health Center to active-duty soldiers was carried out could not be confirmed. An undated press report described the plan; the clinic's current pages still list retirees and family members. It decides how many military retirees and family members around Redstone Arsenal rely on civilian mental health care.

957.title: OI-061 · Could not be confirmed
957.text: What replaced North Alabama Regional Hospital's 74 beds could not be established: whether the 16-bed crisis stabilization units named in Cullman and Huntsville in 2015 still operate, and under what name, and which counties the hospital served. The one Department document found on the closure gives it a single sentence. The report says the region lost its state hospital and cannot say what capacity took its place.

958.title: OI-062 · Could not be confirmed
958.text: Whether two Cullman County arrangements continue could not be confirmed: the 2019 route by which a judge can order a mental health evaluation, and the reentry program The Link of Cullman County began with a 2020 federal grant. The report's table of intercepts marks both as not confirmed.

959.title: OI-063 · Could not be confirmed
959.text: Results of Cullman Regional Medical Center's suicide prevention initiative, Project Zero Suicide, were not found; its 2025 plan says the hospital had recently joined. It is the hospital's main new commitment on mental health.

960.title: OI-064 · Not published, as far as this review found
960.text: An annual operating appropriation from the Madison County Commission to WellStone was not found, and the Commission's budget documents were not found in a form that could be read. Its recorded contributions are a share of the crisis center's capital cost and a $1,000,000 pandemic recovery grant; no local fund for indigent care was found. The county appoints six of WellStone's eighteen board members, and the report cannot say what it pays each year.

961.title: OI-065 · Not published, as far as this review found
961.text: The City of Cullman's budget and the amount of its community service contract with WellStone were not found. The FY2027 budget resolutions name "Cullman Area Mental Health (Wellstone)" among twenty organizations without amounts. The city appoints three board members, and the report cannot state what it contributes.

962.title: OI-066 · Not published, as far as this review found
962.text: Official totals of opioid settlement receipts and full lists of allocations were not found for Madison County, Cullman County or the City of Cullman, and Huntsville's allocations after April 2023 and the utilization reports it requires from recipients were not found. Settlement money is the newest local funding stream, and the report can trace only part of it.

963.title: OI-067 · Not published, as far as this review found
963.text: The shares of the pediatric unit's $9 million cost paid by the state, the Department and donors, the cost and funding of the 2024 Cullman renovation, and the amount of the state grant for the River Crossing detox unit were not found. Capital spending is the best documented part of local financing, and these three projects are the gaps in it.

964.title: OI-068 · Not published, as far as this review found
964.text: The amount of the Department's contract with WellStone and the state operating funds for the Huntsville crisis center and pediatric unit were not found. One state document gives $7,000,000 a year for each crisis center and the enacted budget gives $36,000,000 for six; neither reconciles the two. State money is WellStone's largest source, and the report cannot say how much reaches it.

965.title: OI-069 · Not published, as far as this review found
965.text: WellStone's daily rate under the clinic payment model, the payments it has received and the share of its clients enrolled in Medicaid were not found. The rate is paid for Medicaid enrollees only, so these three numbers decide how much of WellStone's care the new model pays for.

966.title: OI-070 · Not published, as far as this review found
966.text: WellStone's sliding fee schedule, the insurers it accepts and its designated collaborating organizations were not found. They show what an uninsured resident would pay and which partners deliver clinic services on WellStone's behalf.

967.title: OI-071 · Not published, as far as this review found
967.text: Public mental health spending by county or by center was not found: the Medicaid agency's documents as read give eligible people by county and no spending, and the Department's FY2025 annual report gives Medicaid revenue for community mental illness services as one statewide line. A per-person spending figure for the two counties cannot be built from the reports read.

968.title: OI-072 · Not published, as far as this review found
968.text: A current list of WellStone's board members with the body that appointed each, and the membership, remit and consumer and family seats of its Community Advisory Committee, were not found. The committee is known only from the Madison County probate judge's official biography. The state's clinic manual requires people with lived experience to take a meaningful part in governance, and the report cannot say how WellStone meets that rule.

969.title: OI-073 · Not published, as far as this review found
969.text: No document read describes how the thirteen ring counties, or their four mental health centers, take part in decisions about the crisis center, or when and how those counties were assigned to it. The board that governs a fifteen-county crisis center is appointed by four governments in two counties.

970.title: OI-074 · Not published, as far as this review found
970.text: Whether WellStone or the hospital psychiatric units hold accreditation from a national body was not found; WellStone's plan mentions only certification by the Department. Accreditation is a basic quality marker a reader would expect to see stated.

971.title: OI-075 · Not published, as far as this review found
971.text: A community health needs assessment from Huntsville Hospital or Crestwood Medical Center was not found. Cullman's hospital has issued one every three years; Madison County has no hospital equivalent in the sources read.

972.title: OI-076 · Not published, as far as this review found
972.text: A Huntsville or Madison County mental health task force, or a section on behavioral health in a city or county strategic or consolidated plan, was not found; Huntsville's federal housing consolidated plan was not located in readable form. It would be a fourth local planning document beside the three the report describes.

973.title: OI-077 · Not published, as far as this review found
973.text: Yearly activity counts and current staffing and hours for the adult mobile crisis teams in Cullman and Huntsville were not found. The only count is a team member's statement of more than 150 crises in Cullman County in the summer of 2022. Mobile teams are the Department's answer for rural residents who cannot reach the crisis center.

974.title: OI-078 · Not published, as far as this review found
974.text: The number of children and adolescents WellStone serves in total, by program and by county, was not found. The report can give counts for the pediatric unit and the mobile teams and no total for children's services.

975.title: OI-079 · Not published, as far as this review found
975.text: The number of WellStone's residential beds, group homes and supported housing places, and its caseloads for homeless outreach and supported employment, were not found. Housing is named twice among WellStone's unmet needs, and the report cannot say how much it now provides.

976.title: OI-080 · Not published, as far as this review found
976.text: Who operates the Our Place drop-in center in Huntsville, its hours and attendance, and the number of certified peer specialists working in either county were not found. Recovery supports cluster in Huntsville, and the report can list them without saying how much they are used.

977.title: OI-081 · Not published, as far as this review found
977.text: A count of residents trained in Mental Health First Aid or suicide prevention was not found for either county. The only local figure is about 100 faculty and staff trained at the University of Alabama in Huntsville by September 2026. Public education is described in the report and cannot be counted.

978.title: OI-082 · Not published, as far as this review found
978.text: The operator, reach and funding of the SPEAK North Alabama suicide prevention program were not found. It is a local prevention program the report could not describe.

979.title: OI-083 · Not published, as far as this review found
979.text: A count from the ambulance service of psychiatric transports, and of how many children still leave Madison County for psychiatric care since the pediatric unit opened, was not found. The figures of "about 800" and "over 600" children a year come from WellStone and the press. It would measure what the pediatric unit has changed.

980.title: OI-084 · Not published, as far as this review found
980.text: A longer-stay psychiatric option for children in either county was not described in the sources read, and no statement made since the pediatric unit opened says what is still missing or where children go when they need more than a crisis stay. The pediatric unit holds a child for up to two weeks.

981.title: OI-085 · Not published, as far as this review found
981.text: Who takes committed patients from Madison and Cullman counties to Bryce Hospital in Tuscaloosa, how often and at what cost was not found, and neither was any official's statement about the burden of those trips.
