State law lets the probate judge order law enforcement officers to make the trip, and the report cannot say what that costs local deputies.

982.title: OI-086 · Not published, as far as this review found
982.text: Counts of psychiatrists, child psychiatrists, psychologists, counselors and social workers practicing in each county were not found, and neither was a list of local practices using the state's child psychiatry consultation service. The provider ratios in print use different definitions, and the Kids Count profiles give no source for theirs. The report measures the shortage with ratios and anecdotes and cannot count clinicians by profession.

983.title: OI-087 · Not published, as far as this review found
983.text: How many graduates the local training programs produce, where they go to work and whether they stay were not found, and several programs (Oakwood University, Athens State, Calhoun Community College, WellStone's internships and osteopathic school rotations) were not reached. The pipeline is new and its output is unknown.

984.title: OI-088 · Not published, as far as this review found
984.text: A peer support, chaplaincy or wellness program for first responders at the Huntsville police and fire departments or the ambulance service, or a clinician well-being program at the hospitals or WellStone, was not found described in a public source. The report can say only that a resident or a job applicant cannot find out.

985.title: OI-089 · Not published, as far as this review found
985.text: How much care is delivered by telehealth locally (WellStone visits, hospital tele-psychiatry, school tele-therapy) and a figure for broadband coverage in either county were not found. The one account dates from the school closures of spring 2020. The state's clinic manual expects telehealth to support access, and Cullman County is three-quarters rural.

986.title: OI-090 · Not published, as far as this review found
986.text: The number of WellStone clients who lack a payer for medication, the size of the shortfall, and any patient-assistance program specific to psychiatric medicines in either county were not found. Medication for uninsured adults is one of WellStone's three named unmet needs.

987.title: OI-091 · Not published, as far as this review found
987.text: Drug take-back sites in Cullman County and the locations of medication drop boxes in Madison County were not found. It is a small part of the report's account of medicines and overdose prevention.

988.title: OI-092 · Not published, as far as this review found
988.text: Service use, crisis admissions, commitments and jail mental health caseloads by race, language or income were not found for either county. Madison County is a quarter Black, and the report cannot say whether the system reaches residents evenly.

989.title: OI-093 · Not published, as far as this review found
989.text: How WellStone provides interpretation and translation, any north Alabama office of the statewide Hispanic services nonprofit, and any account of Hispanic residents' use of or barriers to mental health care were not found. Hispanic residents are 7.6% of Madison County and 5.8% of Cullman County and almost absent from the service record.

990.title: OI-094 · Not published, as far as this review found
990.text: A Huntsville office or named regional staff of the Department's Office of Deaf Services was not found. The report can say only that deaf residents are served through regional clinicians.

991.title: OI-095 · Not published, as far as this review found
991.text: An advocacy or peer organization based in Cullman County was not found: no NAMI or Mental Health America affiliate, peer-run recovery center, drop-in center, mental health coalition or LGBTQ+ organization appears in the lists read. The report describes Cullman as having services and no organized voice; a local group that is on no state or national list would change that.

992.title: OI-096 · Not published, as far as this review found
992.text: A credible source connecting Cullman's history as a "sundown town" with present-day access to or trust in mental health care was not found; no search was spent on it. It bears on whether Black residents of the region use services in Cullman County.

993.title: OI-097 · Not published, as far as this review found
993.text: Staffing, session limits and use of the counseling centers at the University of Alabama in Huntsville, Alabama A&M, Oakwood University and Wallace State were not found. Students are one of the groups the report says have services built for them.

994.title: OI-098 · Not published, as far as this review found
994.text: A county-level figure for youth suicide or self-harm, or county results from a school survey of students' mental health, was not found for Madison or Cullman. The report can give teen death rates that do not separate suicide, and nothing on what students themselves report.

995.title: OI-099 · Not published, as far as this review found
995.text: Counselor-to-student ratios, the number of WellStone school-based therapists and the students they serve by district, and the Department's list of which school systems partner with which mental health center were not found; the list's link returned an error on 4 October 2026. The districts receiving state funding for mental health coordinators were not named in the memo read. School-based care is split among providers, and no single count of it was found.

996.title: OI-100 · Not published, as far as this review found
996.text: Therapeutic foster care places or providers by county, and any description of how the multi-needs child process works in Madison or Cullman, were not found. They are the parts of a children's system of care the report could not describe locally.

997.title: OI-101 · Not published, as far as this review found
997.text: Mental health screening and services for young people held at Madison County's detention center, where Cullman County youth are held when they need more than short-term detention, counts for the juvenile specialty courts, and the dollar amount of Madison County's youth services diversion grant were not found. The report can list juvenile programs and cannot say what mental health care detained youth receive.

998.title: OI-102 · Not published, as far as this review found
998.text: Which infant and early childhood mental health consultants serve either county, county figures for the home-visiting programs, and a perinatal or postpartum mental health program at Huntsville Hospital for Women & Children were not found. The earliest years are covered by programs whose reach is counted and whose mental health content is not.

999.title: OI-103 · Not published, as far as this review found
999.text: The basis of WellStone's statement that its jail diversion program saves about $300,000 of taxpayer money a year was not found: no method, year or count of people accompanies it. It is the only savings figure attached to diversion in the region.

1000.title: OI-104 · Not published, as far as this review found
1000.text: A current count of crisis-trained Huntsville Police officers and the schedule of the department's crisis intervention community meetings were not found. The latest figures are 94 certified officers and 190 trained in the shorter course, from a report of about 2022. Police crisis training is the best documented form of public education in the region and its current scale is unknown.

1001.title: OI-105 · Not published, as far as this review found
1001.text: Crisis-trained officers, mental health officers or co-responders at the Madison Police Department, the Cullman Police Department and the Cullman County Sheriff's Office were not found on any page read, and the Madison County Sheriff's pages mention no crisis intervention team. Outside Huntsville the report cannot say who responds to a person in crisis; absence from a website is not proof that no officers are trained.

1002.title: OI-106 · Not published, as far as this review found
1002.text: Start years, capacity, participants and graduates were not found for Madison County's Adult Mental Health Court, drug court and veterans court, for the Huntsville municipal mental health court, or for Cullman County's drug, veterans and mental health courts, and no annual report was found for any of them. The courts are known by their launch dates or their judges and not by what they have done.

1003.title: OI-107 · Not published, as far as this review found
1003.text: Waiting times for competency evaluation or restoration for defendants from Madison or Cullman County were not found; press reports give state totals only. Neither county has jail-based restoration, so its defendants wait in the state queue.

1004.title: OI-108 · Not published, as far as this review found
1004.text: An official description of a Huntsville Municipal Court docket for people without housing was not found; the only public description is a citizen's petition, and the city's account is a judge's general statement. The report describes the municipal court's mental health docket and cannot confirm a separate docket for unsheltered people.

1005.title: OI-109 · Not published, as far as this review found
1005.text: How either jail plans discharges and restarts Medicaid or other benefits on release, and counts of people returning to Madison County from state prison, were not found; no Madison County reentry organization with a program described in public was found. Reentry is the intercept the report can describe least in Madison County.

1006.title: OI-110 · Not published, as far as this review found
1006.text: How many of the people supervised by Madison County's Office of Alternative Sentencing and Release or by Cullman County's community corrections program have a mental illness, and what treatment conditions they carry, were not found. Supervision is where a court-ordered treatment condition is enforced.

1007.title: OI-111 · Not published, as far as this review found
1007.text: A family justice center for Huntsville or Madison County was not found in the sources read. It would be part of the trauma side of the justice interface.

1008.title: OI-112 · Not published, as far as this review found
1008.text: Later lawsuits, settlements or consent decrees over deaths or mental health care in either county's jail were not found in the sources read, and the search was thin. One report of a settled suit over an alleged jail beating could not be read, and the only federal opinion found about Cullman's jail concerned a broken hand (Northern District of Alabama, 5:16-cv-01040, dismissed in 2017). The report describes three 2014 suits and cannot say whether anything since binds local practice.

1009.title: OI-113 · Not published, as far as this review found
1009.text: A 2026 point-in-time count and housing inventory for the Huntsville continuum was not found on the federal housing department's site or the local coalition's on 4 October 2026; the only 2026 figure is a press report of "around 575". It would show whether homelessness kept rising after the 718 counted in 2025.

1010.title: OI-114 · Not published, as far as this review found
1010.text: A homelessness count for Madison County alone, or a count of unaccompanied youth for the county, was not found; the federal and coalition reports cover the three-county continuum. Almost everything the report says about homelessness describes three counties together.

1011.title: OI-115 · Not published, as far as this review found
1011.text: The dates and locations of Huntsville's encampment closures and the text of any camping ordinance were not found. An advocacy source says the city gave notice of a fourth closure in four years in October 2024. City policy toward encampments shapes where unsheltered people with mental illness can be found and served.

1012.title: OI-116 · Not published, as far as this review found
1012.text: The status of the Huntsville Housing Authority's voucher waiting list, its wait time and its special-purpose vouchers, and the number of vouchers the Cullman Housing Authority administers, were not found. Vouchers are the main route out of homelessness, and the report can give only a total for Huntsville and a closed list for Cullman.

1013.title: OI-117 · Not published, as far as this review found
1013.text: Medical respite or recuperative care for homeless people leaving hospital in Madison County was not found on the pages read; no dedicated search was made. People discharged from hospital to the street are among those the crisis system sees again.

1014.title: OI-118 · Not published, as far as this review found
1014.text: A county-level estimate of the Medicaid coverage gap for Madison or Cullman was not found. In a state that has not expanded Medicaid, it is the number of adults the clinic payment cannot reach.

1015.title: OI-119 · Not published, as far as this review found
1015.text: The number of TRICARE beneficiaries, VA-enrolled veterans and federal employees in Madison County, and which services each of the VA's three Huntsville sites offers, were not found. An undated press report gives 45,000 beneficiaries and retirees. Madison County has 34,400 veterans and a large military workforce whose care leans on the civilian system at its edges.

1016.title: OI-120 · Not published, as far as this review found
1016.text: Reported complaints about insurers' networks or mental health parity in the Huntsville or Cullman area were not located; no dedicated search was made. One insurer holds 82% of the Huntsville commercial market.

1017.title: OI-121 · Not published, as far as this review found
1017.text: An estimate of what the Medicaid provisions of the 2025 federal reconciliation law mean for WellStone or local hospitals was not found. It would bear on the payer picture the report describes.

1018.title: OI-122 · Not published, as far as this review found
1018.text: Revenue, cost or volume for psychiatric services at Huntsville Hospital, Crestwood or Cullman Regional was not found, and no figure later than a December 2025 forecast was found for the rise in the hospital system's uncompensated care in 2026. The system's finances bear on mental health mainly through what it absorbs.

1019.title: OI-123 · Not published, as far as this review found
1019.text: Descriptions of the behavioral health or employee-assistance benefits of the area's largest employers were not found; no search was spent on it. More than half of Madison County residents are covered through an employer.

1020.title: OI-124 · Not published, as far as this review found
1020.text: Distances or travel times from the ring counties to the Huntsville crisis center, who transports people there and under what agreement, and any statement by a ring center about using or referring to it were not found. For Cullman, WellStone has said its local crisis teams can take people to Huntsville. It would show whether the fifteen-county catchment works in practice or mostly on paper.

1021.title: OI-125 · Not published, as far as this review found
1021.text: Strategic plans for FY2026–27 from CED Mental Health Center and Northwest Alabama Mental Health Center were not found on the Department's index, which still links their earlier plans; CED's residential page was not read. The report describes these two centers from plans a year older than WellStone's.

1022.title: OI-126 · Not published, as far as this review found
1022.text: No source read explains why the ring centers' own counts of people served run higher than the Department's (for example 10,317 in Northwest's plan for 2023 against 3,306 in the Department's FY2025 report). It decides which count fairly describes each center's size.

1023.title: OI-127 · Not published, as far as this review found
1023.text: Any monitoring visit, report or case by the state's protection and advocacy agency concerning a facility in Madison or Cullman County was not found on its public pages. It is the independent body with authority to monitor facilities.

1024.title: OI-128 · Needs a human eye
1024.text: The map position of WellStone's Huntsville campus (4020 and 4040 Memorial Parkway SW) is approximate. Neither geocoder holds the address, and the federal treatment locator gives two different points for it, about 1.7 km apart. The crisis center, the pediatric unit and the Huntsville clinic are the three most important markers on the regional map, and all three use this one point.

1025.title: OI-129 · Needs a human eye
1025.text: Two service locations have no marker on the map: the Huntsville Vet Center (415 Church Street matches both a northwest and a southwest address) and CED Mental Health Center's Cherokee County office in Centre (no geocoder match). Both are named in the report and would otherwise be missing from the map without explanation.

1277.title: Domain 1. Governance, Policy and Legal Foundations
1277.text: Governance. The statewide report describes who decides in Montgomery: the Department, the Legislature, the Governor and the federal courts. This section asks who decides locally. In Madison and Cullman counties that means one nonprofit board, five local governments, two probate courts and a handful of planning documents, and the question in each case is whom the body answers to and what it has put in writing.

1278.title: Domain 2. Financing and Resource Allocation
1278.text: Financing. The statewide report follows the money from the Legislature to the Department. This section follows it the rest of the way: what reaches the two counties, from whom, and how much of that a resident could find out. The answer to the last question shapes the whole section. Capital spending is well documented because ribbon-cuttings are news. Operating money is visible only in fragments, and no Form 990 data for the organization at the center of the system appear in the public database for any year after FY2021 [66].

1279.title: Domain 3. The Service-Delivery Continuum
1279.text: Service continuum. This section follows the continuum the statewide report uses, from prevention through outpatient care, crisis response, inpatient treatment and recovery supports, and asks at each step what exists in Madison and Cullman counties and how much use it gets. The short version is that the front of the system changed a great deal between 2020 and 2025 and the back of it did not.

1280.title: Domain 4. Workforce Development and Well-being
1280.text: Workforce. The statewide report measures Alabama's shortage with federal designations and national ratios. Those tools work poorly at county scale, as this section shows, so it leans on a plainer kind of evidence: what local providers have said they cannot staff. It then looks at where the region's future clinicians are being trained.

1281.title: Domain 5. Medicines, Technology and Infrastructure
1281.text: Infrastructure. This section covers the physical and technical base of the local system: the buildings, the record systems, the medicines, and the means of getting a person from where they are to where the care is. The last of these turns out to be the weakest.

1282.title: Domain 6. Information, Data and Quality Improvement
1282.text: Data. Every other section of this report ends on some version of the same sentence: the number is not published. This section gathers those gaps in one place. It sets out what is measured about mental health in the two counties and by whom, what a planner would want that is missing, and what quality reporting the new clinic model will require.

1283.title: Domain 7. Equity, Inclusion and Cultural Responsiveness
1283.text: Equity. Part I set out who lives in the two counties. This section asks whether the system reaches them evenly: what the data show about differences between and within the counties, which groups have services built for them, and which do not appear in the record at all. The honest summary is that the region can describe its inequities by place and hardly at all by race, language or income, because the data needed for the second kind of description have not been published locally.

1284.title: Domain 8. Community Engagement, Education and Advocacy
1284.text: Engagement. This section describes who speaks for mental health in the two counties, how the public is educated about it, what local advocacy has won, and whether people who have lived with mental illness or addiction have a formal voice in how services are run. Little Orange Fish, the publisher of this report, is the backbone organization of one of the bodies described here, the North Alabama Mental Health Coalition; the coalition is described only from public web pages, its own and its founding organization's, and none of its meeting records were used as sources.

1285.title: Section 9. Children, Youth and Families: A System of Care
1285.text: Children. A child's mental health care is delivered through more doors than an adult's: the school, the pediatrician, the child welfare agency, the juvenile court. The statewide report reads Alabama against the principles of a system of care, in which those doors open onto the same hallway. This section describes each door in Madison and Cullman counties and what is known about how many children pass through it.

1286.title: Section 10. The Justice Interface
1286.text: Justice. The statewide report organizes the meeting points between mental illness and the justice system by the Sequential Intercept Model: community and crisis services, law enforcement, initial detention and court, jails and courts, reentry, and community supervision. This section walks the same six intercepts in Madison and Cullman counties. It deals with deaths and lawsuits as well as programs. People who died or were charged are not named; cases are given by their captions, and what was alleged is kept apart from what a court found.

1287.title: Section 11. Housing, Social Determinants and Community Supports
1287.text: Housing. The statewide report reads Alabama against the five domains of social determinants used in Healthy People 2030: neighborhood and built environment, economic stability, health care access, education access, and social and community context. This section does the same for the two counties. It gives most of its length to housing, because housing is a need WellStone's own plan names twice and the one for which the public record is richest.

1288.title: Section 12. Payers, Coverage and the CCBHC Transition
1288.text: Payers. Who pays shapes who is served. This section sets out how residents of the two counties are covered, how Medicaid pays for mental health care here, what the move to the Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic model has changed, and where the commercial and hospital markets stand. The statewide report explains the rules; this section applies them.

1289.title: Section 13. The Ring: Thirteen Counties, Four Centers
1289.text: The ring. This section has no counterpart in the statewide report. It describes, in outline only, the thirteen counties beyond Madison and Cullman whose crises the state routes to Huntsville, and the four community mental health centers that serve them for everything else. It does not examine their courts, schools, hospitals or housing. Its purpose is to show what the crisis center's wider catchment looks like and how much of that catchment's use of the center is known.
